## Lesson 1.9 — What a Memory Scan Really Finds
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/1/09/
Category: Game Hacking Foundations
Estimated reading time: 18 minutes
Summary: Find, test, and change one gold value in Wesnoth, and see what each scan does and does not prove.

An address names a location, while a type tells a program what its bytes
mean. We will use a memory scanner on Wesnoth: observe a gold value,
search for matching bytes, make one in-game change, and filter the results.

The goal is not merely to reach a final address. The goal is to understand why
each scan removes some candidates and why one test still does not prove that a
candidate is the main game-play value.

## Prepare the target

Use the course build of Wesnoth 1.14.9 in the Windows VM. Start a local match and
pause before recruiting a unit.

<Frame caption="The paused Wesnoth match. The gold number on screen is what the scan will look for.">

![A Wesnoth match showing the gold value](/assets/images/1/5/wesnoth1.png)

</Frame>

Suppose the screen shows 100 gold and the unit you plan to recruit costs 15.
After recruiting, the visible value should become 100 − 15 = 85.

## Attach Cheat Engine to the game process

Open Cheat Engine, choose the process button, and select the running Wesnoth
process.

<Frame caption="Cheat Engine's process list, with the running Wesnoth chosen.">

![Choosing the Wesnoth process](/assets/images/1/5/wesnoth2.png)

</Frame>

Attaching tells Cheat Engine which process address space to read. It does not
yet tell the scanner where gold is or how it is stored.

## Perform the first value scan

<Badge text="Windows VM" variant="note" />

Enter the visible gold amount. Use:

- **Value Type:** <HoverCard kind="explanation" body="Four bytes hold one 32-bit whole number, the same size as Rust’s `i32` or `u32`. The scanner must read all four bytes at an address to see the number the screen shows.">4 Bytes</HoverCard>;
- **Scan Type:** <HoverCard kind="alternative" body="If a game never shows the number, scan for an unknown initial value instead. After each change in the game, keep the addresses that changed, increased, decreased, or stayed the same.">Exact Value</HoverCard>;
- **Value:** the current gold amount.

Start the first scan.

<Frame caption="Straight after the first scan, many addresses hold the same number.">

![The first scan for gold](/assets/images/1/5/wesnoth3.png)

</Frame>

The scan will probably find many addresses. That is expected. The number 100 can
appear in timers, object fields, capacities, interface data, and unrelated
allocations.

At this point, each result proves only this:

> These four bytes were readable as the integer 100 when the scanner checked
> them.

It does not prove that the address controls gold.

## Change the game once

Return to Wesnoth and perform the planned action. Recruit the unit and read the
new gold value off the screen.

<Frame caption="After recruiting, the new gold amount is the next value to search for.">

![Gold after recruiting a unit](/assets/images/1/5/wesnoth4.png)

</Frame>

If the value changed from 100 to 85, return to Cheat Engine, enter 85, and choose
**Next Scan**.

The scanner does not search the whole process from the beginning. It checks the
previous candidate addresses and <HoverCard kind="example" body="Say the first scan found three addresses holding 100: A, B, and C. After the purchase only B and C hold 85, so A is dropped, and the next scan checks just B and C.">keeps only those that now contain 85</HoverCard>. In set
notation:

```text
new_candidates = old_candidates ∩ addresses_currently_equal_to_85
```

You do not need the symbol memorized. It means “keep items that are in both
groups.”

## Repeat with a different change

Make another controlled change with a different result. For example, recruit a
unit with another cost or end a turn if the scenario changes gold in a known
way. Enter the new gold value and perform another **Next Scan**.

<Frame caption="After Next Scan the candidate list is much shorter.">

![A narrowed list of candidate addresses](/assets/images/1/5/wesnoth6.png)

</Frame>

Using different values is important. If you repeat only 100 → 85 → 100, an
unrelated value that happens to follow the same pattern can remain in the list.

Continue until you have a small number of candidates. Do not assume the first
remaining address is correct.

## Test one candidate reversibly

Add one candidate to the address list. Before changing it:

<Steps>

1. copy its current value so you can put it back;
2. confirm the game still shows the expected gold;
3. choose a small replacement value;
4. write the replacement once;
5. observe the screen and one real purchase;
6. <HoverCard kind="recommendation" body="Do this before any other test, even if the change looked harmless. A leftover value can make the next test start from a different state, and then two results can no longer be compared.">restore the original value</HoverCard>.

</Steps>

<Frame caption="Wesnoth after one candidate was edited: the display shows the new value.">

![The edited gold value in Wesnoth](/assets/images/1/5/wesnoth9.png)

</Frame>

Different results support different explanations:

| What happens | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| the number and purchase rules change | strong candidate for game-play state |
| only the text changes | likely a display copy |
| the value changes back on the next update | another system recomputes or owns it |
| nothing visible changes | unrelated value or a copy used elsewhere |
| nearby behavior breaks | wrong address, type, or field width may have been changed |

A single run can mislead, because an unrelated value might change at the same
moment by coincidence. Getting the same result again from the same starting
state makes that explanation less likely.

## Why several copies may all be related

The game can legitimately keep more than one gold-related value:

- the current simulation value;
- a previous value used by an animation;
- text prepared for the interface;
- a value in a replay, event, or network message;
- a temporary calculation.

That is why value scanning is usually the start of reverse engineering. A write
breakpoint later shows which instruction changes the strongest candidate. The
surrounding instructions can reveal the object base and other fields.

## Treat the address as temporary

The address you found belongs to this run of the game. After a restart, gold
may live somewhere else, because the process layout and the heap can change
between runs. A later lesson on [building and loading a program](/pages/1/10/)
explains why some distances stay fixed within one build even when absolute
addresses move. First, a debugger lets us follow the candidate value to the
instruction that changes it.

## What the scan established

The first scan returned readable candidates that matched while it ran;
it did not identify “the gold address.” Each controlled game change
filtered that candidate set. Changing one survivor and then making a
real purchase showed whether it affected gameplay, only the display,
or neither. Restoring the original value leaves the game in a known
state for another run.

The candidate address tells us where to look, but not why the value changes.
When a purchase subtracts gold, which instruction performs the subtraction,
and what decides whether the player can afford it? [What a Debugger Can
Reveal](/pages/2/01/) begins Chapter 2 with that question. We will pause the
program at the change, then learn how source code becomes the instructions
the debugger shows.

---
## Lesson 2.1 — What a Debugger Can Reveal
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/2/01/
Category: Instructions, Debuggers, and Addresses
Estimated reading time: 9 minutes
Summary: Learn what a debugger actually does and why pausing one instruction can answer a big question.

The first scan showed where gold might be stored. This chapter follows that
lead into instructions. A debugger first makes the running program visible;
the build process explains why that view differs from source code; assembly
then gives us the vocabulary to trace a rule. From there we recover a path
to state after addresses move and examine what a temporary control-flow
detour must preserve. The debugger lessons can also be revisited by tool
action: read assembly, set a breakpoint, follow a caller, or check an address
path.

## A debugger can pause and inspect a running program

A memory scanner answers, “Where might this value live?” A debugger answers, “Which instruction just touched it?” In the Lesson 1.9 experiment, a purchase narrowed many candidate addresses to one changing gold value. Suppose it fell from 100 to 75 when you recruited a unit. Which instruction made that subtraction?

The address gives us a route into the running program. A **write
breakpoint** asks the debugger to pause when an instruction stores to
those four bytes. At the pause, we can compare the address and the amount
being subtracted with the gold address and unit price we already know.
One match is a lead; another purchase can test it. Lesson 2.5 performs
the experiment in x64dbg.

When a debugger pauses a process, you can inspect:

- the next instruction the CPU will run;
- register values;
- the call stack;
- nearby memory;
- the condition flags used by branches.

This is not a special “hacking mode.” Developers use the same ideas to find bugs in their own programs.

## Start from a value you can see

Scrolling through thousands of instructions hoping one looks important rarely
works. The visible gold value gives you a way in:

> Which instruction changes my gold when I recruit a unit?

Then:

1. Find the gold address with a memory scanner.
2. Set a breakpoint on writes to that address.
3. Perform exactly one gold-changing action, so the pause can be tied to that
   action.
4. Inspect the instruction that triggered the pause.

You used a visible value as a trail back to the code. The pause is evidence of one execution, not a guarantee that the same instruction serves only recruitment. A later test can distinguish those possibilities.

Different practice targets may use 32-bit or 64-bit code, different calling
conventions, and different build settings. The technique carries over from a
worked example; its addresses and register choices do not.

## Registers hold values the CPU is using now

Lesson 1.2 introduced registers as the CPU's small working places.
The 32-bit Wesnoth build uses x86 registers named `eax`, `ebx`,
`ecx`, and `edx`. In a 64-bit x86 program, their wider relatives
are `rax`, `rbx`, `rcx`, and `rdx`. The diagram shows how one
64-bit register overlaps its smaller views: `eax` names the low 32
bits of `rax`, `ax` its low 16, and `al` its low 8. In the
Wesnoth lab, you will inspect `eax`; the wider view helps when you
meet a 64-bit target later.

<MemoryStrip
  cells="=11|=22|=33|=44|=55|=66|=77|=88"
  groups="0-7:`rax`: all 64 bits, 0x1122334455667788"
  groups2="4-7:`eax`: the low 32 bits, 0x55667788"
  groups3="6-7:`ax`: the low 16, 0x7788"
  groups4="7-7:`al`: 0x88"
  caption="One register, written most significant byte first, the way a debugger shows it. The shorter names are views of its low end, not separate registers. Writing `eax` also clears the upper half of `rax`; writing `ax` or `al` leaves the rest alone."
/>

Each name selects a width of the same working value. When tracing
Wesnoth, use the 32-bit name and ask what instruction last wrote it.

## Memory, registers, and the stack answer different questions

Registers are the values this thread needs immediately. Memory holds far more
data but is slower to access. The stack is one memory area used to organize
function calls.

Suppose the debugger stops here:

```nasm
sub dword ptr [ebx+30h], eax
```

- `eax` contains one immediate input, perhaps a price;
- `ebx` contains a base address, perhaps the start of a player-side record;
- `30h` is an offset, a distance from that base;
- `[ebx+30h]` means “access memory at the calculated address”;
- `dword ptr` says the memory operation is four bytes wide.

<MemoryStrip
  cells="ebx →=side object starts|=· · ·|+30h=gold"
  marks="2"
  groups="0-1:offset `30h`: 48 bytes along"
  caption="`[ebx+30h]` names the four bytes 48 bytes past the address in `ebx`. The instruction subtracts `eax` from them and writes the result back."
/>

The register names alone do not prove those meanings. If `ebx` held
`0x5000`, for example, `ebx+30h` would name `0x5030` because
`30h` is 48 in decimal. Compare the calculated
address with the gold address, compare `eax` with the known unit price, and
repeat the action. If the address equals the gold address and `eax` equals the
price every time, this instruction is the one that spends gold.

The **call stack** answers another question: “Which chain of function calls
brought this thread here?” A low-level update function may be called by a
recruit action, an AI simulation, and a save loader. The caller tells you which
of those uses triggered this pause.

## What actually happens when a debugger attaches

The first trace needs only a verified pause and the values visible there.
To understand how those values reach the debugger, follow the exchange
between the game, Windows, and the debugger.

A debugger is a separate process. It requests the required process and thread
access rights from Windows, and Windows begins sending it **debug events**. An
event can mean:

- a process or thread started;
- a DLL was loaded;
- an exception happened;
- a breakpoint was reached;
- the process exited.

When an event stops a thread, the debugger can ask Windows for that thread’s
**context**. A context is a snapshot of its registers, including the
instruction pointer that says where the CPU will continue. The debugger can
also copy memory from the process and show the copied bytes in friendlier
forms.

The target and debugger do not merge into one program. Windows remains the
gatekeeper between them:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Game as Target game
    participant Win as Windows
    participant Dbg as Debugger
    Game->>Win: a thread reaches a breakpoint
    Note over Game: paused
    Win->>Dbg: debug event: which thread, what happened
    Dbg->>Win: read that thread's context and some memory
    Win-->>Dbg: registers and copied bytes
    Note over Dbg: you inspect and decide
    Dbg->>Win: continue
    Win->>Game: resume
```

Many debuggers pause the rest of the process while you inspect one event. That
prevents other game threads from changing registers and memory while you read
them, but it also means audio, rendering, and network work temporarily stop.

## Disassembly versus debugging

**Disassembly** translates machine-code bytes into assembly instructions. It is a snapshot of what the bytes *could* mean.

**Debugging** watches those instructions run. It lets you see what the registers and memory contain at that exact moment.

Reading code without running it is called **static analysis**. Watching it run
is **dynamic analysis**. They answer different questions:

| View | What it can establish |
|---|---|
| Disassembly | possible instructions, branch targets, referenced constants, and call relationships |
| Live debugging | the path actually taken, concrete register values, live addresses, and the thread that executed it |

Neither view replaces the other. The disassembly shows paths that one test run
did not take. The live debugger shows which path a real game event actually
took, and with which values.

A **decompiler** goes one step further and guesses at higher-level expressions,
loops, and function arguments. Those guesses can be useful, but the machine
code is the final record of what the CPU executes. A friendly decompiler name
such as `player_health` is only a guess until the program's behavior matches
it.

## What a decompiler can recover—and what it cannot

Compilation keeps the effects a computer must perform, but it can discard many
choices that only helped the original programmer. Local names, comments, source
file boundaries, and the exact spelling of a loop may be gone. Optimizations can
inline a function, reuse one register for unrelated values, remove a variable, or
turn a branch into arithmetic.

A decompiler therefore works upward through several reconstructions:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["instruction bytes"] -->|"decode"| B["assembly instructions"]
    B -->|"connect the jumps"| C["basic blocks and<br/>a control-flow graph"]
    C -->|"trace values"| D["expressions, arguments,<br/>and possible types"]
    D -->|"choose readable syntax"| E["pseudocode"]
```

Every upward step is useful, but it adds interpretation. Two different source
programs can compile to the same machine behavior, so exact original source is
often unknowable. What you can recover is a description that matches what the
machine code does, not a perfect transcript of the original source.

Pseudocode is a draft, and most decompilers let you rename values and change
types in it:

- rename a value once its use is clear from the code and from live values;
- change a type when instruction width, signedness, API contracts, and live
  values agree;
- check the control-flow graph — the map of which instruction can run after
  which, built by following every jump — when an `if` or loop looks strange;
- return to assembly when one incorrect type makes later expressions look
  impossible.

This prevents a common failure chain: one guessed pointer becomes a guessed
structure, which gives every field a confident-looking but incorrect name.

## Recover source-level meaning from machine state

At source level, the compiler chooses registers for you. Recall the
guarded purchase in Lesson 1.4: if the player has at least 25 gold,
subtract 25; otherwise, leave gold unchanged. The compiler may express
that decision as a comparison, branch, and subtraction. In a debugger,
you see those pieces and the current register values instead of the
original variable names. Check both an affordable and an unaffordable
attempt: if the subtraction runs only in the first case, you have
evidence for the proposed rule. Before learning the assembly vocabulary,
we need to explain why the programmer's named rule becomes this different
machine-level view.

## A safe first session

Use the VM snapshot and offline target from section one. Attach x64dbg, pause the game, look at the CPU view, then resume without changing anything.

Success for this lesson is simple: you can pause and resume the process, and
you know which panels show instructions, registers, memory, and the stack.
[How Source Becomes a Running Process](/pages/1/10/) explains how those
instructions and addresses were produced. The following assembly lesson
teaches how to read them, and the later [gold-write lab](/pages/2/04/)
returns to the purchase question in x64dbg.

## Lesson 2.2 — How Source Becomes a Running Process
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/1/10/
Category: Instructions, Debuggers, and Addresses
Estimated reading time: 28 minutes
Summary: Compare native compilation, bytecode interpretation, REPLs, and type checking; then follow a native program through linking and loading.

The debugger shows instructions and addresses, while the programmer wrote
functions, fields, and variable names. Why are those two views different?
And why can an address found by a memory scan move after a restart even
though the game still applies the same rule?

These differences come from the stages that turn source into a running
process. First, distinguish several ways a language implementation can
run code. Then we can follow the native executable used in the Windows
memory labs and see which facts survive a restart, which require the
exact build, and which must be rediscovered after an update.

## Source code can take different routes to execution

**Source code** is the text a programmer edits. A CPU eventually executes
machine instructions, but the source does not always become a standalone
machine-code file first. Two routes used in this book are:

**Rust application:** source becomes native code before the program runs.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Rust["Rust source"] --> Native["compile to native code"]
    Native --> Exe["EXE on disk"]
    Exe --> CPU["CPU runs the program"]
```

**Lua script:** source becomes instructions for the Lua virtual machine
when a game loads the script.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Lua["Lua source"] --> VMCode["compile to VM bytecode"]
    VMCode --> VM["Lua VM interprets bytecode"]
    VM --> CPU["CPU runs the Lua VM"]
```

**Compilation** translates code from one representation to another. The
Rust route above compiles ahead of time to native instructions for a
particular target. A **virtual machine** is a program that understands its
own instruction set. Its **bytecode** is instructions for that virtual
machine, not the x86 instructions a debugger shows for the CPU. Lua also
compiles when it loads a source chunk; its virtual machine then
**interprets** the resulting bytecode by carrying out those instructions.
This is why “compiled” and “interpreted” are not mutually exclusive labels.
The [Lua reference manual](https://www.lua.org/manual/5.4/manual.html#3.3.2)
describes this load-and-execute sequence. [Lesson 10.1](/pages/12/01/)
shows what changes when a game embeds a Lua interpreter.

A **REPL** is a way to interact with a language tool: **read** a line,
**evaluate** it, **print** the answer, then **loop** for another line.
For instance, an interactive Lua session can evaluate `2 + 3` and show
`5` immediately. A file can contain the same calculation and be run later.
REPL describes the interaction, not whether the tool uses bytecode,
native compilation, or dynamic typing. The [Lua interpreter
manual](https://www.lua.org/manual/5.4/lua.html) describes both interactive
and file-based use.

## Type checking answers a different question

The route to execution is separate from **when a type mismatch is
detected**. The same job, giving one variable a number and then text, goes
differently in each language:

<CodeGroup sync="language">
<Tab label="Rust: statically typed">

Rust is **statically typed**: every value has a type known to the compiler,
often inferred without an explicit annotation. This fragment fails to compile,
because one variable cannot hold both a `u32` number and a string:

```rust
let mut score: u32 = 7;
score = "seven"; // rejected by the compiler
```

</Tab>
<Tab label="Lua: dynamically typed">

Lua is **dynamically typed**: values have types, and a variable can refer to
a number at one moment and text at another. This code can make both
assignments, but its final arithmetic operation fails when run:

```lua
score = 7
score = "seven"
print(score + 1) -- error: text cannot be used as this number
```

</Tab>
</CodeGroup>

The difference is about where that particular mistake is caught. Rust
can still have run-time errors, and Lua catches some mistakes, such as
malformed syntax, while loading code. Neither typing style alone tells
you whether code is compiled to native instructions, compiled to
bytecode, or entered through a REPL. The [Rust data-types
chapter](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch03-02-data-types.html) and the
[Lua reference manual](https://www.lua.org/manual/5.4/manual.html#2.1)
give the language-specific rules.

The rest of this lesson follows the **native executable** route used for
Rust tools and the Windows game builds in the early memory labs. Lua's
virtual-machine route returns when we study scripting.

## Four stages, each deciding something different

A Windows **EXE** is an executable file for a program. A **DLL** (dynamic-link
library) is compiled code that a running program can load and call. Once
loaded, either one is a **module** with a starting address and a range of
code and data in the process.

<Scene name="source-to-process" />

Each stage keeps what the next stage needs. A release build may omit
information that helped the programmer but is unnecessary for execution.
Debug information can preserve some names separately; we will distinguish
that case below.

## The compiler decides layout, and stops needing your names

The compiler translates source into object code, often stored in `.obj`
files by the Microsoft toolchain used for these Windows C++ examples. Two
of its decisions matter throughout this book.

First, it chooses a compiled layout according to the language's rules.
For an example player structure, it may leave unused bytes between fields
<HoverCard kind="example" body="In a C or C++ structure, a one-byte field followed by a four-byte field normally puts the second at offset 4, so the 3 bytes between them are padding: 1 + 3 = 4.">so each field starts at an address suited to its type</HoverCard>. Those gaps are
**padding**, explored in the later [object-layout lesson](/pages/3/03/).
If health begins 48 bytes into the object, an instruction can identify it
by that distance rather than its name. A debugger may write this as
`[ecx+0x30]`: read at the address held in the `ecx` register, plus hexadecimal
`0x30`, which is decimal 48. The assembly lesson explains this notation in
detail; here it shows why a compiled field can survive without the word
`health`.

Second, the machine instruction no longer needs the word `health`. The
name helped the programmer refer to the field; the instruction uses its
distance from the object base. A normal release executable often omits
local and field names, though debug information can preserve them. A
missing name is not evidence that it was encrypted or hidden.

Function names survive slightly longer, because the linker still has work to do
with them.

## The linker resolves names, then it does not need them either

Your game is many object files plus libraries, and one file's call to a function
defined in another may still be an unresolved reference. The **linker** matches
references to definitions it has, lays the sections out into the final image,
and records the references that a loader must finish later. A call to an
internal game function can be resolved here; a call into a DLL still needs the
DLL's address at run time.

After that, many internal names have served their purpose. Debug
information can be kept — the Microsoft toolchain often puts it in a
separate `.pdb` file — but the EXE does not need it to run. Imports and
exports can still carry names in the executable; the next section shows
why an imported function name may remain.

This explains why a debugger may show an imported Windows function's name
but only a numeric address for an internal game function. A binary without
debug symbols is not necessarily obfuscated; it may simply lack source
names that execution does not require.

## Two things the linker deliberately leaves unfinished

Not everything can be decided at build time, and the two exceptions are exactly
the ones later chapters spend time on.

**Where the module will be.** The linker does not know which address Windows
will choose, so it records a preferred base and includes a table of every
location that would need adjusting if a different base is used. An offset
measures a distance from the beginning of that module. The later
[address-movement lesson](/pages/2/08/) uses the distinction: for the same
build, that distance can stay fixed while the loader chooses a different
starting address.

**Where the DLL functions will be.** The linker knows the game calls
`MessageBoxW` in `user32.dll`, but not the address, which will not exist until
the DLL is mapped. So it writes down the requirement — which DLL, which
function — and leaves a table of slots for the loader to fill with real
addresses. That table is the <HoverCard kind="reference" href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/debug/pe-format" body="Microsoft's PE format specification describes the import tables, including the Import Address Table, field by field.">Import Address Table</HoverCard>:

<MemoryStrip
  column
  cells="on disk=a reference to the name MessageBoxW in user32.dll|in memory=the address of MessageBoxW, written by the loader"
  marks="1"
  caption="One Import Address Table slot. The game's code calls through the slot, so the call works only once the loader has written the real address there."
/>

Lesson 6.5 hooks a program's own copy of this table — a technique that works
precisely because the linker left the address for someone else to fill in.

## The loader turns a file into a process

The loader maps the sections into memory with the right permissions, applies
those relocations if it picked a different base, fills in the import table,
prepares **thread-local storage** (data kept separately for each thread), and
runs the initialisation code. The later [loader-boundary lessons](/pages/11/02/)
follow these details. They explain why a DLL's `DllMain` initialisation
function cannot safely perform every task a normal function can.

The [executable-file chapter](/pages/7/01/) will compare the two layouts:
content arranged for storage on disk and content arranged for execution
in memory. The loader is the connection between them; file positions do
not automatically equal positions in the running process.

### Follow one location across two runs

<Example title="One location across two runs">

Suppose the linker placed an instruction `0x1350` bytes from the beginning of
the game's module. In one run, Windows loads that module at `0x00400000`; in
another, it loads it at `0x00600000`. The instruction did not move *within the
module*, even though its absolute address changed:

| Run | Module base | Instruction offset | Instruction address |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| first | `0x00400000` | `0x1350` | `0x00401350` |
| second | `0x00600000` | `0x1350` | `0x00601350` |

The same distinction applies inside an object, but the starting point is
different. If the compiler put `health` at `+0x30` within a player object,
and that object begins at `0x01A2B000` in the first run, its health field is at
`0x01A2B030`. A newly created player at `0x0208C000` puts the same field at
`0x0208C030`. The module offset measures from the **loaded module**; the field
offset measures from **that particular object**. Neither offset alone is a
complete address. Later pointer work uses this distinction every time it adds
an offset to a base address.

</Example>

## How updates affect locations

The practical payoff is knowing which kinds of location survive a new game
version.

| What you found | Safe to reuse? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A raw address from one run | No reliable reuse after a restart | The module or object may have a different base |
| An offset from the module base | Usually after a restart of the same build | The linker fixed its place within that image |
| A field offset like `+0x30` | Usually for objects of that type in the same build | The compiler chose the layout |
| A byte pattern | Verify it in each build | Compilation or linking can change its bytes |
| "Health is 48 bytes in" | Recheck after a rebuild | A new field earlier in the structure may shift it |

That last row is the one Lesson 11.4 turns into a migration procedure. In
this fixed-order example, inserting a field moves the later fields and
leaves the earlier ones in place. Other layout rules can change more, so
measure the new build rather than assuming the same shift everywhere:

<MemoryStrip
  cells="+0x00=id|+0x04=health|+0x08=max_health|+0x0C=gold"
  caption="The player structure in one build."
/>

<MemoryStrip
  cells="+0x00=id|+0x04=armor|+0x08=health|+0x0C=max_health|+0x10=gold"
  marks="1"
  groups="2-4:each moved 4 bytes later"
  caption="The next build adds `armor`. `id` keeps its offset; every field after the new one moves."
/>

## Optimization is why the code does not match the source

One more consequence, and it explains a lot of confusing disassembly. An
optimising build is allowed to produce anything that behaves the same. It can
paste a small function into each of its callers so no call remains, keep a
variable only in a register so it never touches memory, drop a variable whose
result is never used, reorder work, and merge two identical functions.

So when a function you expected is missing, the usual explanation is not that
it was hidden. It is that the compiler decided the fastest way to do that work
did not involve a separate function. This is also why a debug build and a
release build of the same source can be so different to read, and why an
address or offset belongs to the exact build it came from.

## Why the stages matter in a debugger

The compiler chooses field layouts and may remove or transform source
functions. The linker fixes positions within a native image and records
DLL imports; the loader chooses a run-time base and fills in external
addresses. A module-relative offset can therefore survive a restart of
the same build while a raw address changes. Rebuilding after a field
insertion can shift later offsets, so old offsets need rechecking.
Release binaries may omit source names even while import names or
separate debug information remain.

We now know why a debugger can show addresses and transformed operations
instead of the source's original names. [How Assembly Describes a Running
Game](/pages/2/02/) gives those operations a readable vocabulary and follows
a small rule through its comparisons, branches, and arithmetic.

---
## Lesson 2.3 — How Assembly Describes a Running Game
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/2/02/
Category: Instructions, Debuggers, and Addresses
Estimated reading time: 30 minutes
Summary: Understand what assembly is, how the CPU executes it, and how registers, memory, flags, stacks, and calls fit together.

## What assembly actually is

A CPU does not run source code or even the words `mov` and `sub`. It runs **machine code**: bytes whose bit patterns mean operations for one CPU architecture. Continue the 100-to-75 gold purchase from Lesson 2.1: this first instruction loads its price, 25, into a register. Later instructions will compare and subtract it.

Assembly language is a human-readable spelling of those operations. For 32-bit x86, these five bytes:

<MemoryStrip
  cells="=B8|=19|=00|=00|=00"
  groups="0-0:opcode|1-4:the number 25, little endian"
  caption="`B8` means “put the 32-bit number that follows into `eax`.” The four bytes after it are that number."
/>

can be shown as:

```nasm
mov eax, 25
```

The byte `B8` selects one form of `mov`. The next four bytes hold `25` as a little-endian 32-bit number. The readable instruction and the bytes describe the same CPU action at different levels.

:::note
🔍 **Reading tip:** each instruction changes only a few things, usually one register or one memory location, and sometimes the flags. Taken one instruction at a time, a function becomes ordinary bookkeeping.
:::

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S["source code"] -->|"compiler"| B["machine-code bytes<br/>in the EXE"]
    B -->|"Windows maps them<br/>into memory"| C["the CPU executes them"]
    B -->|"disassembler"| A["assembly text<br/>for a human"]
    A -->|"assembler"| B
```

An **assembler** travels from assembly text to machine code. A **disassembler** travels from machine code to assembly text. A debugger includes a disassembler and also shows the live register and memory values while the instructions execute.

Assembly preserves machine effects, not the author's original explanation. A
release build usually does not retain friendly variable names, comments, source
loops, or the exact class boundaries that produced it. Optimization may inline two
functions into one, remove a variable completely, or replace multiplication with a
different but equivalent instruction sequence.

Therefore, disassembly shows what the machine does; it is not recovered source code. A decompiler
can suggest source-like structure, but you still verify its types, signs, widths,
branches, and calling convention against the actual instructions.

## Assembly depends on the CPU architecture

This book’s historical game builds are 32-bit x86 programs. Their main registers are named `eax`, `ebx`, `ecx`, `edx`, `esi`, `edi`, `esp`, `ebp`, and `eip`.

A 64-bit x86 program uses wider names such as `rax` and `rip`. ARM uses a different instruction set and different register names. Assembly is not one universal language; it is the readable face of a particular processor architecture.

The examples use **Intel syntax**, where the destination normally appears before the source:

```nasm
mov eax, ebx       ; copy ebx into eax
```

Other tools may display AT&T syntax with a different order and punctuation. Pick one syntax while learning so the notation does not hide the idea.

## Read the whole disassembly row

A debugger may show:

```text
007CCD91  29 42 04  sub dword ptr [edx+4], eax
```

<MemoryStrip
  cells="address=007CCD91|bytes=29 42 04|mnemonic=sub|destination=dword ptr [edx+4]|source=eax"
/>

Read it from left to right:

<Panel title="The parts of a disassembly row">

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `007CCD91` | address of the first instruction byte in this run |
| `29 42 04` | the three machine-code bytes |
| `sub` | mnemonic: the short human name for the operation |
| `dword ptr [edx+4]` | destination: a four-byte value in memory |
| `eax` | source: the four-byte value to subtract |

</Panel>

In plain English: “Take the 32-bit number stored four bytes after the address in `edx`, subtract `eax`, and store the answer back in that same memory location.”

This one sentence is far more useful than memorizing that opcode `29` means a form of subtraction.

## The CPU repeats a tiny cycle

At a simplified level, one thread repeatedly:

<Steps>

1. uses `eip` to find the next instruction;
2. fetches its bytes from executable memory;
3. decodes what the bytes mean;
4. reads the required registers or memory;
5. performs the operation;
6. writes the result;
7. advances `eip` or jumps somewhere else.

</Steps>

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    F["fetch the bytes<br/>at eip"] --> D["decode them"]
    D --> R["read registers<br/>or memory"]
    R --> X["do the operation"]
    X --> W["write the result"]
    W --> N["advance eip,<br/>or jump"]
    N --> F
```

`eip` is the **instruction pointer**. It is not a normal game variable. It tells the CPU where this thread is executing. A jump, call, return, exception, or debugger action can change it.

## Registers hold the CPU's current working values

Registers are tiny, very fast storage locations built into the CPU. On 32-bit x86, each general-purpose register below holds 32 bits:

<Panel title="x86 registers at a glance">

| Register | Common historical role | Important warning |
|---|---|---|
| `eax` | return value and arithmetic | a function may use it for anything temporary |
| `ebx` | preserved general value | “preserved” depends on the calling convention |
| `ecx` | counter or `this` pointer | not every use is a counter or object |
| `edx` | arithmetic or extra argument | meaning comes from surrounding instructions |
| `esi` / `edi` | source/destination pointers | compilers also use them as ordinary storage |
| `esp` | top of the current thread’s stack | unbalanced changes usually crash on return |
| `ebp` | stack-frame reference in some builds | optimized code may use it as a normal register |
| `eip` | address of the next instruction | controlled by branches, calls, and returns |

</Panel>

The role column is a clue, not a promise. Ask what the current function actually reads and writes.

## Bits do not carry their own meaning

The register value `0xFFFF_FFFF` is only 32 one-bits. An instruction may interpret those bits as:

- unsigned integer `4,294,967,295`;
- signed integer `-1`;
- four bytes;
- part of a pointer;
- a bit mask where every switch is on.

<MemoryStrip
  cells="=FF|=FF|=FF|=FF"
  groups="0-3:as a `u32`: 4,294,967,295"
  groups2="0-3:as an `i32`: −1"
  caption="The bits are identical. Only the instruction that uses them chooses the reading."
/>

Source-level types give those bits a declared meaning. In disassembly, only the instruction that uses the bits, and the code around it, tells you which meaning applies.

You do not need to memorize the whole x86 instruction set. Start with a handful of verbs, but always connect each verb to the CPU, registers, memory, and control flow described above.

## The debugger changes the view, not the bytes

The same four bytes can be displayed as hexadecimal, a signed integer, an
unsigned integer, a float, four characters, or an instruction. Changing the
debugger's display format does not convert the target's memory. It changes only
the question you ask about those bits.

Use the program's operations to choose the view:

- a floating-point instruction supports a float interpretation;
- sign extension or a signed conditional jump supports a signed integer;
- a memory dereference supports an address interpretation;
- repeated one-byte reads ending at zero support a C-string interpretation;
- bytes that decode into valid-looking instructions are code only if control
  flow actually reaches them.

This last point matters because a code section can contain alignment bytes,
constants, and jump tables. A disassembler can produce a plausible instruction
from almost any byte sequence. What makes bytes code is that execution reaches
them: a jump, call, or fall-through from other code leads there, or a debugger
sees the CPU run them.

## Moving data

`mov destination, source` copies data:

```nasm
mov eax, 25        ; eax now contains 25
mov ebx, eax       ; ebx now contains 25
```

Square brackets mean “use the memory at this address”:

```nasm
mov eax, [rcx]     ; read 4 bytes from the address in rcx
mov [rcx], eax     ; write 4 bytes to that address
```

Without brackets, `rcx` is a number. With brackets, that number is treated as an address.

For the 32-bit course games, the same examples usually use `ecx` instead of `rcx`:

```nasm
mov eax, [ecx]     ; read four bytes from memory
mov [ecx], eax     ; write four bytes to memory
```

<MemoryStrip
  cells="0x5000=64|0x5001=00|0x5002=00|0x5003=00"
  groups="0-3:`mov eax, [ecx]` copies these four bytes: `eax` = 100"
  caption="Suppose `ecx` holds `0x5000`. `mov eax, ecx` copies the number `0x5000` itself. The brackets in `mov eax, [ecx]` go to that address and copy what is stored there."
/>

The instruction decides the size. `byte ptr` means one byte, `word ptr` means two, `dword ptr` means four, and `qword ptr` means eight.

## Little endian explains “backward” bytes

x86 stores a multi-byte integer with its least-significant byte first. The value `0x12345678` appears in memory as:

<MemoryStrip
  cells="+0=78|+1=56|+2=34|+3=12"
  groups="0-3:the value `0x12345678`"
/>

The number is not reversed when the CPU uses it. This is only the byte order in memory. The conversion helpers `u32::from_le_bytes` and `to_le_bytes` make the chosen byte order explicit.

## Doing math

```nasm
add eax, 10        ; eax = eax + 10
sub eax, 3         ; eax = eax - 3
inc eax            ; eax = eax + 1
dec eax            ; eax = eax - 1
```

The source-level equivalent is easier to read:

```rust
let mut value = 25_i32;
value += 10;
value -= 3;
value += 1;
value -= 1;
```

Starting at 25, those four operations leave `value` at 32: add 10, subtract
3, add 1, subtract 1. The assembly operations would do the same arithmetic
if `eax` started at 25. The debugger lets us check the actual register value
before and after each instruction instead of assuming that starting point.

## Comparing and branching

`cmp` performs a comparison and updates flags. A jump reads those flags:

```nasm
cmp eax, 0
je player_is_dead
```

`je` means “jump if equal.” Common jumps include:

<Panel title="Jumps after a compare">

| Instruction | Meaning after `cmp left, right` |
|---|---|
| `je` / `jz` | equal / zero |
| `jne` / `jnz` | not equal / not zero |
| `jg` | greater, signed |
| `jl` | less, signed |
| `ja` | above, unsigned |
| `jb` | below, unsigned |
| `jmp` | always jump |

</Panel>

Signed and unsigned matter because the same bits can be read in different ways. `0xFFFF_FFFF` is `4,294,967,295` as a `u32`, but `-1` as an `i32`.

That choice decides which branch actually runs. Imagine a price of
`0xFFFFFFFF` arriving at a gold check while the player holds 100 gold:

```text
jb  (unsigned): is 100 below 4,294,967,295?   yes -> refuse the purchase
jl  (signed):   is 100 less than -1?          no  -> allow it, then subtract
                                                     -1, which adds a gold
```

Identical bits, identical `cmp`, opposite outcomes. When you are reading a
check that guards something valuable, the signedness of the jump is not a
footnote — it is very often the entire bug.

The type makes that choice visible:

```rust
let signed = -1_i32;
let unsigned = u32::MAX;

assert_eq!(signed.to_ne_bytes(), unsigned.to_ne_bytes());
```

The assertion passes because `-1_i32` and `u32::MAX` have the same four-byte
pattern on this target. A signed jump treats that pattern as −1; an unsigned
jump treats it as 4,294,967,295. The branch instruction determines which
meaning controls the next step.

## Flags are one-bit answers from the last operation

`eflags` is a register containing many one-bit results. Common ones include:

| Flag | Plain-English question it helps answer |
|---|---|
| ZF, zero flag | Was the result zero? |
| CF, carry flag | Did unsigned arithmetic carry or borrow? |
| SF, sign flag | Is the result’s top bit set? |
| OF, overflow flag | Did signed arithmetic overflow its range? |

`cmp eax, ebx` behaves like a subtraction that throws away the numeric answer but keeps the flags. `je`, `jg`, `ja`, and the other conditional jumps interpret those flags in different combinations.

This is why signed and unsigned jumps differ even though the register bits are identical.

Here are the flags after the two comparisons in the gold check at the end of
this lesson:

<MemoryStrip
  cells="ZF=0|CF=0|SF=0|OF=0"
  caption="Gold 100 compared with price 25: 100 − 25 = 75. The result is not zero and nothing was borrowed, so `je` and `jb` both fall through."
/>

<MemoryStrip
  cells="ZF=0|CF=1|SF=1|OF=0"
  marks="1-2"
  caption="Gold 20 compared with price 25: 20 − 25 needs a borrow. CF = 1 makes `jb` jump. SF differs from OF, which makes `jl` jump as well."
/>

## Calls, returns, and the stack

`call` jumps into a function and remembers where to return. `ret` goes back.

```nasm
call calculate_damage
; execution continues here after `ret`
```

The stack is a last-in, first-out area used for return addresses, saved registers, and some local values:

```nasm
push rbx
; use rbx
pop rbx
ret
```

On 32-bit x86, the stack grows toward lower addresses. `push eax` subtracts four from `esp` and stores `eax` there. `pop eax` loads four bytes and adds four back to `esp`.

<MemoryStrip
  column
  cells="0x0019FF30=older data, where esp pointed before|0x0019FF2C=25, the value in eax"
  marks="1"
  groups="1-1:`esp` after `push eax`"
  caption="`push eax` with `eax` = 25. The stack pointer moves down four bytes and the value lands there. `pop eax` reads it back and moves `esp` up again."
/>

`call target` is roughly:

```text
push address_of_the_next_instruction
jump target
```

`ret` roughly pops that saved address into `eip`. If a hook adds an unmatched `push`, `ret` may treat some unrelated value as an address and jump into nonsense.

Follow the `call calculate_damage` above through its return. The saved address
belongs to the caller's next instruction; it is separate from the address of
`calculate_damage`:

<Scene name="call-and-return" />

## Calling conventions are agreements between functions

A **calling convention** answers questions such as:

- Where are arguments placed: stack or registers?
- Which registers must the called function preserve?
- Who removes stack arguments?
- Where is the return value placed?

The course’s 32-bit games commonly expose `cdecl`, `stdcall`, and `thiscall` boundaries. The three differ mainly in who removes the arguments from the stack after the call. `cdecl` leaves that job to the caller, which is also what lets a `cdecl` function such as `printf` accept a varying number of arguments—only the caller knows how many it pushed. `stdcall` makes the callee remove its own arguments before returning. In a typical 32-bit `thiscall`, `ecx` carries the object pointer—the value an object method treats as `self` or `this`—while other arguments use the stack, and the callee cleans up like `stdcall`.

Do not identify a calling convention from one register alone. Inspect how the caller prepares arguments and how the callee returns. A wrong convention can leave `esp` incorrect even when the function address is right.

On 64-bit Windows, ordinary integer and pointer arguments start in `rcx`, `rdx`,
`r8`, and `r9`; floating-point arguments use the matching XMM argument
registers. The caller also reserves stack space for the register arguments and
keeps the stack correctly aligned. There is one main Windows x64 convention,
so do not carry the old 32-bit `cdecl` versus `stdcall` cleanup distinction into
64-bit code.

A calling convention is more than an argument list. It is the complete border
contract between caller and callee:

```text
arguments + return location + preserved registers + stack shape + unwind rules
```

Read both sides of a call. Code before `call` explains what the caller offers;
the callee's first uses explain what it expects; code after the return shows what
the caller believes survived.

## Address calculations

This pattern appears constantly:

```nasm
mov eax, [rcx+30]
```

Read it as: “Start at the address in `rcx`, move forward `0x30` bytes, then read a 32-bit value.” If `rcx` points to a player object, offset `0x30` might be a field such as health.

A typed struct expresses the idea by name:

```rust
#[repr(C)]
struct PlayerSnapshot {
    id: u32,
    team: u32,
    health: u32,
}
```

`#[repr(C)]` asks the compiler for a predictable C-compatible field layout. We only rely on a layout after confirming its offsets; guessing a struct from one screenshot is not enough.

## `lea` does math, not a read

`lea` stands for “load effective address.” It works out the address the brackets
describe and stores that number, instead of reading whatever lives there. It is
the one common instruction where brackets do not mean a memory access:

```nasm
mov eax, [rcx+rdx*4]  ; eax = the four-byte value stored at rcx + rdx*4
lea rax, [rcx+rdx*4]  ; rax = the address rcx + rdx*4 itself; nothing is read
```

The `mov` reads into `eax` because the elements are four bytes wide. Reading
into the eight-byte `rax` would take the next element along with it.

The `*4` is a strong hint that this is array indexing: `rcx` holds the start of
an array, `rdx` holds an index, and each step of the index moves four bytes
because each element is four bytes wide. So this `lea` computes “the address of
element number `rdx`,” which is exactly what code does just before handing one
element to another function.

<MemoryStrip
  cells="rcx+0=10|rcx+4=20|rcx+8=30|rcx+12=40"
  marks="2"
  groups="2-2:element 2"
  caption="An array of four-byte numbers, with `rdx` = 2. `lea rax, [rcx+rdx*4]` puts the address `rcx+8` in `rax`. `mov eax, [rcx+rdx*4]` reads the number stored there, 30."
/>

Compilers also use `lea` as a quick way to do plain arithmetic, since it can
multiply and add in one instruction without disturbing the flags. Do not assume
every `lea` result is a pointer.

## A five-question reading method

For each instruction, ask:

1. What is read?
2. What is written?
3. How many bytes are involved?
4. Is a number signed or unsigned?
5. Where can execution go next?

Answer those five questions one instruction at a time. A long function becomes a trail of small facts.

## Trace both data flow and control flow

Reading only downward through the listing works for a tiny straight-line function.
Larger functions need two connected maps.

**Data flow** asks where a value came from and where it goes next. If `eax` is
compared, trace backward to the instruction that last wrote `eax`. If `[ecx+0x30]`
is changed, trace how `ecx` obtained the suspected player address and who later
reads that field.

**Control flow** asks which instruction can run next. A straight sequence with one
entry and one exit is often called a **basic block**. Conditional jumps connect
blocks into a graph:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["read gold"] --> B["compare with price"]
    B --> C{"enough?"}
    C -->|"yes"| D["subtract"]
    D --> E["success"]
    C -->|"no"| F["failure"]
```

The graph explains the decision even when the compiler has rearranged the blocks.
Source-level `if`, `match`, loops, early returns, and error paths all become control-flow
edges of this kind.

Use both maps together. A branch tells you *when* a write occurs; data flow tells
you *what* it changes. Guessing from only one of them is how a nearby animation
counter gets mislabeled as health or a failure path gets mistaken for the normal
path.

## Trace a complete tiny function

Suppose `ecx` points to a player and gold is the four-byte field at offset `4`:

```nasm
mov eax, [esp+4]          ; read the price argument
cmp dword ptr [ecx+4], eax
jb cannot_afford         ; unsigned gold < price
sub dword ptr [ecx+4], eax
mov eax, 1               ; return true
ret 4                    ; return and remove one 4-byte stack argument

cannot_afford:
xor eax, eax             ; eax = 0, meaning false
ret 4
```

The same listing as a control-flow graph. Each box is a basic block, and the
only decision is the `jb`:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["mov eax, [esp+4]<br/>cmp dword ptr [ecx+4], eax<br/>jb cannot_afford"] -->|"gold is not below the price"| B["sub dword ptr [ecx+4], eax<br/>mov eax, 1<br/>ret 4"]
    A -->|"gold is below the price, unsigned"| C["cannot_afford:<br/>xor eax, eax<br/>ret 4"]
```

Three details in that listing puzzle almost everyone the first time.

**Why `[esp+4]` and not `[esp]`?** The `call` that reached this function pushed
a return address onto the stack, so that address is now sitting at `[esp]`. The
argument the caller pushed just before the call is one slot further in, at
`[esp+4]`. Whenever you see a function collecting its arguments from `+4`, `+8`,
`+12`, the saved return address is what those offsets are stepping over.

<MemoryStrip
  column
  cells="0x0019FF34=the caller's own data|0x0019FF30=the price argument, 25|0x0019FF2C=the return address, pushed by call"
  marks="2"
  groups="1-1:`[esp+4]`|2-2:`[esp]`"
  caption="The stack as the function begins. `esp` points at the return address, so the argument the caller pushed just before the call is one slot further in."
/>

**Why `xor eax, eax` instead of `mov eax, 0`?** Both leave zero in `eax`. Any
value exclusive-ORed with itself is zero, and the `xor` form assembles to fewer
bytes, so compilers emit it constantly. Read `xor register, register` as “set
this register to zero” and keep going.

**Why does `ret` have a number after it?** `ret 4` returns *and* discards four
bytes of arguments from the stack, so the function cleans up after itself. A
plain `ret` leaves that job to the caller. Which form a function uses is fixed
by its calling convention, and getting it wrong corrupts `esp`: execution
returns to the correct place, and from that point on the caller's stack is off
by four bytes.

Trace it with `gold = 100` and `price = 25`:

| Step | Important state |
|---|---|
| enter | `ecx = player`, `[ecx+4] = 100`, `[esp+4] = 25` |
| `mov` | `eax = 25` |
| `cmp` | flags describe `100 - 25`; unsigned-below is false |
| `jb` | branch is not taken |
| `sub` | `[ecx+4] = 75` |
| `mov` | `eax = 1` return value |
| `ret 4` | caller resumes and the argument is removed |

Now trace `gold = 20`. The `jb` branch skips the subtraction and returns zero. That is assembly comprehension: follow state changes and rebuild the higher-level decision.

<Quiz
  id="assembly-gold-branch"
  type="multiple-choice"
  title="Trace the branch"
  prompt="In the example above, `gold` is 20 and the price is 25. What happens after the unsigned comparison?"
  options="The subtraction runs and produces −5||The below branch is taken and the function returns zero||The CPU changes 20 into 25 before comparing||The return instruction repeats the comparison"
  answer="1"
  explanation="For unsigned values, 20 is below 25, so `jb` takes the failure path. That path clears the return register to zero. The important habit is to follow the flags and branch instead of mentally executing every line in order."
/>

## What the debugger is showing

Assembly text is a readable rendering of machine bytes for one CPU
architecture; x86 and ARM bytes need different decoders. In the x86 trace,
`eip` locates the next instruction, `esp` marks the stack top, and `eflags`
holds one-bit results that branches can use. Brackets such as `[edx+4]` mean
read or write memory at the calculated address; `edx+4` without brackets is
only an address calculation. A `call` saves a return address on the stack,
and `ret` uses it to resume the caller. The calling convention completes that
contract by fixing where arguments and results go and who removes arguments
from the stack. Breakpoints in the next lesson let you inspect those facts
while a real instruction is paused.

---
## Lesson 2.4 — Breakpoints: One Moment of Program State
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/2/03/
Category: Instructions, Debuggers, and Addresses
Estimated reading time: 12 minutes
Summary: Pause on an instruction or memory access, inspect registers, memory, and the call stack, and continue without losing the thread.

## What a breakpoint does

A breakpoint asks the debugger to pause when a specific event happens. The two kinds we use most are:

- **code breakpoint** — pause when the CPU reaches an instruction;
- **memory breakpoint** — pause when code reads, writes, or executes at an address.

The pause is useful because the thread's register state and instruction location
are still available. A code breakpoint normally stops before its instruction;
a data watchpoint may report an access after the instruction performed it.
Inspect the triggering access and the state at the pause before deciding which
side of that instruction the debugger shows.

A breakpoint tells you that one condition happened, not why. A write breakpoint
on health may fire for damage, healing, loading, respawning, and
initialization, all through the same instruction. The action you performed just
before the pause, and the call stack at the pause, tell those uses apart.

## A pause is one instant on one thread

A process can contain many threads. When one thread hits a breakpoint, another may have updated nearby state just before the debugger stopped everything. The snapshot is real, but it is not automatically the whole causal story.

Four kinds of context explain a pause:

- **time:** what player action immediately preceded the pause;
- **thread:** which thread executed the instruction;
- **data:** which registers and memory locations the instruction used; usually only two registers matter, the one that forms the memory address and the one the value moves into or out of;
- **control:** which call path and branches led here.

Repeating the same action shows whether the breakpoint is useful. A useful breakpoint fires at a consistent point for the behavior you are studying. A noisy breakpoint may still be correct, but it needs a stronger filter such as a specific thread, object pointer, call site, or condition.

This is the difference between a **trace** and an **explanation**. A trace records what executed. An explanation connects that execution to a game rule and survives repeated tests.

## Memory breakpoints

A hardware breakpoint uses CPU debug registers to watch a small address range. It is ideal when you know the gold address but not the instruction that changes it.

<MemoryStrip
  column
  cells="DR0=0x0550A034|DR1=unused|DR2=unused|DR3=unused|DR7=which of DR0 to DR3 are on, what each watches, and how many bytes"
  marks="0"
  caption="One thread's debug registers with a write watchpoint on four bytes of gold. Four address slots are all there are."
/>

The debug registers can watch for a write, for a read *or* write, or for an
execute — x86 has no read-only setting. A debugger that offers a pure read
breakpoint implements it another way, usually with page protection.

Choose the narrowest event that answers your question:

- **write** when looking for code that changes a value;
- **read** when looking for code that uses a value;
- **access** only when you truly need both.

Access breakpoints can fire constantly. More pauses do not automatically mean more understanding.

Hardware watchpoints are limited resources—x86 provides only a small number of
debug-address registers per thread—and supported widths/alignment are
restricted. A debugger may emulate larger memory watches with guarded pages,
which is noisier because unrelated data on the same page can trigger.

Be precise about the event:

- an instruction **reads** when it needs the old bytes;
- it **writes** when it stores new bytes;
- a read-modify-write instruction such as `sub [address], eax` does both;
- **execute** means the watched bytes are being treated as code.

Watching four bytes does not tell the debugger that they are a `u32`. Width is
about overlapping addresses. Type meaning still comes from the instruction and
behavior.

## Code breakpoints

Once a memory breakpoint identifies the instruction that writes gold, a
code breakpoint can stop at that instruction on later runs. That makes
it easier to compare its callers and branch conditions without watching
every write to the field.

On x86, a debugger often implements a software breakpoint by temporarily replacing the first byte of an instruction with `0xCC`, the `int3` instruction.

Use a concrete three-byte subtraction as the byte-level example below:
`sub dword ptr [edx+4], eax` subtracts the value in `eax` from a four-byte
field at address `edx+4`. The debugger changes only its first instruction byte
to set the breakpoint.

<MemoryStrip
  cells="0x007CCD91=29|=42|=04"
  groups="0-2:`sub dword ptr [edx+4], eax`"
  caption="The three-byte subtraction before a software breakpoint is installed."
/>

<MemoryStrip
  cells="0x007CCD91=CC|=42|=04"
  marks="0"
  groups="0-0:`int3`"
  caption="The same bytes with a breakpoint set. The CPU now executes `int3` and stops; the debugger keeps the original `29` to put back."
/>

When the CPU executes `int3`, Windows reports a breakpoint exception. The debugger:

1. pauses the process;
2. restores the original byte;
3. lets you inspect or step;
4. replaces the breakpoint when execution continues.

That bookkeeping is why you should remove breakpoints through the debugger instead of editing the byte by hand.

It also means a software breakpoint is not invisible. While it is set, the
program's own code genuinely contains `0xCC` where the original byte used to
be, and nothing prevents the program from reading its own bytes and noticing.
A routine that adds up the bytes of a function and compares the total against
a figure recorded when the game was built will disagree the moment you place a
breakpoint inside that function.

Notice what such a routine has actually established: that its code changed. It
has not detected a debugger, and it cannot tell your breakpoint apart from any
other modification to those bytes. Chapter 13 returns to this, because it is
the same self-checking idea used to notice a patch.

## How a software breakpoint pauses and resumes

The original instruction still has to execute. A debugger normally handles the
`0xCC` pause in two events:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["the CPU executes int3"] --> B["breakpoint event"]
    B --> C["restore the original byte"]
    C --> D["move the instruction pointer back<br/>to the restored instruction"]
    D --> E["turn on one-instruction stepping"]
    E --> F["the real instruction runs"]
    F --> G["single-step event"]
    G --> H["write 0xCC back"]
    H --> I["turn stepping off, then<br/>continue or pause for the user"]
```

The instruction pointer needs rewinding because the CPU has already consumed
the one-byte `int3`. The one-instruction step lets the real instruction run
before the breakpoint byte is restored. [Lesson 5.7](/pages/7/07/) models this as explicit
`Armed` and `Stepping` states so the byte is never restored at the wrong time.

On x86, single stepping uses the **trap flag** in the thread’s flags register.
When set, the CPU raises a debug exception after the next instruction. The flag
belongs to one thread, which is why debugger state records thread IDs.

Follow the subtraction example through both events. The saved `29` byte must
be executable for one instruction before `CC` can safely be installed again:

<Scene name="breakpoint-restore" />

## Step, step over, and run to return

When paused at a `call`, <HoverCard kind="tip" body="In x64dbg, F7 steps into, F8 steps over, Ctrl+F9 runs until the function returns, and F9 resumes. F2 sets or clears a breakpoint on the selected instruction.">you have choices</HoverCard>:

| Action | What it does |
|---|---|
| Step into | Enter the called function |
| Step over | Run the called function and pause after it |
| Run to return | Continue until the current function returns |
| Resume | Continue until another event pauses the process |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P["paused at<br/>call calculate_damage"] -->|"step into"| I["first instruction<br/>inside calculate_damage"]
    P -->|"step over"| O["the instruction<br/>after the call"]
    I -->|"run to return"| O
```

Step into code you need to understand. Step over code that is not part of your question.

“Step over” is not one special CPU instruction. At a `call`, the debugger can
place a temporary breakpoint at the instruction after the call and resume. If
the call never returns normally, that temporary breakpoint may never fire.

“Run to return” relies on the current call frame and can be confused by tail
calls, exceptions, corrupted stacks, or optimized code. These controls are
convenient ways to express a debugging goal, not guarantees about source-level
functions.

## `nop`: do nothing once

`nop` means “no operation.” Replacing an instruction with one or more
`nop` bytes is a quick, temporary way to test what that instruction does.
This is a separate action from setting a breakpoint: it changes what
the game executes after you resume.

```nasm
sub [ecx+30h], eax
```

If this removes gold and you temporarily replace the whole instruction with `nop` bytes, recruiting may stop costing gold. That result supports your theory.

NOPing an instruction removes all of its effects, including effects that are
easy to overlook. Arithmetic instructions often update flags used by the next
conditional branch. A floating-point store may also pop a value from an x87
stack. A test that appears visually correct can still damage later control flow
or machine state.

<MemoryStrip
  cells="=29|=41|=30"
  groups="0-2:`sub [ecx+30h], eax`: three bytes"
  caption="The original instruction."
/>

<MemoryStrip
  cells="=90|=90|=90"
  marks="0-2"
  groups="0-0:`nop`|1-1:`nop`|2-2:`nop`"
  caption="All three bytes replaced. The subtraction is gone, and so are the flags it would have set."
/>

<MemoryStrip
  cells="=90|=90|=30"
  marks="2"
  groups="0-1:two `nop`s|2-2:leftover"
  caption="Only two bytes replaced. The CPU decodes the leftover `30` as the start of an `xor` instruction that swallows the bytes after it."
/>

Before patching, ask:

1. How many complete bytes does the instruction occupy?
2. Which registers, memory, flags, or special stacks does it change?
3. Does later code rely on those changes?
4. What should visibly change in the game if the patch works?
5. How will the original bytes be restored?

:::danger
Always save a copy of the original bytes before patching, so they can be written back. An incomplete replacement can make the CPU decode the remaining bytes as a completely different instruction.
:::

## Represent debug events as explicit states

Later, our debugger will receive the same breakpoint events from Windows. We will model them with an enum:

```rust
enum DebugEvent {
    Breakpoint { thread_id: u32, address: usize },
    ProcessExited { code: u32 },
    Other,
}
```

An enum gives each event a clear shape. Pattern matching then forces us to decide how every event should be handled instead of silently ignoring surprises.

The next lesson uses x64dbg's built-in breakpoint controls rather than a
custom debugger. Start with the gold address, watch a write, and use the
paused registers and instruction to test the purchase rule. The enum
becomes useful later when we write our own event-handling code.

<Quiz
  id="breakpoint-evidence"
  type="multiple-choice"
  title="One instruction, several uses"
  prompt="A write breakpoint on the player's health fires while damage is taken. What is the best next step?"
  options="Assume the instruction only handles damage||Delete every other breakpoint and patch immediately||Check the call stack, then heal, load, and respawn to see which of those also reach the same instruction||Change all writable values near the address"
  answer="2"
  explanation="A breakpoint tells you that the condition happened; it does not tell you every role of the instruction. The same write can run for damage, healing, loading, and respawning, and the call stack at each pause shows which path led there."
/>

## Lesson 2.5 — From a Game Value to the Code That Changes It
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/2/04/
Category: Instructions, Debuggers, and Addresses
Estimated reading time: 20 minutes
Summary: Follow a known gold address backward to the exact instruction that changes it.

## Find the instruction that changes gold

In the previous memory lab, we found the current gold. Now we want to know:

> Which instruction subtracts the price of a recruited unit?

Use the same offline Wesnoth 1.14.9 target and restore your clean VM snapshot before starting.
For a concrete run, suppose you start at 100 gold and recruit a unit
costing 15. The expected result is 85. Use the actual price and gold
shown in your match when checking the paused instruction.

## Attach x64dbg

Launch Wesnoth, begin a local match, and find the gold address again. Then attach <HoverCard kind="reference" href="https://help.x64dbg.com/en/latest/" body="The x64dbg documentation covers every view and menu used in this lesson.">x64dbg</HoverCard> to the running process.

<Frame caption="x64dbg's Attach command hooks the debugger to the running game.">

![The Attach command in x64dbg](/assets/images/2/4/reversing1.png)

</Frame>

<Frame caption="Choose the Wesnoth process from the list.">

![Selecting the Wesnoth process](/assets/images/2/4/reversing2.png)

</Frame>

The CPU view contains four useful areas:

- disassembly—the instructions near the current position;
- registers—the CPU’s current scratch values;
- dump—raw memory;
- stack—return addresses and temporary data.

<Frame caption="The CPU view: disassembly, registers, dump, and stack.">

![The main x64dbg view](/assets/images/2/4/reversing3.png)

</Frame>

Attaching may pause in Windows system code. That is normal. Resume the process before triggering your experiment.

## Go to the gold address

Open the dump view’s “go to expression” command and enter the address found by the memory scanner.

<Frame caption="Go to expression in the dump, with the address the scanner found.">

![Going to an address in the dump](/assets/images/2/4/reversing5.png)

</Frame>

<Frame caption="The dump at the gold address, showing the value's bytes.">

![The player gold address in memory](/assets/images/2/4/reversing7.png)

</Frame>

The bytes in the dump are little-endian. If the gold is `100`, the 32-bit value `0x00000064` appears as:

```text
64 00 00 00
```

The least-significant byte comes first.

## Break on writes

Set a hardware breakpoint on **write**, covering four bytes at the gold address.
The lesson uses x64dbg, but any debugger that can watch an address will do:

<Tabs sync="debugger">
<Tab label="x64dbg">

Select the four bytes in the dump, right-click, and choose **Breakpoint**, then
**Hardware, Write**, then **Dword**.

</Tab>
<Tab label="WinDbg">

Type `ba w4` followed by the address, for example `ba w4 0A3C1230`, to break on a
four-byte write. Then type `g` to let the game run.

</Tab>
<Tab label="Cheat Engine">

Right-click the gold entry in the address list and choose **Find out what writes
to this address**. Cheat Engine lists each instruction that writes it, with a
count.

</Tab>
</Tabs>

A hardware memory breakpoint does not replace the game’s instruction bytes.
The debugger programs special CPU debug registers with an address, access type,
and width. When an instruction writes across that watched range, the CPU raises
a debug exception and Windows reports it to the debugger.

The width matters. Gold is believed to be a four-byte value, so watch all four
bytes. Watching one byte can still trigger, but it hides whether the game wrote
the complete integer or only part of it.

This breakpoint watches a **data address**, not one fixed instruction. If three
different functions write gold, the same watch can reveal all three. A software
breakpoint placed on a code address answers the opposite question: “When does
this exact instruction execute?”

<Frame caption="Select the four bytes, right-click, then Breakpoint, Hardware, Write, Dword.">

![Setting a write breakpoint on gold](/assets/images/2/4/reversing8.png)

</Frame>

Resume the game and recruit one unit. The debugger should pause close to an instruction that resembles:

```nasm
sub dword ptr [reg+offset], eax
```

Do not copy the exact register or offset from this page. Read the
instruction in your own debugger. A hardware data breakpoint can report
an access after the instruction has run, so the highlighted next
instruction may not be the one that wrote gold. Use the breakpoint's
access information and nearby disassembly to identify the triggering
write, then confirm that its calculated destination is your gold
address. Builds and runs can differ.

<Frame caption="The debugger paused at the instruction that changes gold.">

![The instruction that changes player gold](/assets/images/2/4/reversing11.png)

</Frame>

## Ask the five assembly questions

Apply the five questions to the paused instruction:

1. **What is read?** The current gold and the price in a register.
2. **What is written?** Four bytes at the gold field.
3. **How many bytes?** `dword ptr` means 32 bits.
4. **Signed or unsigned?** Test nearby comparisons before deciding.
5. **Where next?** The following instruction unless a branch changes the path.

Now compare the price register with the unit’s price. In the example
run, it should be 15 and the destination should be the gold address
that changed from 100 to 85. Matching both is stronger evidence than
recognizing `sub` alone.

## Read an instruction as state transition

For `sub dword ptr [reg+offset], eax`, the complete before-and-after effect is:

```text
address = register value + offset
old = 32-bit value read from address
new = old - low 32 bits of eax
store new at address
update arithmetic flags
```

That last line matters. Later branches may inspect zero, sign, carry, or overflow flags. Replacing the subtraction changes both the stored gold and those flags. Before a temporary patch, step forward and check whether nearby conditional jumps consume them.

The effective address calculation does not dereference `reg` and then add an offset to the loaded value. It adds the offset to the register first, then reads memory at the resulting address. Keep “calculate an address” separate from “read the value at that address.”

## Read the brackets as an address calculation

For an instruction such as:

```nasm
sub dword ptr [esi+30h], eax
```

read it from the inside outward:

1. take the address currently stored in `esi`;
2. add hexadecimal offset `0x30`;
3. treat the four bytes at that final address as the destination;
4. subtract the lower 32 bits of `eax` from that destination;
5. store the result back to the same four bytes;
6. update CPU flags for later branches.

The bracketed expression accesses memory. Without brackets, `esi+30h` would be
an address calculation rather than a read or write of the bytes at that
address.

Read the live value of `esi` in the register panel and add `0x30` yourself. For
example, if `esi` holds `0x0A3C1200`, the destination is
`0x0A3C1200 + 0x30 = 0x0A3C1230`. If the sum equals the candidate gold address,
this instruction writes the gold you found.

## Test with a reversible patch

Copy the original instruction bytes first, so you can write them back. Then temporarily replace the **entire** subtraction instruction with <HoverCard kind="example" body="The length comes from the encoding. `sub [edx+4], eax` is the three bytes `29 42 04`, so it takes three `90` bytes. `sub [edx+0x1234], eax` is the six bytes `29 82 34 12 00 00`, so it takes six. The disassembly's bytes column shows the count.">the same number of `nop` bytes</HoverCard>.

<Frame caption="Fill the whole instruction with nop bytes.">

![Filling the instruction with NOP bytes](/assets/images/2/4/reversing12.png)

</Frame>

Resume and recruit another unit. If gold no longer decreases, this instruction is the one that subtracts the price. Restore the original bytes immediately afterward.

<Frame caption="The instruction after patching: only nop bytes remain.">

![The patched instruction](/assets/images/2/4/reversing14.png)

</Frame>

## Turn one discovery into a repeatable patch

Our tools will not hardcode “whatever address worked once.” They will:

1. open the controlled process;
2. locate a module or scan a known pattern;
3. confirm the expected original bytes;
4. apply a temporary patch;
5. restore the bytes on exit.

Checking the original bytes is crucial. Refusing to patch an unknown version is safer than writing to the wrong place.

## Clean up

Remove the breakpoint through x64dbg’s Breakpoints tab and confirm the original instruction is restored.

<Frame caption="The Breakpoints tab lists every breakpoint and removes it.">

![The Breakpoints tab](/assets/images/2/4/reversing15.png)

</Frame>

The scan gave us a candidate *value*; the write breakpoint gave us a
specific instruction and the register values from one recruitment.
The reversible patch checked its effect, but the instruction may also
run for other gold-changing actions. [Lesson 2.6](/pages/2/05/)
follows the call path to find which rule brought execution here.
