## Lesson 2.6 — Tracing a Game Rule Through Its Callers
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/2/05/
Category: Instructions, Debuggers, and Addresses
Estimated reading time: 23 minutes
Summary: Follow callers and dependencies from one gold-changing instruction to the menu decision that caused it.

Finding one instruction is useful. Understanding the surrounding feature is better.

## Start from a known anchor

In an offline Wesnoth 1.14.9 match, recruiting a unit reduces the player's
four-byte gold value by that unit's price. The instruction that writes the
reduced gold is our **anchor**. Set a code breakpoint on the instruction you
verified in the debugger, recruit one unit, and let the breakpoint fire.

<Frame caption="The breakpoint paused on the gold subtraction during a recruit.">

![A breakpoint on the gold subtraction](/assets/images/2/5/wesnoth4.png)

</Frame>

The current function probably handles a small part of recruitment. To discover who asked for that work, look at the call stack or run until the function returns.

<Frame caption="Run until return: execution continues until the current function finishes.">

![Running until the current function returns](/assets/images/2/5/wesnoth6.png)

</Frame>

Now you are back in the caller. Repeat this carefully to move from the low-level write toward the broader decision that requested it.

## Why the caller is visible

When x86 executes `call`, it places a return address on the stack before jumping to the callee. That address points to the instruction the caller expects to run next. A debugger’s call stack combines return addresses with known module ranges and function information to show the nested route that reached the breakpoint.

The call stack a debugger shows is a reconstruction, and it may be incomplete. Optimizations can inline functions, reuse stack space, or omit traditional frame pointers. Confirm an important caller by returning to it or placing a breakpoint at its call site and reproducing the action.

## Recognize dispatcher code

Menus often use a chain of comparisons:

```nasm
cmp eax, MENU_RECRUIT
je handle_recruit
cmp eax, MENU_DESCRIPTION
je show_description
cmp eax, MENU_CANCEL
je close_menu
```

The constants will not have friendly names in the debugger. You create those names from experiments.

Triggering one menu item at a time shows which branch each one takes. In one run
of this book's build:

```text
Action: Recruit
Compared value: 3
Taken destination: 0x00CC_A140

Action: Terrain description
Compared value: 5
Taken destination: 0x00CC_AF20
```

Those destinations belong to one run of one build, and yours will not match.
What carries over is the shape: two actions, two constants, two different
branch targets, all from the same comparison chain.

Once each constant is matched to an action, the anonymous numbers become an
enum:

```rust
#[repr(u32)]
enum MenuAction {
    Recruit = 3,
    TerrainDescription = 5,
}
```

The enum is your model, not a claim about the original source type.

The comparison value alone is not enough. Where it came from matters: a register, a stack argument, or a field inside a menu object, and whether another branch changed it before the dispatcher. Those details distinguish “menu command ID” from a temporary loop counter that merely happened to equal `3`.

## Separate “where” from “why”

The gold instruction tells you **where** a change happens. The menu dispatcher tells you **why** execution reached it.

That distinction matters:

- patching the subtraction changes one cost rule;
- changing a branch may select a different feature;
- hooking the dispatcher lets you observe every menu action.

Do not make all three changes at once. Test one layer at a time.

This is also a lesson about **abstraction levels**. The subtraction is a low-level side effect. The recruitment function groups validation and side effects into one operation. The dispatcher chooses among operations. Moving upward explains more behavior but also adds more unrelated branches, so stop when the original question is answered.

## Follow dependencies, not just nearby instructions

“Backward” does not simply mean scrolling upward in the disassembly. It means following the facts that had to be true for the anchor instruction to run.

- A **data dependency** asks where an operand came from. If `eax` is the price, find the instruction or argument that produced `eax`.
- A **control dependency** asks which comparison allowed this block to run. If a branch skipped the subtraction, determine what value controlled that branch.
- A **call dependency** asks which caller requested this operation and what arguments it supplied.

Compilers can move calculations away from the source statement that inspired them. The instruction immediately above the anchor may be unrelated, while the important value was loaded twenty instructions earlier or passed by the caller. Track one value and one decision at a time.

A practical stopping rule is: stop tracing callers when you can name the input, the decision, and the observable result in plain English. Going farther may reveal the whole menu framework, but it no longer answers the focused gold question.

### The three questions, asked once

Put the anchor from Lesson 2.5 back on screen and ask all three of them about
it. Writing `sub dword ptr [esi+0x30], eax` in the middle, each question pulls
in a different direction:

```text
        call dependency          who asked for this work?
                 |               (the caller, and what it passed)
                 v
   data  -->  sub [esi+0x30], eax  <--  control
  where did                             which comparison let
  esi and eax                           this line run at all?
  come from?
```

They are genuinely different searches, and the answers usually live in
different places. `eax` may have been loaded two instructions above, or handed
in by the caller and untouched since. `esi` is the one that matters most here:
find where it was set and you have the object the field belongs to, which is
the whole of Lesson 2.8. The comparison that guarded the block may sit
immediately above, or in the caller, having already decided this purchase was
affordable before the call was made.

Answering them one at a time matters. The common way to get lost is to chase `eax` upward, notice an interesting branch
on the way, follow that instead, and end up unable to say which question you
were answering.

<Frame caption="A branch in the code that chooses between menu operations.">

![Code branching between menu operations](/assets/images/2/5/wesnoth9.png)

</Frame>

## Restore before changing direction

Use x64dbg’s restore command after every temporary patch.

<Frame caption="Restoring the original selection after a temporary patch.">

![Restoring the original selection](/assets/images/2/5/wesnoth11.png)

</Frame>

Then verify:

1. original bytes are back;
2. the normal menu behavior works;
3. no stale breakpoint remains.

## A plain-English function sketch

The recovered behavior fits in a few lines of pseudocode:

```text
when the player chooses a menu item:
    if it is Recruit:
        check the tile
        check the price
        create the unit
        subtract gold
    otherwise:
        run the matching menu action
```

Pseudocode separates the idea from register names and addresses, so the same sketch describes the function in any build even though every address changes. Parts whose purpose is not known yet can keep neutral names instead of invented ones:

```text
if candidate_action == 3:       # Recruit in all three trials
    check unknown_flag          # the branch exists; its purpose is unknown
    call create_unit_candidate  # a unit appeared every time this ran
    subtract gold
```

## From a write to a menu rule

The gold write supplied a known starting instruction. Its return address and
call stack led to the caller; recruiting and opening Terrain Description
supplied contrasting cases for the menu branch. The small pseudocode model
names only behavior those cases supported. That route from an observed write
to a caller, branch, and named rule also works when the compiler has removed
the original source names.

That explanation names a rule, but the address of its instruction still belongs
to one run. The next question is how to find the same game state after a restart:
why addresses move, and which relationships between objects can survive the
move. Once those are clear, we can return to changing control flow itself.

---
## Lesson 2.7 — Why Addresses Move
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/2/08/
Category: Instructions, Debuggers, and Addresses
Estimated reading time: 18 minutes
Summary: Understand dynamic allocation, module bases, ASLR, and why a pointer path survives when one raw address does not.

## The disappearing-address problem

You find gold at `0x1234_5678`, restart the game, and the address is different. Nothing is broken. The address was never a permanent identity.

Two common reasons are:

- **dynamic allocation** — the game asks for memory while it runs;
- **ASLR**, short for Address Space Layout Randomization — Windows loads modules at different base addresses between runs.

Virtual addresses belong to one process. The same numeric address in two different processes can name completely different physical memory, and a freed address can later be reused for another allocation in the same process.

Every address involves three separate things, **location, identity, and lifetime**:

- a location is the virtual address used for this access;
- an identity is the game object or field that lives there;
- a lifetime is the interval during which that mapping remains valid.

An address gives only the first item. The code that uses it, the objects that
point to it, and repeated access patterns show the identity. Allocation and game events determine the
lifetime. A reusable tool must rediscover or validate the location instead of
treating yesterday's address as permanent identity.

## Relative locations

ASLR can load a module at a different base address on another run. Within one
exact executable build, a global's relative virtual address (RVA) in the image
is fixed even when the module base changes. The loader maps sections at their
defined relative locations and applies relocations where needed. Thus a tool
can rediscover the base and add the verified RVA; it must not assume ASLR picks
a new base on every launch or that a rebuilt game keeps the same RVA:

```text
module base + relative offset = current address
```

If `wesnoth.exe` loads at `0x1400_0000` and a global pointer is at offset `0x01A2_B3C0`, the current address is:

```text
0x1400_0000 + 0x01A2_B3C0 = 0x15A2_B3C0
```

`usize` is the integer type normally used for an address-sized number:

```rust
fn absolute_address(module_base: usize, offset: usize) -> Option<usize> {
    module_base.checked_add(offset)
}
```

`checked_add` returns `None` if the addition overflows instead of silently wrapping.

## Pointer chains

A stable module location may hold a pointer to an object, which holds a pointer to another object, which contains gold:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["module + offset"] -->|"read pointer"| B["player manager"]
    B -->|"+ 0x18, read pointer"| C["current player"]
    C -->|"+ 0x30"| D["gold"]
```

Each arrow that says “read pointer” means:

1. calculate an address;
2. read a pointer-sized value from it;
3. treat the result as the next address.

The last step may be a field address rather than another pointer.

Pointer size follows the target architecture. A 32-bit process stores a pointer in four bytes; a 64-bit process normally uses eight. Reading eight bytes from a 32-bit pointer field consumes neighboring data, while reading four from a 64-bit pointer truncates the address. The reader must use the target’s bitness, not the host’s.

At every link, distinguish three different numbers:

- the address where a pointer is stored;
- the pointer value read from that address;
- the field offset added to that pointer value.

Writing the chain as numbered equations makes accidental double-dereferences visible.

Walked with real numbers, the chain in the diagram above looks like this:

```text
module base                    0x1400_0000
+ root offset 0x01A2_B3C0  ->  0x15A2_B3C0    an address holding a pointer
read the pointer there     ->  0x0453_1180    the player manager

0x0453_1180 + 0x18         ->  0x0453_1198    an address holding a pointer
read the pointer there     ->  0x0691_A200    the current player

0x0691_A200 + 0x30         ->  0x0691_A230    the address of the gold field
read four bytes there      ->  250            the value you wanted
```

Notice the rhythm: add, read, add, read — and then at the last step, add and
stop. That final `+ 0x30` produces the address *of* gold, not a pointer to
somewhere else. Reading a pointer there instead would take the number 250,
treat it as an address, and try to read memory at `0x0000_00FA`.

That is the “one dereference too many” mistake, and it has a recognizable
signature: the error names a very small address. Ordinary game values —
health, gold, ammunition — are small numbers, so when one is mistakenly used
as an address it points at the very bottom of the address space, where nothing
is mapped. An error mentioning an address below a few thousand almost always
means you dereferenced a value instead of a pointer.

## Pointer scan results need checking

Cheat Engine can search for pointer paths automatically:

<Frame caption="Cheat Engine's pointer scan searches for pointer paths automatically.">

![Cheat Engine’s pointer scan feature](/assets/images/2/8/CheatEngine1.png)

</Frame>

A result is not automatically correct. Validate it across several clean restarts. Prefer paths that:

- begin inside a known module;
- use a short chain;
- work on the exact documented game version;
- end at the expected value;
- fail safely when a pointer is null or unreadable.

A pointer scan finds numeric relationships that existed in its snapshots. It does not prove ownership. Large offsets, very long chains, and links through short-lived allocations are more likely to be coincidences. Normal gameplay tests—opening menus, changing maps, loading a save—exercise those ownership assumptions.

## Give addresses a checked type

Do not scatter raw address math around a program. Give it a type:

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
struct Address(usize);

impl Address {
    fn offset(self, amount: usize) -> Option<Self> {
        self.0.checked_add(amount).map(Self)
    }
}
```

This wrapper does not prove that an address is readable. It does stop us from accidentally mixing an address with an ordinary game value, and it gives one place for overflow checks.

The operating-system call that reads another process still belongs behind a carefully reviewed `unsafe` boundary. The rest of the pointer-chain algorithm can remain safe, ordinary code.

## Walk a chain without losing the meaning

Use a function whose name says whether the final offset is dereferenced:

```rust
fn walk_to_field(
    process: &Process,
    module_base: usize,
    root_offset: usize,
    pointer_offsets: &[usize],
    field_offset: usize,
) -> anyhow::Result<usize> {
    let root = module_base.checked_add(root_offset)
        .context("root address overflowed")?;
    let mut object = process.read_pointer(root)?;

    for &offset in pointer_offsets {
        anyhow::ensure!(object != 0, "null object pointer");
        let link = object.checked_add(offset)
            .context("pointer-link address overflowed")?;
        object = process.read_pointer(link)?;
    }

    anyhow::ensure!(object != 0, "null final object pointer");
    object.checked_add(field_offset)
        .context("field address overflowed")
}
```

The final field address is returned without reading another pointer. Keeping that distinction in the function signature and variable names prevents the common “one dereference too many” mistake.

The change from loose arithmetic to a deliberate chain is easier to see as a
diff:

```diff
 fn read_gold(process: &Process, module_base: usize) -> anyhow::Result<u32> {
-    let gold = process.read_u32(module_base + root + a + b + field)?;
+    let root_address = module_base.checked_add(root_offset)
+        .context("root address overflowed")?;
+    let mut object = process.read_pointer(root_address)?;
+    object = process.read_pointer(object.checked_add(a)
+        .context("first link overflowed")?)?;
+    let field_address = object.checked_add(field_offset)
+        .context("field address overflowed")?;
+    let gold = process.read_u32(field_address)?;
     Ok(gold)
 }
```

:::note[Why this version?]
Offsets describe different jobs. `root_offset` locates
the first pointer, link offsets locate the next pointer, and `field_offset`
locates data inside the final object. Naming those stages prevents addition
from being mistaken for dereferencing. It also places an error at the exact
link that failed instead of returning one mysterious “bad address” message.
:::

  id="pointer-chain-walk"
  lab="pointer-walk"
  label="Interactive pointer-chain walkthrough"
/>

<Quiz
  id="pointer-chain-dereference"
  type="short-answer"
  title="Name the pointer action"
  prompt="What computer-science word means ‘read the address stored here, then follow it to the next object’?"
  answer="dereference"
  alternatives="dereferencing||pointer dereference"
  explanation="To dereference a pointer is to use the address it contains. In a pointer chain, link offsets usually lead to another pointer that must be dereferenced; the final field offset often leads directly to data and should not be followed again."

## Lesson 2.8 — How Pointer Paths Survive Restarts
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/2/09/
Category: Instructions, Debuggers, and Addresses
Estimated reading time: 20 minutes
Summary: Trace the player object back to a verified starting point and prove the pointer path across restarts.

## Start from behavior

Use offline, 32-bit Wesnoth 1.14.9. Find the current player's gold again and
set a write breakpoint on its four bytes. Instead of recruiting, end a turn
so income changes that value.

<Frame caption="Wesnoth's income display at the end of a turn.">

![Wesnoth’s income display](/assets/images/2/9/wesnoth1.png)

</Frame>

When the breakpoint fires, inspect the instruction that reached the gold field. In the 32-bit Wesnoth 1.14.9 build used by this book, income reaches:

<Frame caption="The breakpoint fires on the instruction that adds income.">

![A breakpoint triggered by income](/assets/images/2/9/wesnoth2.png)

</Frame>

```nasm
009B4D00  add dword ptr [eax+4], edx
```

Read that line like a sentence: “add the income in `edx` to the 32-bit number four bytes after the object in `eax`.” `eax` points at the current side record, `eax + 4` is its gold field, and `edx` contains the income.

These addresses are exact only for Wesnoth 1.14.9 32-bit. If your instruction differs, use your build’s values instead of forcing these numbers onto it.

## Trace the object pointer

Set a breakpoint on the call above the income write. At entry, `eax` is zero; after stepping over the call, it holds the side-record pointer. Step into that call on the next turn. The useful path begins with:

```nasm
mov eax, dword ptr [ecx+60]
; later, follow that pointer and add 0xA90
; the gold field is another 4 bytes into the side record
```

At `0x009AE7F7`, read `ecx`. Restart Wesnoth, recreate the same local match, and break there again. In this book’s build, `ecx` remains `0x017EECB8`. The complete path is:

```text
[[0x017EECB8 + 0x60] + 0xA90] + 0x4
```

Because `0x017EECB8 + 0x60` is `0x017EED18`, later labs use the shorter form:

```text
[[0x017EED18] + 0xA90] + 0x4
```

Square brackets mean “read the pointer stored here.” A plus sign means “move this many bytes from that address.”

## A pointer path is a route through an object graph

Each dereference moves from one object to another. The observed root
`0x017EED18` is an **absolute address for the pinned course build**, not an
RVA. Confirm that it still points into the expected module in your run. A
portable profile would store the root's RVA and first discover the module's
current base, as Lesson 2.7 explained. The heap objects reached afterward may
move between runs, which is why the path reads their current addresses rather
than saving yesterday's final address.

A path is stable only under stated conditions. It may depend on:

- the exact executable build;
- a local match being active;
- the current player or side object existing;
- the same layout and pointer width;
- each intermediate page being readable at the moment of use.

Validate every edge, not only the final gold. A non-null pointer can still be stale or point to the wrong object. Check module ranges, page protections, alignment, and a few field invariants before trusting the final value.

## Build the chain manually

In Cheat Engine, add a pointer entry by hand using the module and the offsets you observed.

<Frame caption="Adding a pointer entry by hand: the module, then each offset.">

![Adding a pointer path manually](/assets/images/2/9/wesnoth7.png)

</Frame>

Be careful about order. A displayed list of offsets may be applied from the module outward or shown in reverse depending on the tool. For this exact build, enter base address `0x017EED18`, first offset `0xA90`, and final offset `0x4`. The resolved value should equal the gold shown in the game.

<Frame caption="The finished pointer entry, resolving to the gold value.">

![The completed pointer entry](/assets/images/2/9/wesnoth8.png)

</Frame>

## Restart tests

One successful run proves very little. Test:

<Steps>

1. close Wesnoth completely;
2. start it again;
3. begin a new local match;
4. confirm the pointer entry resolves;
5. repeat at least three times.

</Steps>

Also test a state where no match is active. A good tool should report “player object unavailable,” not crash or read address zero.

## Write the algorithm before the API

The code follows this plain algorithm:

```text
read the 32-bit pointer stored at 0x017EED18
if it is null, stop with a useful error
add 0xA90 and read the next 32-bit pointer
if it is null, stop with a useful error
add the final gold-field offset
read the 32-bit gold value
```

We can model failures precisely:

```rust
#[derive(Debug)]
enum ResolveError {
    ModuleNotFound,
    NullPointer { step: usize },
    AddressOverflow,
    ReadFailed { address: usize },
}
```

Here is the resolver without any Windows API noise. `read_u32` can use `ReadProcessMemory` in an external tool or direct reads inside an injected DLL:

```rust
const PLAYER_ROOT: usize = 0x017E_ED18;
const GAME_OFFSET: usize = 0xA90;
const GOLD_OFFSET: usize = 0x4;

fn wesnoth_gold_address(
    mut read_u32: impl FnMut(usize) -> Result<u32, ResolveError>,
) -> Result<usize, ResolveError> {
    let player = read_u32(PLAYER_ROOT)? as usize;
    if player == 0 {
        return Err(ResolveError::NullPointer { step: 0 });
    }

    let game_slot = player.checked_add(GAME_OFFSET)
        .ok_or(ResolveError::AddressOverflow)?;
    let side = read_u32(game_slot)? as usize;
    if side == 0 {
        return Err(ResolveError::NullPointer { step: 1 });
    }

    side.checked_add(GOLD_OFFSET)
        .ok_or(ResolveError::AddressOverflow)
}
```

The `Result` type makes failure data we must handle, not a surprise we hope never happens.

## What counts as “stable”

The path is stable only for the target version and states you tested. The
absolute root in this example also depends on the module loading where it did
in the verified course run; a relocated module requires base-plus-RVA
resolution. Game updates can change layouts and offsets. Document:

- game version and architecture;
- module name;
- offsets in traversal order;
- the expected final type;
- how many restarts passed;
- known states where the chain is unavailable.

Chapter 3 turns this verified path into an external program. First, the final
two lessons in this chapter ask a different question: what must be preserved
when execution takes a temporary detour through new instructions?

---
## Lesson 2.9 — How Detours Change Control Flow
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/2/06/
Category: Instructions, Debuggers, and Addresses
Estimated reading time: 14 minutes
Summary: Understand how a small detour can run extra instructions and still return the game to its original path.

## The problem with replacing code

The pointer path gives us a repeatable way to find data, but it cannot add
behavior. Replacing the gold-changing instruction with `nop` was useful for
one quick test, but it could only remove behavior. What if we want to observe
values, add a check, or run several instructions and then resume the game?

A **code cave** is a spare executable area used for extra code. A **detour** redirects execution there and then returns.

The road-diversion image behind the name is worth taking literally, because
every part of it maps onto something you have to get right. You put a sign at
one junction sending traffic down a side road that rejoins the main road
further along. You have not demolished the main road, so traffic can be
restored by removing the sign. The side road must rejoin — a diversion that
just stops leaves everyone stranded, which is what a detour with no return jump
does. And the sign has to replace a whole junction, not half of one, which is
the instruction-boundary problem below.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["original code runs<br/>up to the hook site"] --> B["hook site: a jump now sits<br/>where whole instructions were"]
    B --> C["cave: save registers and flags"]
    C --> D["cave: run the extra logic"]
    D --> E["cave: restore registers and flags"]
    E --> F["cave: replay the replaced instructions"]
    F --> G["jump back to the return address"]
    G --> H["original code continues"]
```

## A detour needs five parts

A responsible detour has:

1. **hook site** — the instructions being replaced;
2. **saved bytes** — an exact copy of those original instructions;
3. **cave** — memory where the new code can execute;
4. **extra logic** — the observation or change;
5. **return address** — the first untouched instruction after the hook.

If any one is wrong, the game may crash or behave strangely.

## Instructions are not all the same size

On x86, one instruction may be 1 byte and another may be 7 bytes. A typical near jump needs 5 bytes. You must replace **whole instructions** until you have enough room.

The reason is that the CPU keeps no map of where instructions begin. It starts
decoding at whatever address it is handed and reads forward, letting each
opcode announce how many bytes it consumes. Start it one byte late and every
instruction from that point on is decoded from the wrong position.

Take the six-byte span this lesson hooks:

<MemoryStrip
  cells="0x1000=8B|=01|0x1002=8D|=74|=26|=00"
  groups="0-1:`mov eax, [ecx]`|2-5:`lea esi, [esi]`"
  caption="Two whole instructions, six bytes."
/>

A five-byte jump written over it covers `8B 01 8D 74 26` and strands the final
`00`. When the cave later returns to `0x1005`, the CPU does not see “the
leftover tail of a `lea`.” It sees a fresh byte stream beginning with `00`,
which starts a completely different instruction that swallows whatever follows
as its operands. Execution continues confidently into nonsense, and the crash
usually surfaces somewhere unrelated a few instructions later — which is what
makes this mistake so hard to diagnose after the fact.

<MemoryStrip
  cells="0x1000=E9|=??|=??|=??|=??|0x1005=00"
  marks="5"
  groups="0-4:`jmp` to the cave|5-5:stranded"
  caption="Bad: exactly five bytes copied. The cave returns to `0x1005`, and the CPU starts a new instruction at the orphaned `00`."
/>

<MemoryStrip
  cells="0x1000=E9|=??|=??|=??|=??|=90"
  groups="0-4:`jmp` to the cave|5-5:`nop`"
  caption="Good: both whole instructions covered, the spare byte filled with `nop`. The cave returns to `0x1006`, the first untouched byte."
/>

So you round up to the next instruction boundary: cover all six bytes and fill
the spare sixth byte with a `nop`. The return address is the hook address plus
the total number of whole bytes replaced.

## Follow the detour before writing a DLL

For the pinned Wesnoth 1.14.9 build, the Terrain Description menu reaches a
six-byte span at `0x00CC_AF8A`: `8B 01 8D 74 26 00`. The first two bytes
encode `mov eax,[ecx]`; the other four encode an alignment `lea`. A jump
needs five bytes, so it must cover both whole instructions and resume at
`0x00CC_AF90`, the first untouched byte.

This short x86 sketch puts code beside the flow diagram above. The two
instructions near the end replay the behavior removed from the hook site;
the final jump lands after all six covered bytes:

```nasm
pushfd                 ; save the interrupted flags
pushad                 ; save the 32-bit general registers
call extra_logic       ; observe or change something
popad
popfd
mov eax, [ecx]         ; replay the first covered instruction
lea esi, [esi]         ; replay the second covered instruction
jmp 0x00CCAF90        ; first untouched Wesnoth instruction
```

`extra_logic` is a placeholder, not a ready-to-install hook. The exact
implementation also has to verify the original bytes, encode a reachable
relative jump, and restore the patch when disabled.

Lesson 2.10 uses x64dbg to trace that route with breakpoints before adding
behavior. [Lesson 6.4](/pages/8/03/#apply-it-to-wesnoth-1149) then builds the
full DLL version: checked gold pointer path, naked x86 cave, relative jump
bytes, saved registers and flags, injector commands, F1 toggle, and restoration.
The exact code and stack diagram live beside that runnable implementation.

## Why assembly is still required

A detour begins and ends at machine-code boundaries. The surrounding program can:

- allocate and own buffers;
- calculate and verify addresses;
- decode instructions with a library;
- build a patch plan;
- restore original bytes automatically;
- expose a small safe API.

The final jump bytes and an in-process hook still require `unsafe` code and a
small amount of assembly. Typed code manages the larger, error-prone lifecycle:

```rust
struct Patch {
    address: usize,
    original: Vec<u8>,
    replacement: Vec<u8>,
}

impl Patch {
    fn is_compatible_with(&self, found: &[u8]) -> bool {
        found == self.original
    }
}
```

Before writing, compare the bytes in memory with `original`. If they differ, stop. The target may be a different version or another tool may already have changed it.

## Restore is part of the design

A patch is not complete until it has a cleanup path. Plan restoration before applying the detour:

- store the exact original bytes;
- restore them when the feature is disabled;
- restore them when the tool exits normally;
- make repeated enable/disable operations safe.

This habit will shape the wrappers we build later.

The key distinction is **lifecycle code versus boundary code**. The manager owns
the patch, validates the target, reports failures, and restores state. Assembly describes
the few CPU instructions that must run at the exact hijacked boundary.

<Quiz
  id="detour-instruction-boundary"
  type="multiple-choice"
  title="Make room for a detour"
  prompt="A jump needs five bytes, but the fifth byte lands in the middle of the next CPU instruction. What should the patcher do?"
  options="Overwrite the five bytes anyway||Move the return address back one byte||Cover enough whole instructions, save them, and replay their meaning before jumping back||Fill the instruction fragment with random padding"
  answer="2"
  explanation="The CPU decodes instructions from byte boundaries. Returning into half an instruction changes the byte stream into nonsense. A safe detour covers complete instructions, preserves their original behavior in the cave, and resumes at the first untouched instruction."
/>

## Lesson 2.10 — What a Working Detour Must Preserve
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/2/07/
Category: Instructions, Debuggers, and Addresses
Estimated reading time: 17 minutes
Summary: Build a temporary debugger-only detour, prove every hop, and restore the target.

This lesson follows the Terrain Description menu in offline, 32-bit Wesnoth
1.14.9. A six-byte instruction span in that path will become a temporary
detour. Use x64dbg to trace every hop before automating its lifecycle in
Lesson 6.4.

## Detour vocabulary before touching bytes

A **hook site** is the address where normal execution is redirected. A
**detour** is that redirection. A **code cave** is executable storage holding
the added instructions. A **return address** is the first untouched instruction
where normal execution resumes.

Some tools use the word **trampoline** for a small block that replays displaced
instructions and jumps back. Names vary, but every working detour must answer
the same questions:

```text
Where do we leave the original path?
Which complete instructions did we remove?
Where will the new code live?
What machine state must it preserve?
Where does normal execution resume?
How will every changed byte be restored?
```

The CPU has no concept of “our patch.” It only follows the instruction pointer.
A single wrong length or destination sends that pointer into unrelated bytes.

## Choose a harmless trigger

Right-click a tile and open **Terrain Description** to trigger this path. It
gives us an easy local-menu event without changing competitive or networked
behavior.

<Frame caption="The terrain-description function that the detour starts from.">

![The terrain-description function](/assets/images/2/7/wesnoth2.png)

</Frame>

Pause the game and choose a hook site with enough complete instructions for a jump. Building the detour takes five facts about that site. For the exact course build they are:

```text
Hook address:          0x00CC_AF8A
Original instructions: mov eax,[ecx] / alignment lea
Original bytes:        8B 01 8D 74 26 00
Total byte length:     6
Return address:        0x00CC_AF90
```

The byte count comes from instruction decoding, not subtraction by guesswork. `8B 01` is the two-byte `mov eax,[ecx]`, and `8D 74 26 00` is a four-byte `lea` that changes nothing and exists only as alignment padding, so the two instructions cover 2 + 4 = 6 bytes. The return address is the first byte after them: `0x00CCAF8A + 6 = 0x00CCAF90`, because `0x8A` is 8 × 16 + 10 = 138, and 138 + 6 = 144 = 9 × 16 = `0x90`.

Do not continue until the return address points to the first untouched instruction.

x86 instructions have different lengths. A five-byte jump cannot safely replace
the first five bytes of a six-byte instruction. The overwrite must end exactly
on an instruction boundary, even when that means replacing six, eight, or more
bytes and filling unused space with `nop`.

## Find a suitable cave

For this historical debugger exercise, locate executable padding inside the controlled module.

<Frame caption="Empty-looking padding near the end of the module, where a cave can fit.">

![An empty-looking area near the end of the module](/assets/images/2/7/wesnoth1.png)

</Frame>

“Looks empty” is enough for this one debugger experiment, not for a repeatable
hook installer. A detour installed whenever the game starts should allocate
its own cave, request the needed page protection, verify the hook bytes, and
release or restore everything during shutdown. Here we use existing padding so
you can see the control-flow idea before building that machinery in chapter 6.

## Build the smallest detour

Start with no extra behavior:

```nasm
; cave
; replay the complete instructions removed from the hook
jmp return_address
```

At the hook site, write a jump to the cave and fill any remaining whole bytes with `nop`.

<Frame caption="A jump written at the hook site that leads into the cave.">

![A jump from the hook into the cave](/assets/images/2/7/wesnoth4.png)

</Frame>

Set breakpoints at:

- the hook;
- the first cave instruction;
- the return address.

Trigger the menu once. You should see the breakpoints in that order. This proves the path before new logic complicates it.

## Preserve the interrupted calculation

The hook interrupts a function in the middle of its work. Registers, flags, and
stack entries may already carry values needed by later instructions.

The cave must normally:

1. save any register or flag it will change but the original code expects;
2. run the added behavior;
3. restore that machine state;
4. replay the complete displaced instructions exactly once;
5. jump to the first untouched instruction.

Replaying an instruction twice is just as wrong as skipping it. Changing the
stack pointer without undoing the change can make a later `ret` jump to garbage.
These delayed failures are why a hook may appear to work once and crash later.

<Frame caption="The breakpoint firing inside the cave.">

![The cave breakpoint firing](/assets/images/2/7/wesnoth6.png)

</Frame>

## Add one observable change

Only after the round trip works, add a tiny change such as writing a known value to the already-identified gold field.

<Frame caption="The cave with a tiny test change added.">

![A cave containing the test change](/assets/images/2/7/wesnoth7.png)

</Frame>

Trigger once, observe once, and stop. If the wrong action triggers it, your hook is too broad or your model is wrong.

## Diagnose by symptom

<Panel title="Detour symptoms">

| Symptom | Likely place to check |
|---|---|
| Crash before cave | Hook bytes or jump destination |
| Cave never runs | Wrong trigger or hook not reached |
| Crash after cave | Saved instruction or return address |
| Game acts oddly later | Register, flag, or stack state was changed |
| Runs more than once | Trigger path or re-entry assumption |

</Panel>

Change one variable per retry.

## Restore the target

Before closing the debugger:

<Steps>

1. pause the game;
2. restore the hook’s original bytes;
3. remove breakpoints;
4. verify the original behavior;
5. restore the VM snapshot if anything is uncertain.

</Steps>

The lasting result is your map of the detour, not the temporary patch.

After this debugger-only round trip, [Lesson 6.4](/pages/8/03/#apply-it-to-wesnoth-1149)
implements the same map in a DLL. It verifies the six bytes, replaces them
with `E9 rel32 90`, runs a naked x86 cave, sets Wesnoth gold to `888`, replays
the removed behavior, jumps to `0x00CCAF90`, and restores the bytes when
disabled. The complete source is also in
[`game_hooks.rs`](/windows-labs/src/windows_impl/game_hooks.rs).

<GitHub path="windows-labs/src/windows_impl/game_hooks.rs" />

Chapter 3 uses the verified addresses and types from this chapter to build an
external memory tool. The DLL hook remains a later application of this same
control-flow model.
