## Lesson 7.12 — Render Snapshots and Feature Integration
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/8/08/
Category: 3D Space, Rendering, and Tool Design
Estimated reading time: 24 minutes
Summary: Combine camera and player observations, graphics features, versioned profiles, and reversible hooks without mixing frames or losing game state.

The [tool-architecture lesson](/pages/8/10/) gave snapshots, commands,
features, and cleanup separate owners. Rendering adds a timing constraint:
positions and the camera that projects them must describe the same captured
update. A well-organized tool can still draw incorrect markers if those values
come from different moments.

This lesson applies that architecture to radar, overlays, aim analysis, and
render hooks. The snippets describe interfaces inside a combined tool; the
complete dispatcher and patch owners are linked below.


## One frame, one snapshot

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Target observer"] --> B["Validated frame snapshot"]
    B --> C["Radar model"]
    B --> D["Overlay labels"]
    B --> E["Aim analysis"]
    C --> F["Renderer"]
    D --> F
    E --> F
```

Read and validate target data once per update. Features consume the same owned
snapshot. In this excerpt, `PlayerSnapshot` is a local record of the player's
identity, position, and other validated fields; `Mat4` holds the camera
transform. Neither type borrows a pointer into the game:

```rust
struct FrameSnapshot {
    local: PlayerSnapshot,
    players: Vec<PlayerSnapshot>,
    matrix: Mat4,
    viewport: (f32, f32),
}
```

Every feature receives the same owned set of fields from one bounded
observation pass. If the radar reads the player list on one pass while the
overlay independently reads the camera matrix a few milliseconds later, the
features describe different updates, and markers can land where enemies used
to be. Bundling the fields means both features use the same captured values.
It does **not** make the reads atomic: the game can update an entity between
two reads within that pass. Validate the resulting snapshot and, if the game
exposes a tick or generation counter, check it before and after the copy or
retry when it changes.

The camera matrix and viewport travel with the players for that exact reason.
Projecting this frame's positions through last frame's camera is wrong in a way
that looks almost right — everything is drawn slightly behind where it belongs,
worst when you turn quickly, which makes it easy to blame the projection maths
instead of the timing.

`Vec<PlayerSnapshot>` is owned rather than borrowed, so nothing here points back
into the game. A feature holding a reference into an entity the game then frees
is the stale-pointer failure from Lesson 1.8, arriving through the back door.
Copy once, then let every feature read from the copy.

## Give render features a lifecycle

A radar overlay needs a different per-frame action from a recoil patch, but
both must answer the same lifecycle questions: when is it enabled, what does
it do with this frame's snapshot, and how does it undo its own changes? The
interface below makes those moments explicit for every feature:

```rust
trait Feature {
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
    fn enable(&mut self) -> anyhow::Result<()>;
    fn update(&mut self, frame: &FrameSnapshot) -> anyhow::Result<()>;
    fn disable(&mut self) -> anyhow::Result<()>;
}
```

Only patching or hooking features need setup or restoration in `enable` and
`disable`. A pure observer still implements those required methods, but they
can return `Ok(())`; its useful work lives in `update`. The owner checks the
result before reporting that a toggle succeeded.

## Model configuration with enums

Three booleans named `show_teammates`, `show_opponents`, and
`show_everyone` could all become true after a sequence of clicks. Yet the
overlay can display only one of those modes at a time. Store that choice as
one enum value, alongside the independent radar and debug switches:

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
enum OverlayMode {
    Off,
    Teammates,
    Opponents,
    Everyone,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Settings {
    overlay: OverlayMode,
    show_radar: bool,
    show_debug_values: bool,
}
```

An enum prevents impossible combinations such as three different overlay booleans being true at the same time.

## Route input as commands

A key press should request a change, not let the input thread reach into a
feature while the update loop is using it. The input side can send a small
command; the update loop then applies it to its own `Settings`. For example,
`CycleOverlay` takes `Off` to `Teammates` and eventually back to `Off`:

```rust
enum Command {
    ToggleRadar,
    CycleOverlay,
    ToggleDebugValues,
    Stop,
}

// The update loop uses true to leave the loop and enter cleanup.
fn apply_command(settings: &mut Settings, command: Command) -> bool {
    match command {
        Command::ToggleRadar => settings.show_radar = !settings.show_radar,
        Command::CycleOverlay => {
            settings.overlay = match settings.overlay {
                OverlayMode::Off => OverlayMode::Teammates,
                OverlayMode::Teammates => OverlayMode::Opponents,
                OverlayMode::Opponents => OverlayMode::Everyone,
                OverlayMode::Everyone => OverlayMode::Off,
            };
        }
        Command::ToggleDebugValues => {
            settings.show_debug_values = !settings.show_debug_values;
        }
        Command::Stop => return true,
    }
    false
}
```

The input thread sends commands through a channel. The update loop owns and
changes the settings, avoiding shared mutable globals. A `true` return means
it should stop taking frames and enter cleanup. The menu receives an
acknowledgement after an enabled feature has actually changed state.

## Contain a render feature's failure

If a frame lacks a valid projection matrix, the overlay may fail while the
radar and debug reader can continue. Each feature's `update` returns a result.
The owner records the error, marks that feature disabled, and calls its
restoration path. Subsequent updates skip it; an error message alone would
leave it running again on the next frame.

That local decision is valid only when the rest of the snapshot remains sound.
A closed process or an invalid entity list stops every consumer. A missing
camera may disable only screen projection. If a failing feature cannot restore
its hook or patch, keep that failure visible and enter the shared shutdown
path rather than treating a disabled checkbox as successful cleanup.


## Shut down in reverse order

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["stop accepting input"] --> B["signal update workers"]
    B --> C["wait for workers to finish"]
    C --> D["disable features"]
    D --> E["restore patches and<br/>graphics hooks"]
    E --> F["close handles"]
    F --> G["exit or unload"]
```

Do not unload code while another thread may still execute it. Restoration must
also happen on the thread or render boundary that owns the changed state.
Stop the worker, wait for it to finish, and remove only the hooks this tool
installed. A render callback may still be executing after the menu closes.

## Keep verified graphics facts with their target build

An offset is a fact about one supported executable, not a universal property
of an overlay. A profile joins build identity, module-relative locations,
object layouts, and expected instruction bytes. Each feature receives verified
facts from that profile rather than embedding another copy of an address.

A profile should make the supported game and version obvious. These constants join the concrete labs used by this combined tool; the complete project uses `Option<usize>` for facts a game does not need.

```rust
const ASSAULTCUBE_1202: TargetFacts = TargetFacts {
    process: "ac_client.exe",
    local_player_ptr: Some(0x0050_9B74),
    entity_list_ptr: Some(0x0050_F4F8),
    entity_count: Some(0x0050_F500),
    trigger_call: Some(0x0040_AD9D),
    no_recoil_patch: Some(0x0045_BAAD),
    radar_patch: Some(0x0040_9FB3),
    esp_hook: Some(0x0040_BE7E),
    draw_elements_hook_offset: None,
};

const URBAN_TERROR_434: TargetFacts = TargetFacts {
    process: "Quake3-UrT.exe",
    local_player_ptr: None,
    entity_list_ptr: None,
    entity_count: None,
    trigger_call: None,
    no_recoil_patch: None,
    radar_patch: None,
    esp_hook: None,
    draw_elements_hook_offset: Some(0x16),
};
```

At startup, verify an original instruction signature at every address you plan to use. The finished DLL dispatches by the current executable and exposes only hotkeys that belong to that exact game:

| Target | F1 | F2 | F3 | F4 | F5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wesnoth 1.14.9 | terrain gold cave | second-player stat text | reveal map | — | — |
| AssaultCube 1.2.0.2 | triggerbot | no recoil | reveal radar | aimbot | internal ESP |
| Urban Terror 4.3.4 | memory wallhook | OpenGL wallhack | OpenGL chams | — | — |

**End** stops the worker and restores every active patch. Flare and Wyrmsun, the offline automation targets from Chapter 4, use their dedicated in-game loops instead of this function-key table.

Load one supported profile after fingerprinting the target. Features receive
verified addresses and layouts instead of hardcoding them. If a profile has
no address for a capability, that control must remain unavailable; `None` is
not an invitation to reuse an address from another game.

The complete dispatcher and lifecycles are in [`dll.rs`](/windows-labs/src/windows_impl/dll.rs). The patch-owning primitives are in [`local_patch.rs`](/windows-labs/src/windows_impl/local_patch.rs); dropping each `LocalPatch` restores the bytes it captured only after an exact pre-patch verification.

<GitHub path="windows-labs/src/windows_impl/dll.rs" />

<GitHub path="windows-labs/src/windows_impl/local_patch.rs" />

## Check the combined render path

The complete dispatcher and feature lifecycles bring the separate effects
into one DLL, called the **multihack** in the original course. Test the
connections as well as each effect:

- radar and overlay consumers use the same captured player values;
- camera and viewport changes cannot silently mix with an older frame;
- a disabled feature is skipped until the user deliberately enables it again;
- each render callback restores the graphics state it changed;
- each hook restores only its own verified original bytes;
- an unsupported game or build exposes no active feature controls;
- shutdown waits for workers and callbacks before unloading code.

Keep a log of target, build, feature, address, expected bytes, found bytes,
action, and restoration result, separate from the visible menu. Those records
let a failed cleanup remain inspectable even after its UI closes.

The next lesson draws the menu inside the game's frame. Its placement changes;
the ownership, commands, and restoration rules still apply.

## Lesson 7.13 — In-Game Menus and Text Rendering
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/8/09/
Category: 3D Space, Rendering, and Tool Design
Estimated reading time: 36 minutes
Summary: Understand what a game's interface is made of, how its text function can draw a small menu, and why input edges, frame timing, and string lifetimes matter.

## A third option between a window and an overlay

Lesson 6.8 put the menu in its own window, which is the right default: it
cannot corrupt the game's graphics state, and you can close the game without
losing it.

But you have already met a function that draws text *inside* the game. In
Lesson 3.8 you traced Wesnoth's print function; Lesson 6.4 then used its call
site for a verified, reversible text hook. In Lesson 7.9 you called
AssaultCube's print function at `0x0041_9880` to label players. That function already knows
the font, the scale, the screen size, and the right moment in the frame to
draw. Calling it is the cheapest way to put a menu on screen, because the
hard graphics work is done and you are only supplying strings.

The trade is that you are now running inside the game's render path, so
the hook must finish quickly. A file read, sleep, or blocking channel receive
there delays the game's next frame; Lesson 4.11 measures the same cost in a
per-frame recorder.

## What a game's interface is made of

Before borrowing the game's text function, it helps to know what it sits on top of. A
game's interface is drawn by the same pipeline as its world (Lesson 7.2), in a last pass
that ignores the 3D camera: flat rectangles and text, placed in screen units.

- **Text.** A font is turned into a **glyph atlas**, a texture holding every character as a
  small image (the atlas idea from Lesson 7.2). To draw "Gold", the engine draws one quad
  per letter, each showing that letter's rectangle in the atlas, and moves along by each
  letter's **advance width**. If the advances of G, o, and l are 12, 9, and 4 pixels, the
  letter d starts 12 + 9 + 4 = 25 pixels to the right of where the G started.
- **Layout.** Elements sit in boxes. **Anchoring** pins a box to part of the screen: a
  200 × 50 box anchored to the bottom-right corner of a 1280 × 720 screen with a 20-pixel
  margin is at `x = 1280 − 20 − 200 = 1060` and `y = 720 − 20 − 50 = 650`. In a **flex**
  layout, boxes in a row share the space by weight: in a 600-pixel row, three boxes with
  weights 1, 2, and 1 get 150, 300, and 150 pixels. A **grid** layout assigns boxes to rows
  and columns, and size limits keep a box between a smallest and a largest size.
- **Scaling.** Interfaces are usually designed for a reference size, such as 1920 × 1080, and
  scaled by the smaller of `width ÷ 1920` and `height ÷ 1080`. On a 1280 × 720 screen both
  are 0.6667, so a 300-pixel button is drawn 200 pixels wide. The window's scale factor from
  Lesson 6.7 multiplies the result again.
- **Stretchable art.** A button picture with decorated corners cannot simply be stretched.
  **Nine-slice** drawing cuts it into a 3 × 3 grid: the four corners keep their size, the
  four edges stretch in one direction, and the centre stretches in both. Drawing a picture
  with 16-pixel corners as a 200 × 60 button gives four 16 × 16 corners, top and bottom
  edges 200 − 32 = 168 wide, side edges 60 − 32 = 28 tall, and a 168 × 28 centre.
- **Order and clipping.** Elements are drawn back to front by a layer number. **Clipping**
  hides whatever falls outside a box, which is how a scrolling list works: the items are
  moved up by the scroll amount, and only the part inside the list's box is drawn.
- **Input and focus.** A click is tested against each box's rectangle, the 2D picking of
  Lesson 7.5, and the topmost box under the cursor gets it. For a keyboard or gamepad, the
  game keeps a **focus**, the element that will respond, and moves it to the nearest
  element in the direction pressed. A **text box** keeps a string and a cursor position and
  receives typed characters. Sliders, checkboxes, and buttons are each a small state
  machine: a value, and whether they are hovered, pressed, or focused.
- **Popups.** A **context menu** is a box created at the cursor when the right button is
  pressed and sized to fit its items. If it would run off the screen it is moved back: a 150
  pixel wide menu opened at `x = 1200` on a 1280 pixel screen is placed at
  `min(1200, 1280 − 150) = 1130`.
- **Where it is drawn.** Most interface is drawn over the finished 3D picture. It can also be
  drawn into a texture and placed on a surface in the world, such as a screen on a wall, and
  a label that follows an object uses the projection from Lesson 7.9.

Lesson 6.8 contrasts the two ways such code is written: an **immediate-mode** interface
redraws every element on every frame from the current state, and a **retained-mode**
interface keeps a tree of elements in memory and changes them when something happens.

## Hook a per-frame site, then call the text function

The obvious idea is to hook the text function itself. That is the one thing
that cannot work:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["your hook runs"] --> B["you want to draw a menu line"]
    B --> C["you call the text function"]
    C --> D["...which is hooked"]
    D --> A
```

The hook calls the text function, and the text function runs the hook again:
recursion with no base case, the same failure as a wrapper that forwards to
itself in [Lesson 7.3](/pages/5/03/#keep-the-original-function). Every nested
call adds a stack frame, so the stack overflows while the hook is still trying
to draw its first menu line.

Hook a site that runs **once per frame** instead, and call the text function
from there as an ordinary function:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Game draws its HUD"] --> B["Your detour at a per-frame site"]
    B --> C["Replay the displaced instructions"]
    C --> D["Call the text function once per menu line"]
    D --> E["Return to the game"]
```

Lesson 7.9 already identified such a site in AssaultCube: the final print hook
at `0x0040_BE7E`, resuming at `0x0040_BE83`. Drawing there puts your lines in
the same pass as the game's own HUD, so they inherit its ordering and never
appear underneath the world.

## Reconstruct the contract before you call it

Calling a function you found is Lesson 6.1's problem, not a new one. Before
the first call, answer its four parts:

- which arguments it takes, and in what order — typically a screen position
  and a string;
- where those arguments go, which for a 32-bit game usually means `cdecl` on
  the stack, or `thiscall` with the renderer object in `ecx`;
- what it returns, if anything;
- whether it **copies** the string or merely stores the pointer.

That last question is the one that bites. If the function keeps the pointer and
draws later in the frame, a string you built on the stack is gone by then:

```rust
// ❌ The buffer dies at the end of this function. If the game reads the
//    pointer later in the frame, it reads freed stack space.
let line = format!("radar [on]");
draw_text(10, 10, line.as_ptr());
```

Keep an owned buffer alive for at least as long as the frame, and give the
function a pointer into that:

```rust
// ✅ `lines` outlives the call, and the trailing zero is explicit because a
//    C-style text function reads until it finds one.
struct MenuText {
    lines: Vec<std::ffi::CString>,
}
```

`CString` is the same tool Lesson 3.8 used at the C boundary, and for the same
reason: it guarantees the terminating zero and rejects interior zero bytes
instead of silently truncating your text.

## Colour is usually a marker inside the string

Many engines let a string carry its own formatting. The mechanism is nearly
always the same: a marker byte the renderer watches for, followed by an index
that selects a palette entry. AssaultCube uses the form feed character,
`0x0C`, followed by a digit.

<MemoryStrip
  cells="=0C|=33|=52|=61|=64|=61|=72"
  groups="0-0:marker (form feed)|1-1:palette index '3'|2-6:visible text: `Radar`"
  caption="AssaultCube's colour marker in front of the string `Radar`. The marker and index are consumed by the renderer, not drawn, so these 7 bytes show only 5 visible characters."
/>

Two consequences follow, and both matter.

The marker and index are **consumed**, not drawn, so the string's byte length
is larger than the number of visible characters. That is the same distinction
Lesson 3.8 drew between bytes, code units, scalars, and what a reader sees; a
menu that lines up columns by counting bytes will be crooked.

And the exact marker is a fact about one build. Confirm it by drawing a string
containing a candidate byte and watching what happens, rather than trusting the
number above.

## The menu itself is a small state machine

<GitHub path="rust-labs/src/bin/text_menu_lab.rs" />

Everything above is about getting characters on screen. The part that actually
misbehaves is the bookkeeping, so
[`text_menu_lab.rs`](/rust-labs/src/bin/text_menu_lab.rs)
models it in portable safe Rust with no graphics API involved:

```powershell
cd rust-labs
cargo run --bin text_menu_lab
cargo test --bin text_menu_lab
```

### A wrapping cursor underflows if you write the obvious thing

Moving the cursor up from the first row should land on the last. The natural
expression is wrong:

```rust
self.cursor = (self.cursor - 1) % self.items.len();   // ❌
```

When `cursor` is `0`, `0 - 1` on an unsigned integer panics in a debug build
and produces `usize::MAX` in a release build, which then indexes far outside
the list. Handle the boundary explicitly and the intent is visible:

```rust
self.cursor = if self.cursor == 0 { last } else { self.cursor - 1 };
```

<MemoryStrip
  cells="0=item 0|1=item 1|2=item 2|3=item 3"
  marks="0"
  caption="For example, four menu rows with the cursor on the first. Pressing up should wrap to the last row, not compute `0 - 1` on an unsigned index."
/>

<MemoryStrip
  cells="0=item 0|1=item 1|2=item 2|3=item 3"
  marks="3"
  caption="After the explicit boundary check, the cursor wraps to the last row instead of underflowing."
/>

### `GetAsyncKeyState` reports a level, not a press

Lesson 6.7 made this point about input paths and it decides how a menu feels.
`GetAsyncKeyState` answers "is this key down right now?", which is true on
every frame of one press. A menu that acts on that answer scrolls the whole
list in a fraction of a second.

What a menu needs is the *edge* — the frame where the key changed from up to
down — which means remembering the previous frame:

```rust
let pressed = current.down && !previous.down;
```

The lab test holds the key for ten frames and asserts the cursor moved exactly
one row. That is the behavior to aim for, and it is the same edge-versus-level
distinction Lesson 4.10 used for bot events.

### Build the strings without allocating every frame

The render path runs thousands of times per second. Clear and reuse one buffer
rather than allocating a fresh `Vec` per frame; the lab asserts the buffer's
capacity is unchanged after a second render.

The menu should also own only its own state. Keep the same split Lesson 6.8
used: the menu produces settings and commands, and the worker reads them. A
menu that reaches directly into game memory while the render thread is drawing
has put a second writer on the same data.

## Restore the site, not just the feature

Closing the menu is a display change. Unloading the tool is a lifetime change,
and Lesson 7.12's ordering applies without modification: stop the worker, wait
for it to leave the hooked path, restore the displaced bytes, then release the
DLL. While an in-flight frame is still executing the detour, the hook is
**draining**: no new calls should enter, but the current call must finish before
its code is removed. Lesson 6.10 established this lifetime rule for a general
hook manager; the render hook is another application of it.

<LessonVideo
  title="Combined tools running in AssaultCube"
  src="/assets/images/5/10/cube.mp4"
  duration="12 seconds"
  caption="The original multihack recording combines features from the preceding AssaultCube lessons. Compare their visible effects with the independent settings a menu exposes: changing a setting and drawing that setting are separate responsibilities."
/>

## Scope

This is the same offline, version-pinned lab used since Chapter 7, and the same
menu model as Lesson 6.8 rendered somewhere else. The transferable skill —
calling a function you recovered, with a contract you proved, from a hook that
runs at a known point in a frame — is what a debug HUD, a benchmarking overlay,
and an accessibility tool all do.

## Lesson 8.1 — Messages, Streams, and Multiplayer
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/6/01/
Category: Messages Across Networks and Processes
Estimated reading time: 25 minutes
Summary: See how a client and server turn a move into framed bytes, and why TCP transport does not define a game's message boundaries.

## Client and server

Imagine two players looking at copies of the same game board. One presses north while their character is at `(10, 15)`. Their computer can draw a possible new position immediately, but the other player cannot know about that move until information crosses the network. The server checks the move against the game's rules and replies with the accepted position, `(10, 14)`.

A **client** collects your input, sends requests, receives state, and draws what you see. A **server** applies the shared rules. Both hold their own changing game state; a message carries information between the copies.

This chapter follows that message from intent to bytes, from captured bytes
to a parsed event, and from one event to a legal session transition. A local
chat client and proxy put the pieces together. The final lessons ask how two
programs on one computer can exchange equally well-defined messages without
using a network socket.

<div class="diagram-on-dark">

![A basic client/server model](/assets/images/1/2/ClientServer.png)

</div>

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Game client
    participant S as Local test server
    C->>S: "I want to move north"
    S->>S: Validate the request
    S-->>C: "Position is now (10, 14)"
    C->>C: Draw the new state
```

The client's “move north” is an **intent**: a request for a change, not the final truth. The reply reports what the server actually accepted. If a wall blocked the move, the reply might still say `(10, 15)`, and the client would correct its display.

The client and server are not one program with a slow shared variable. The server may accept, reject, reorder, or combine requests according to its rules, while the client may predict a result before confirmation arrives. The next question is how the reply's bytes become one complete message at the other end.

## TCP is a stream

TCP is a common transport for a connection between the two programs. It delivers an ordered **stream** of bytes. A program calls `read` to take some bytes that have arrived from that stream. TCP does **not** preserve the game's message boundaries for that call.

One call to `read` may return:

- half of one message;
- exactly one message;
- one message plus part of the next;
- several messages.

Concretely: if the sender writes two length-prefixed messages back to back, the
receiver has no say in how they turn up.

```text
sent:       [00 00 00 02][41 42]  [00 00 00 03][43 44 45]

read #1 ->  00 00 00 02 41 42 00 00      one message, plus half a header
read #2 ->  00 03 43 44 45               the remainder
```

<MemoryStrip
  cells="0=00|1=00|2=00|3=02|4=41|5=42|6=00|7=00|8=00|9=03|10=43|11=44|12=45"
  groups="0-3:length 2|4-5:`AB`|6-9:length 3|10-12:`CDE`"
  groups2="0-7:read #1: 8 bytes|8-12:read #2: 5 bytes"
  caption="The 4 + 2 + 4 + 3 = 13 bytes on the wire, numbered from 0. In ASCII, `41 42` is `AB` and `43 44 45` is `CDE`. Read #1 stops after box 7, halfway through the second length field, so the receiver must keep boxes 6 and 7 until read #2 brings boxes 8 and 9."
/>

Neither read lands on a message boundary. The receiver has to hold what it has
in a buffer, remove complete messages when enough bytes have arrived, and keep
the leftover for next time. A parser that assumes one `read` equals one message
works flawlessly over a fast loopback connection while you are testing, then
breaks the moment timing changes.

This is why a protocol needs framing.

```rust
use std::io::{self, Read};

fn read_frame(stream: &mut impl Read, max_size: usize) -> io::Result<Vec<u8>> {
    let mut length_bytes = [0_u8; 4];
    // Wait for the whole header, even if it arrives across several reads.
    stream.read_exact(&mut length_bytes)?;
    let length = u32::from_be_bytes(length_bytes) as usize;

    // Check an untrusted size before allocating its payload buffer.
    if length > max_size {
        return Err(io::Error::new(
            io::ErrorKind::InvalidData,
            "frame is too large",
        ));
    }

    let mut payload = vec![0_u8; length];
    // A successful result contains one complete payload, without the header.
    stream.read_exact(&mut payload)?;
    Ok(payload)
}
```

`stream` supplies incoming bytes and `max_size` is the caller's permitted payload
limit. A successful call returns one payload as a `Vec<u8>`; a truncated header
or payload produces an I/O error through `?`. For a header `00 00 00 02` followed
by `41 42`, the returned vector contains just `41 42`. The maximum size prevents
a bad length field from requesting absurd amounts of memory. This blocking
helper also needs an appropriate timeout on a real socket so a peer cannot
make it wait indefinitely.

TCP reliability ends at delivering an ordered byte stream to the receiving socket. It does not prove the application parsed a complete message, accepted the request, saved the state, or sent a meaningful reply. Those guarantees belong to the application protocol. Define acknowledgments, request IDs, timeouts, and retry rules at that layer when the behavior needs them.

## Byte order is part of the protocol

The same integer has more than one possible byte order. Decimal `258` is
1 × 256 + 2, so as a four-byte number it has one byte worth 256 (`01`), one byte
worth 1 (`02`), and two zero bytes. Wesnoth’s four-byte frame length is big
endian, which puts the byte worth the most first:

<MemoryStrip
  cells="+0=00|+1=00|+2=01|+3=02"
  groups="0-0:× 16,777,216|1-1:× 65,536|2-2:× 256|3-3:× 1"
  groups2="0-3:1 × 256 + 2 × 1 = 258"
  caption="Big endian, the order Wesnoth sends on the wire."
/>

On little-endian x86 memory, a native `u32` with the same value would usually
appear in the opposite order:

<MemoryStrip
  cells="+0=02|+1=01|+2=00|+3=00"
  groups="0-0:× 1|1-1:× 256|2-2:× 65,536|3-3:× 16,777,216"
  groups2="0-3:2 × 1 + 1 × 256 = 258"
  caption="Little endian, the order of a native `u32` in x86 memory: the same value with its four bytes reversed."
/>

Read with the wrong order, the wire bytes `00 00 01 02` become `0x02010000`,
which is 2 × 16,777,216 + 1 × 65,536 = 33,619,968: a frame length of more than
33 million bytes. Network code must follow the protocol, not the host CPU’s default. That is why the reader uses `u32::from_be_bytes` rather than a pointer cast.

## Packets and protocols

A **packet** is a chunk of bytes sent across a network. That part is
straightforward.

“Protocol” is usually defined with words like *rules* or *agreement*, which
sound reasonable and tell you nothing. Be concrete instead. A **protocol** is
the set of specific questions both programs must already know the answers to
before a single byte means anything. There are four:

1. **Where does one message end and the next begin?** A TCP connection is one
   long stream of bytes with no natural gaps, so something has to mark the
   boundaries.
2. **What is each part of a message?** Which bytes are the length, which are the
   message type, which are the payload, and how each of those is encoded.
3. **Which messages are allowed right now?** A login reply makes no sense before
   a login request. People routinely forget this is part of the protocol at all.
4. **What happens when something is wrong?** An unknown message type, a length
   that does not fit, a message arriving out of turn.

None of that can be worked out by staring at the bytes, because none of it is
written in them. Both programs have to know it in advance. That is precisely why
reverse engineering a protocol means recovering those four answers — and why a
byte layout on its own only ever answers the second one.

:::note
📦 **Watch for:** the same bytes can be perfectly valid at one point in a
conversation and meaningless at another. A protocol model has to check *when* a
message is legal, not only what it contains.
:::

A simple framed message might contain:

```text
[4-byte length][1-byte kind][payload bytes...]
```

A typed message models the decoded meaning:

```rust
enum Message {
    Chat { sender: String, text: String },
    Move { unit_id: u32, x: i32, y: i32 },
    Ping,
}
```

This enum is a declaration fragment, not a network reader. After framing and
validation, a parser can turn a move's fields into `Message::Move` with a unit
ID and two coordinates; the game logic receives named values instead of raw
byte offsets. The bytes are untrusted until parsing succeeds.

## One message is wrapped in several layers

Several layers cooperate when the bot sends one chat message:

```text
chat meaning:      sender and text
serialization:     WML fields and tags
compression:       gzip bytes
framing:           four-byte length plus payload
transport:         ordered TCP byte stream
network:           loopback IP packets
```

**WML**, Wesnoth Markup Language, is Wesnoth’s own tagged text format for structured data — chat messages, maps, units, and more all get written as bracketed tags such as `[message]` and `[/message]` wrapping quoted `key="value"` fields. It is the serialization format this chapter keeps reversing.

When something fails, ask which layer broke. A correct TCP connection does not prove the WML is valid. A valid gzip stream does not prove the length prefix used the right byte order.

The receiver undoes the layers in the opposite order, and each step has its own
way to fail:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Bytes arrive from the TCP stream"] --> B["Framing: split off one frame<br/>using the big-endian length"]
    B --> C["Compression: gunzip the payload"]
    C --> D["Serialization: parse the WML tags"]
    D --> E["Meaning: build a typed Message"]
    B -.->|"length above the maximum"| X["Stop with an error<br/>that names the layer"]
    C -.->|"not a valid gzip stream"| X
    D -.->|"unbalanced or unknown tags"| X
```

**Serialization** turns structured values into bytes. **Framing** tells the receiver where one serialized message ends. **Transport** moves bytes between endpoints. Keeping those jobs separate makes both the explanation and the code easier to test.

<Scene name="receive-to-event" />

## Messages can feed a data pipeline

A multiplayer service handles more than packets. It may keep durable account
and inventory records in a **database**, reuse expensive results in a **cache**,
and build a **search index** for queries such as finding a match by region and
mode. Those are different access patterns: keep data across restarts, avoid
repeating work, and find selected records efficiently. They are not three names
for the authoritative state of a running match.

Processing is **asynchronous** when the sender can continue before the work
finishes. A request can enter a queue, then a worker handles it later. A queue
acknowledgment might mean “received”; it does not by itself mean “validated,
applied, and saved.” The protocol must say which stage each reply confirms.

There are also two common ways to process a sequence of events:

| Processing style | Game-service example | What it must account for |
|---|---|---|
| Stream processing | Update a match's statistics as accepted events arrive | Ordering, late events, duplicates, and how quickly the result is needed |
| Batch processing | Recompute a leaderboard from a collected set of finished-match results | Which results belong to the batch, when it runs, and how to repeat it safely |

“Stream processing” here means processing ongoing events; it does not mean the
TCP byte stream discussed earlier. A service can obtain events from many
connections, files, or queues. A batch deliberately waits for a group of data
and processes that group together. Neither approach implies that a game can
delay its immediate rules until a leaderboard job finishes.

For example, a match event might carry `match_id`, `event_id`, and a score
change. If a sender retries it after a lost acknowledgment, the receiver must
recognise the same event rather than add the score twice. Event identity and
retry behaviour belong to the model and protocol, not to whether TCP delivered
the underlying bytes correctly.

### Modularity and scaling follow the dependencies

Keep receiving, parsing, rule validation, and persistence as identifiable jobs.
Then measure where time is spent. A slow disk write, repeated full-player
search, and long logging operation need different remedies; adding workers
does not remove a shared bottleneck automatically.

Several independent matches can often run on separate workers. Within one
match, operations on shared state still need a defined order. Moving one job
to another process also adds a message boundary, possible failures, and delay.
Start with a small correct local service, preserve these contracts, and
distribute work when measurements and the use case justify it.

Bound queues as well as messages. If input arrives faster than it can be
processed, an unbounded queue consumes memory and makes results increasingly
stale. A newer position snapshot may replace an older one under a documented
policy; a one-time item grant needs different handling. That is a decision
about message meaning, not a universal “drop old data” rule.

## UDP is made of datagrams

UDP preserves datagram boundaries but does not guarantee delivery, order, or uniqueness. Fast games often tolerate those tradeoffs for time-sensitive state.

A later position update can make an older one useless, so freshness may matter more than retransmission. In contrast, a one-time inventory change may need explicit ordering and acknowledgment. Choose behavior per message kind instead of labeling an entire game “reliable” or “unreliable.”

Do not assume a game uses only one protocol. It might use TCP for login/chat and UDP for movement.

## Ports and sockets

A socket represents a network endpoint. This complete helper opens a TCP
connection to our local test server, or returns an error:

```rust
use std::{io, net::{SocketAddr, TcpStream}};
use std::time::Duration;

fn connect_local() -> io::Result<TcpStream> {
    let address = SocketAddr::from(([127, 0, 0, 1], 15000));
    // This bounds connection establishment, not later read/write operations.
    TcpStream::connect_timeout(&address, Duration::from_secs(3))
}
```

`127.0.0.1` means the same computer; `15000` selects the server's listening
port. We use loopback and a local test server for this section. A successful
result is a connected stream; framing and protocol checks still remain.

## Encryption changes what you can see

If a protocol uses modern encryption correctly, a packet capture shows encrypted bytes, addresses, sizes, and timing—not readable messages. Do not try to defeat encryption or certificate checks.

For learning, use:

- your own toy protocol;
- a local open-source server;
- captured bytes provided by a challenge;
- application logs you control.

## Captures in this chapter stay local

The capture, replay, and proxy examples use loopback or a local test server. That keeps timing, state changes, and failures observable while you learn what each protocol layer contributes.

Now that the message boundary and its byte order have a purpose, Lesson 8.2 records a real local exchange and asks which captured bytes correspond to one controlled action.

## Lesson 8.2 — Protocol Capture and Message Framing
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/6/02/
Category: Messages Across Networks and Processes
Estimated reading time: 17 minutes
Summary: Learn how a short local capture reveals message direction, boundaries, and the bytes associated with one game action.

## Separate network layers before capturing

Lesson 8.1 showed that one game message can arrive across two TCP reads. A packet capture lets us inspect the bytes on the way, but its packet rows are not automatically game-message rows. We will send one distinctive lobby message, then follow its bytes in both directions.

An application message is not the same thing as an IP packet or TCP segment.
Each layer has a different job:

```text
game protocol message   login, chat, lobby update
TCP byte stream         ordered, reliable bytes between two sockets
IP packet               routed data between host addresses
link/loopback capture   what the capture interface records
```

TCP may split one game message across several segments or combine bytes from
several messages in one segment. Retransmissions can repeat packet data. The
receiving application sees an ordered stream, so protocol parsing needs its own
framing rule such as a length prefix or delimiter.

A **socket** is an operating-system object representing one endpoint. A TCP
connection is identified by source address, source port, destination address,
and destination port—the four-tuple used below.

## Capture answers “what crossed,” not “why”

A network trace records bytes and timing at one capture point. It does not contain the sender's variable names, the receiver's interpretation, or any record of which UI action caused which packet. That link comes from changing one thing at a time:

1. capture a quiet baseline;
2. perform exactly one distinctive local action;
3. repeat the action with one changed input;
4. compare both directions and several repetitions;
5. confirm the candidate fields in the open-source client or server.

## Build a controlled capture

Use the course’s local Wesnoth server setup or your own toy client and server. Keep both endpoints inside the lab VM.

<Frame caption="A local multiplayer lobby: client and server on the same machine.">

![A local multiplayer lobby](/assets/images/6/2/bot1.png)

</Frame>

Start Wireshark, <HoverCard kind="tip" body="On Windows the loopback adapter comes from Npcap, which the Wireshark installer offers. Wireshark lists it as “Adapter for loopback traffic capture”; older versions called it “Npcap Loopback Adapter”.">choose the loopback adapter</HoverCard> when client and server share the machine, and begin capture before connecting.

Capturing on the wrong interface produces an empty-looking experiment. Traffic
to `127.0.0.1` stays on the loopback path rather than crossing the physical Wi-Fi
or Ethernet adapter.

<Frame caption="The Wireshark interface, where the capture starts.">

![The Wireshark interface](/assets/images/6/2/bot6.png)

</Frame>

## Reduce noise

Filter by the known local port. Wireshark has two filter boxes, and each has its
own syntax for the same job:

<CodeGroup sync="filter">
<Tab label="Display filter (hides rows afterwards)">

```text
tcp.port == 15000
```

</Tab>
<Tab label="Capture filter (never records the rest)">

```text
tcp port 15000
```

</Tab>
</CodeGroup>

A display filter can be changed at any time, because everything was recorded. A
capture filter keeps the file small, but a packet it dropped cannot be
recovered, so use the display filter while you are still learning what to look
for.

For the Wesnoth 1.14.9 lab, keep `15000`: that is `wesnothd`’s default listening port. Launch `wesnothd.exe`, choose **Connect to Server** in the game, and enter `localhost:15000`.

Perform the actions at known times, so each burst of packets can be matched to the action just before it:

```text
00:00 connect
00:02 enter username
00:05 join lobby
00:08 send "hello-17"
00:12 disconnect
```

A distinctive message such as `hello-17` is easier to find than “hi.”

## Direction matters

One connection has one four-tuple, and each direction reads it the other way round:

```text
client IP : client port → server IP : server port
server IP : server port → client IP : client port
```

The client port is often temporary. The server port is the stable listening port.

The server first owns a **listening socket** on port `15000`. Accepting a client
creates a separate connected socket while the listener remains available for
other clients. The client normally receives an ephemeral local port selected by
Windows.

## Follow the stream

Wireshark’s “Follow TCP Stream” view reassembles TCP bytes <HoverCard kind="tip" body="To open it, right-click any packet of the connection and choose Follow, then TCP Stream. The shortcut is Ctrl+Alt+Shift+T.">for easier inspection</HoverCard>.

<Frame caption="Follow TCP Stream shows the reassembled bytes of one connection.">

![Following a TCP stream](/assets/images/6/2/bot8.png)

</Frame>

Remember: this is still a stream, not necessarily a list of messages. Look for:

- fixed-size headers;
- length fields;
- magic bytes;
- repeated separators;
- readable text;
- compressed-looking regions;
- request/response pairs.

“Follow TCP Stream” performs reassembly for inspection. Your client still
has to handle partial reads: `read()` may return fewer bytes than requested even
when more bytes will arrive later. `read_exact` is appropriate only after a
validated frame length tells you exactly how many bytes belong to the next
piece.

Reassembly also chooses an order from sequence numbers and removes retransmitted overlap. Preserve the original packet capture alongside any exported stream fixture so later questions about direction, timing, or retransmission can still be answered.

## Export a tiny fixture

Save only the bytes for one clearly labeled action. A small binary fixture is excellent for parser tests.

```rust
#[test]
fn parses_recorded_local_chat_frame() {
    let bytes = include_bytes!("fixtures/local-chat-frame.bin");
    let message = parse_frame(bytes).expect("fixture should parse");
    assert!(matches!(message, Message::Chat { .. }));
}
```

Do not store secrets, account tokens, or other people’s traffic in fixtures.

## Compare two captures

Repeat the same action with exactly one changed input:

```text
Capture A: send "red"
Capture B: send "blue"
```

Compare lengths and differing byte ranges. If only one region changes, it may contain the text. If the whole payload changes, compression or encryption may be involved.

<Frame caption="A server message identified in the stream.">

![A server message identified in the stream](/assets/images/6/2/bot14.png)

</Frame>

## Identify the real Wesnoth handshake

Add this display filter so Wireshark shows client/server data rather than every TCP acknowledgement:

```text
tcp.port == 15000 && tcp.flags.push == 1
```

The first client payload in a Wesnoth 1.14.9 connection is exactly four zero bytes:

```text
00 00 00 00
```

Replay only those four bytes from a tiny TCP client. The local server responds with 41 bytes across the observed replies, proving that the zeros begin protocol negotiation. The next client frame identifies version `1.14.9`; the following frame logs in with the chosen username.

After the four-byte frame length, both of those later frames begin with gzip magic bytes `1F 8B`. For example, a captured version frame begins:

```text
00 00 00 2F  1F 8B 08 00 ...
└─ length 47 ┘  └─ gzip data
```

Do the same controlled capture with usernames `IEUser` and `FFFAAAKKKEEE`. The second name makes repeated-character compression easier to notice. Put together, the Wesnoth 1.14.9 connection works like this:

```text
target: Wesnoth 1.14.9 + local wesnothd
transport: TCP
server: 127.0.0.1:15000
negotiation: 00 00 00 00
normal frame: u32 big-endian compressed length + gzip(Simple WML)
login order: negotiation → version → username → lobby
```

## Capture facts the parser needs

A useful frame fixture records:

- the start of one frame;
- the field that gives its size, or another reliable delimiter;
- its direction;
- one input and the bytes that changed because of it.

---
## Lesson 8.3 — Message Parsing and Serialization
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/6/03/
Category: Messages Across Networks and Processes
Estimated reading time: 30 minutes
Summary: Connect raw chat frames to typed messages through bounded parsing, serialization, and round-trip checks.

## Parse the real Wesnoth frame

The controlled captures from Wesnoth 1.14.9 reveal this frame:

```text
u32 big-endian compressed length
gzip-compressed Simple WML payload
```

The first four bytes do **not** include themselves in the length. If the header ends in `4E`, the following gzip member is 78 bytes and the complete TCP payload is 82 bytes.

This four-byte prefix solves a problem TCP does not solve for us: message boundaries. A TCP `read` might return two header bytes now and the rest later, or it might return several complete frames together. The receiver therefore accumulates bytes until it has four, interprets the advertised length, then accumulates exactly that many payload bytes.

Big-endian means the most significant byte comes first. A length of 78 is hexadecimal `0x0000004E`, so the wire contains `00 00 00 4E`. `u32::from_be_bytes` documents that agreement directly; shifting bytes by hand would be harder to review.

The header is a claim from the sender, not permission to allocate whatever
it asks for. Compare two headers followed by four bytes currently available:

```text
00 00 00 04  61 62 63 64   -> claims 4 bytes; four are present
FF FF FF FF  61 62 63 64   -> claims 4,294,967,295 bytes
```

<MemoryStrip
  cells="=00|=00|=00|=04|=a|=b|=c|=d"
  groups="0-3:claimed length: 4|4-7:four payload bytes"
  caption="An acceptable four-byte payload: the header and available payload agree."
/>

<MemoryStrip
  cells="=FF|=FF|=FF|=FF|=a|=b|=c|=d"
  marks="0-3"
  groups="0-3:claimed length: 4,294,967,295|4-7:four payload bytes seen so far"
  caption="The header is structurally valid but exceeds the configured size limit. More TCP bytes could arrive; waiting for this advertised size is still unacceptable."
/>

The second header is four valid bytes, but its advertised size is not an
acceptable frame for this parser. Code that allocates from that claim
could request nearly four gigabytes. First reject any length above the
configured maximum; only then wait for the advertised number of payload
bytes, with a bounded buffer and a way to stop a stalled connection.
Having only four payload bytes *so far* does not by itself prove a
network frame is false, because TCP may deliver the rest later.
After a complete frame is assembled, the parser checks its exact
length before decoding it. This separates byte validation from the
later question of whether the decoded chat message makes sense.

## Keep five layers separate

A protocol message has several nested layers, and each layer has its own rule:

```text
TCP byte stream
  -> frame: one length plus exactly that many bytes
  -> compressed payload: one gzip member
  -> document: Simple WML text and tree structure
  -> game meaning: a lobby chat message
```

Each layer answers a different question. TCP delivers ordered bytes, not chat
messages. Framing finds one complete compressed unit. Gzip recovers plain bytes.
UTF-8 and WML give those bytes text structure. Only the game-level schema says
that `sender`, `room`, and `message` form a chat event.

This separation is a debugging tool. If the first four bytes advertise an impossible
size, inspect framing. If decompression fails, inspect the wrapper and payload. If
WML is malformed, inspect serialization. If valid WML is ignored by the game,
inspect the expected message fields and connection state. Calling every failure a
“packet problem” hides the layer that actually broke.

<Frame caption="Several controlled chat messages in the capture.">

![Several controlled chat messages](/assets/images/6/3/packet1.png)

</Frame>

## Read with a cursor

The four-byte length at the front of the captured frame must be read before
the compressed body, and every read must stop at the captured buffer's end.
A cursor pairs the borrowed bytes with the next unread position. If a read
fails, the position stays where it was, so an error cannot leave a parser
halfway through a claimed field:

```rust
#[derive(Debug)]
enum ParseError {
    Truncated,
    TooLarge(usize),
    TrailingBytes,
    InvalidGzip(std::io::Error),
    InvalidUtf8,
}

struct Cursor<'a> {
    bytes: &'a [u8],
    position: usize,
}

impl<'a> Cursor<'a> {
    fn take(&mut self, count: usize) -> Result<&'a [u8], ParseError> {
        // 📏 Calculate and validate the complete range before changing position.
        // A failed read therefore cannot leave the parser half-advanced.
        let end = self.position.checked_add(count).ok_or(ParseError::Truncated)?;
        let slice = self.bytes.get(self.position..end).ok_or(ParseError::Truncated)?;
        self.position = end;
        Ok(slice)
    }

    fn u32_be(&mut self) -> Result<u32, ParseError> {
        // 📦 The protocol says network byte order (big-endian), regardless of
        // the little-endian x86 CPU running the game.
        Ok(u32::from_be_bytes(
            self.take(4)?.try_into().map_err(|_| ParseError::Truncated)?,
        ))
    }
}
```

This cursor replaces direct indexing and hopeful conversion:

```diff
 fn parse_payload(bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<&[u8], ParseError> {
-    let length = u32::from_be_bytes(bytes[0..4].try_into().unwrap());
-    let payload = &bytes[4..4 + length as usize];
+    let mut cursor = Cursor { bytes, position: 0 };
+    let length = cursor.u32_be()? as usize;
+    let payload = cursor.take(length)?;
+    if cursor.position != bytes.len() {
+        return Err(ParseError::TrailingBytes);
+    }
     Ok(payload)
 }
```

:::note[Why this version?]
Network input is allowed to be short, oversized, or
malformed. Indexing panics when a boundary is wrong, and `unwrap()` erases the
difference between bad input and a programmer bug. The cursor makes failure a
normal `Result`, advances only after a successful bounded read, and lets the
caller reject hidden trailing data after one complete frame.
:::

The lifetime `'a` says every slice returned by the cursor borrows from the original input. The cursor owns only a position number; it does not copy payloads or create references that outlive the frame.

`take` is the one place that advances parsing state. It first calculates the end with `checked_add`, asks the slice for a bounded range with `get`, and advances only after both checks succeed. This gives later field readers a simple promise: success consumes exactly the requested bytes; failure consumes nothing useful and returns an error.

`try_into()` converts a four-byte slice into `[u8; 4]`, the fixed-size array required by `from_be_bytes`. The conversion can only succeed after `take(4)`, but keeping the error path explicit makes the invariant visible instead of using `unwrap()`.

Every read checks its boundary. Now decompress only the advertised bytes and cap the output:

```rust
use std::io::Read;
use flate2::read::GzDecoder;

const MAX_FRAME: usize = 1_048_576;

fn decode_wesnoth_frame(bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<String, ParseError> {
    let mut cursor = Cursor { bytes, position: 0 };
    let compressed_len = cursor.u32_be()? as usize;
    // 🛡️ Reject the advertised allocation before slicing or decompressing.
    if compressed_len > MAX_FRAME {
        return Err(ParseError::TooLarge(compressed_len));
    }

    let compressed = cursor.take(compressed_len)?;
    if cursor.position != bytes.len() {
        return Err(ParseError::TrailingBytes);
    }

    let mut decoder = GzDecoder::new(compressed);
    let mut plain = Vec::new();
    // 📏 Read one byte beyond the limit. Reaching that extra byte proves the
    // decompressed message is oversized without allocating without bound.
    decoder.by_ref().take((MAX_FRAME + 1) as u64)
        .read_to_end(&mut plain)
        .map_err(ParseError::InvalidGzip)?;
    if plain.len() > MAX_FRAME {
        return Err(ParseError::TooLarge(plain.len()));
    }

    String::from_utf8(plain).map_err(|_| ParseError::InvalidUtf8)
}
```

There are two separate size limits here:

- `compressed_len` limits how many bytes the parser accepts from the frame;
- the `take(MAX_FRAME + 1)` wrapper limits how many bytes decompression may produce.

Both matter because a small compressed input can expand into a very large output. Reading one byte beyond the limit lets the parser distinguish “exactly at the limit” from “too large” without allocating an unbounded vector.

There is a third limit outside this pure function: the connection's accumulated
input buffer. A peer could advertise a legal one-megabyte frame and then send one
byte every few seconds. The stream reader needs a maximum buffered size, read
timeouts or cancellation, and a policy for a connection that never finishes its
frame. Parsing bounds protect completed inputs; transport bounds protect the time
and memory spent waiting for them.

The trailing-byte check makes this function parse **one complete frame**. Without it, a valid prefix could hide extra bytes that the caller mistakenly ignores. A streaming connection reader should split the stream into exact frame slices first and call this parser once per slice.

Decompressing a captured chat frame reveals readable Simple WML:

```text
[message]
  message="a"
  room="lobby"
  sender="FFFAAAKKKEEE"
[/message]
```

That is the actual structure we will rebuild.

Simple WML is a tree-shaped text format. Bracketed tags open and close nodes;
quoted assignments store fields. This lesson handles the one chat-message shape
needed by our local Wesnoth proxy. If you extend the tool to inspect maps,
units, or arbitrary add-on messages, use a real tokenizer that handles escaping,
nested nodes, repeated fields, and comments instead of adding more substring
searches.

The receiver also has an expected **schema**, even when no formal schema file
exists. That schema includes field names, allowed repetitions, value types, and
which fields are required. The sender writes one version of that agreement; the
receiver reads according to the version it understands.

When a game update adds a field, ask two different compatibility questions:

- Can the new reader still understand old messages?
- Can the old reader safely ignore or default the new field?

Those questions are not the same. A tolerant tree format may ignore an unknown
optional field, but renaming a required field can break both directions. For a
versioned research tool, keep captured fixtures from every supported game build and
record which message shape each fixture uses instead of guessing that one parser is
universal.

## Compress and frame a real chat message

Use `flate2`:

```toml
[dependencies]
flate2 = "1"
```

With the gzip encoder available, the next function accepts a chat field as
text and rejects quotes or line breaks that would change the simple WML
structure. Only validated fields go into the message before compression
and length framing:

```rust
use flate2::{Compression, write::GzEncoder};
use std::io::Write;

fn simple_field(value: &str) -> Result<&str, &'static str> {
    if value.chars().any(|ch| matches!(ch, '"' | '\n' | '\r')) {
        return Err("quotes and newlines are not allowed in this lab field");
    }
    Ok(value)
}

fn encode_wesnoth_frame(wml: &str) -> Result<Vec<u8>, &'static str> {
    let mut encoder = GzEncoder::new(Vec::new(), Compression::default());
    encoder.write_all(wml.as_bytes()).map_err(|_| "gzip write failed")?;
    let compressed = encoder.finish().map_err(|_| "gzip finish failed")?;
    let length = u32::try_from(compressed.len()).map_err(|_| "frame too large")?;

    let mut frame = Vec::with_capacity(4 + compressed.len());
    frame.extend_from_slice(&length.to_be_bytes());
    frame.extend_from_slice(&compressed);
    Ok(frame)
}

fn encode_chat(sender: &str, message: &str) -> Result<Vec<u8>, &'static str> {
    let sender = simple_field(sender)?;
    let message = simple_field(message)?;
    encode_wesnoth_frame(&format!(
        "[message]\nmessage=\"{message}\"\nroom=\"lobby\"\nsender=\"{sender}\"\n[/message]"
    ))
}
```

Encoding runs the decoding pipeline in reverse:

1. validate values before placing them inside quoted WML fields;
2. serialize the typed message into UTF-8 text;
3. finish the gzip stream so its footer is present;
4. convert the compressed size to `u32` without truncation;
5. reserve one vector for header plus payload;
6. append the big-endian length and compressed bytes.

`Vec::with_capacity` is an optimization, not a safety requirement. It avoids reallocating as the two pieces are appended. `u32::try_from` *is* a correctness requirement because `as u32` could silently discard high bits for an oversized buffer.

`GzEncoder` produces the correct gzip wrapper; a plain zlib stream is not interchangeable here. The first two compressed bytes should be `1F 8B`.

Gzip and zlib can both use the DEFLATE compression algorithm but wrap it in different headers and checksums. “Same compression algorithm” does not mean “same wire format.” Matching the observed wrapper is part of implementing the protocol.

## Round-trip tests

Feed the serializer one sender and one message, then give its frame to the
decoder. If the resulting WML still contains both values, the length,
compression wrapper, UTF-8 text, and field quoting agree between these two
functions for this case:

```rust
#[test]
fn chat_round_trip() {
    let frame = encode_chat("lab-user", "hello-17").unwrap();
    let decoded = decode_wesnoth_frame(&frame).unwrap();
    assert!(decoded.contains("message=\"hello-17\""));
    assert!(decoded.contains("sender=\"lab-user\""));
}
```

Also test an empty input, a truncated gzip member, an oversized length, invalid UTF-8 after decompression, extra trailing bytes, and rejected quote/newline characters.

A round trip proves that the encoder produces something this decoder accepts. It does **not** prove compatibility by itself, because two functions could share the same mistake. Keep at least one captured fixture from the real local session and verify that the decoder accepts it. Then send an encoded message to the controlled server and confirm that another capture has the expected four-byte prefix and gzip header.

Use a small failure matrix:

| Test input | Expected failure |
|---|---|
| Fewer than four bytes | `Truncated` while reading the length |
| Length larger than remaining bytes | `Truncated` while taking the payload |
| Length above the cap | `TooLarge` before decompression |
| Valid frame plus one extra byte | `TrailingBytes` |
| Broken gzip checksum | `InvalidGzip` |
| Decompressed non-UTF-8 bytes | `InvalidUtf8` |
| Quote inside a simple field | Rejected before serialization |

<Frame caption="Comparing one changed message field.">

![Comparing one changed message field](/assets/images/6/3/packet14.png)

</Frame>

The goal is not merely to make one capture parse. It is to define exactly which byte strings are accepted and how malformed data fails.

The buildable protocol module is [`wesnoth_protocol.rs`](/windows-labs/src/wesnoth_protocol.rs). It contains bounded frame reads, gzip encode/decode, output-size caps, strict trailing-byte checks, WML field sanitation, `send_wml`, `encode_chat`, and round-trip/error tests. Both the real chatbot and proxy import this same implementation instead of copying a shortened lesson version.

<GitHub path="windows-labs/src/wesnoth_protocol.rs" />

## Read the module by responsibility

Start with the pure functions that accept and return byte vectors; they are easiest to test. Next read the exact stream functions that repeatedly call `read_exact` for a header and payload. Finally read `send_wml`, which owns the complete serialization-and-write transaction.

This order keeps three kinds of failure distinct:

- transport failure: the socket closed or timed out;
- framing failure: the advertised message length was impossible;
- content failure: gzip, UTF-8, or WML data was invalid.

Preserving those categories in error messages is part of the explanation. If everything becomes “chat failed,” a learner cannot tell whether to inspect Wireshark, the frame cursor, or the message serializer.
