## Lesson 15.1 — Why Games Need Anti-Cheat
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/15/01/
Category: Anti-Cheat: How Games Defend Themselves
Estimated reading time: 7 minutes
Summary: Separate a player's requests from the game's decisions, and connect prevention, detection, and fair enforcement.

A multiplayer game asks several computers to agree on one world. Each
player controls a **client**, the program that sends their input and draws
their view. The player also controls the machine running it. That machine
cannot be the sole authority for rules that affect everyone else.

**Anti-cheat** is the collection of controls that protects those rules from
unauthorized advantages. It includes game design, server validation,
client protection, investigation, and enforcement. A scanner alone cannot
repair a game that accepts any score a client sends.

## Requests cross an authority boundary

An **authority boundary** separates a request from the party allowed to
decide its result. In [Lesson 8.9](/pages/6/09/), a Source client predicts
movement, while the server owns the accepted simulation.

Consider a toy game with three points already earned. One uncollected coin
is worth one point. A client claims that its score is now 99. The server
ignores that claimed total. It checks whether the player's simulated
position reaches the available coin. A valid pickup removes the coin and
adds its reward: `3 + 1 = 4`.

<Scene name="server-authority" />

The boundary prevents this score manipulation even if the client display
has been changed. Detection can still help explain the attempted request,
but protecting the result does not have to wait for an account ban.

<MarginNote kind="brief">Protect the shared result first. Decide what a suspicious request means using its context.</MarginNote>

## Different advantages leave different observations

An information advantage exposes something the player should not know,
such as an opponent behind a wall. An input advantage automates decisions
or timing that the rules reserve for the player. A state advantage changes
movement, damage, inventory, or another accepted result.

Other problems involve message order and volume, account abuse, or the
game's economy. A reward request arriving twice may be a normal retry after
packet loss. The game must prevent duplicate rewards before deciding
whether the repetition was malicious.

These categories overlap. They describe the violated rule, rather than a
particular brand of tool. An accessibility device and an automation tool
may both produce unusual inputs. Policy, supported controls, and the
actual advantage matter when interpreting them.

## Prevent, detect, and respond

**Prevention** stops an invalid effect. A server rejects movement through
a solid wall or refuses a purchase without sufficient currency.
**Detection** identifies an observation worth investigating. A sequence
of inconsistent movement commands may trigger a recorded flag.
**Deterrence** makes abuse less attractive through credible rules and
consequences. **Mitigation** reduces harm while a case is being resolved.

These jobs need different evidence. A malformed request can be rejected
immediately. An irreversible accusation needs stronger support than an
unusual mouse movement. Publicly accusing a player also exposes them to
harassment, so a defender should separate internal investigation from
public messaging.

## A false flag has a cost

A **false positive** is an honest case incorrectly marked suspicious.
A **false negative** is cheating that the detector misses. Neither rate
can be understood by looking only at players already banned.

**Telemetry** is recorded information about a running system. Useful
telemetry includes the rule version, server state, command timing, and
the reason a check failed. It lets an investigator reproduce a decision
and notice when a game update changes legitimate behavior.

An enforcement system also needs corrections and appeals. Keep the
evidence needed to review a case, limit who can access it, and stop
collecting data that does not help protect the game. This chapter studies
defenses in owned offline examples. It does not require testing a live
service or another player's machine.

---
## Lesson 15.2 — What the Server Can See
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/15/02/
Category: Anti-Cheat: How Games Defend Themselves
Estimated reading time: 8 minutes
Summary: Validate commands against server-owned state, withhold hidden information, and use replays carefully.

The server receives requests and runs the shared simulation. It can see
the accepted position, inventory, cooldowns, and command history. It does
not directly see what a player was thinking or every program on their
computer. Build checks around what the server actually knows.

## Validate an action in the current world

**Validation** checks that data satisfies the rules before using it.
For a movement command, check the input's finite numeric values and allowed
range. Then simulate movement using server-owned speed, collision, and
time. A client-reported final position cannot replace those steps.

The permitted range must come from the game's rules. A knockback, vehicle,
or teleport ability changes what movement is possible. Checking only a
single speed ceiling can mistake a valid ability for cheating.

A purchase needs the player's identity, the item's current price, and
their server-owned balance. Apply the debit and reward together. Otherwise,
two concurrent requests could both spend the same old balance, like the
lost-update problem in the threading lessons.

## Bound how much work a client causes

A **rate limit** bounds work or requests within a period. Limit expensive
queries, parser allocation, and accepted actions separately. Receiving a
burst after network delay does not mean the player earned extra simulation
time.

[Lesson 8.1](/pages/6/01/) separated framing, parsing, and session rules.
Keep that order here. Reject an invalid length before allocating its
claimed buffer. Reject an action in the wrong session state before changing
the world. Handle duplicates according to the action's documented retry
rules.

Record the original server timing as well as the command's claimed timing.
Source's lag-compensation checks in Lesson 8.9 illustrate why the server
must bound and compare those claims rather than accepting arbitrary history.

## Withhold information the client does not need

**Fog of war** is a disclosure rule: hide game information until the player
is entitled to observe it. A server that sends every hidden enemy position
and merely hides the corresponding drawing has already disclosed the data.

In the toy picture, a wall blocks the observer's sightline. The server
knows the enemy's position but sends none to this client. The enemy moves
above the wall. Only after the new sightline clears the wall does its
position enter the client's observation.

<Scene name="server-visibility-filter" />

Real visibility systems must account for more than this one line.
Animation, sound, team information, latency, and other players' perspectives
can make an entity relevant. Reveal it early enough to avoid visible
pop-in, but do not disclose unrelated hidden state.
[Lesson 7.8](/pages/5/08/) applies the same ownership rule to radar markers.

<MarginNote kind="alternative">Ask what the client needs to draw now. Construct that observation on the server before sending it.</MarginNote>

## Replays preserve useful context

A **replay** records enough accepted state and input to inspect a past
sequence. Store the game version and timing rules alongside it. A video
from one client can omit information available to the server and include
prediction or interpolation differences.

Replay review helps distinguish an impossible state from an unusual but
legal tactic. It also reveals what a check was unable to observe. A replay
that omits raw input edges cannot prove the timing of those omitted edges.

**Machine learning** fits a model to examples instead of using only hand-
written rules. It can rank large numbers of replay segments for review.
Its training labels can contain mistakes, and a new game update can change
the input distribution. Test on held-out legitimate matches, different
devices, and the updated game. A model score is a signal with measured
limits, not an explanation of guilt by itself.

---
## Lesson 15.3 — Server Plugins, Counters, and False Flags
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/15/03/
Category: Anti-Cheat: How Games Defend Themselves
Estimated reading time: 10 minutes
Summary: Read Macrodox and other SourceMod designs as measurement systems, separating button edges, weighted history, and enforcement.

**SourceMod** lets a Source server run plugins that observe game events and
player commands. A plugin is code loaded through the server's supported
extension system. It sees the engine's reported state and the inputs
reaching that server. It does not gain a trustworthy view of all client
software.

The command boundary from [Lesson 8.9](/pages/6/09/) explains both its power
and its limits. A plugin can compare movement requests with accepted state.
It cannot conclude which program created a request from its timing alone.

## Macrodox counts button edges

The inspected Macrodox version is 1.9, from the source supplied for this
book revision. Its original forum discussion describes a detector built
for Counter-Strike: Source bunnyhop servers. **Bunnyhopping** chains jumps
to maintain movement speed under a game's movement rules.

Macrodox remembers whether a player's jump button was already held. A new
press increments its counter only when the input changes from released
to held. Repeated commands with the same held button do not each become
a new press.

For the five toy samples `0, 1, 1, 0, 1`, zero means released and one means
held. The first `0 → 1` adds one press. The second consecutive one adds none.
The later release allows the final `0 → 1` to add another. There are two
fresh presses, because there are two rising edges.

<Scene name="detector-input-window" />

A **rising edge** is that transition from zero to one. Separating levels
from edges matters in ordinary game input too. A held key can span many
commands while describing one physical press.

## Its histories answer different questions

At a game-reported jump event, Macrodox records the counted presses and
horizontal speed. It retains a circular array of recent jump counts.
A **circular array** reuses its oldest slot when the write position reaches
the end. The inspected declaration reserves 30 slots; that is a chosen
storage capacity, not a universal detection rule.

Other measurements use a **weighted average**, which gives older and newer
observations different influence. The source updates these averages with
`(old × 9 + sample) ÷ 10`. Dividing each term by ten shows the weights:
`0.9 × old + 0.1 × sample`.

For an illustrative old value of `0.5` and a new sample of `1`, the result
is `(0.5 × 9 + 1) ÷ 10 = 5.5 ÷ 10 = 0.55`. The older value still contributes.
This is not a ratio computed over exactly the last fifteen jumps.

The perfect-jump measurement samples fresh presses using the previous and
current ground state. A press on the transition to grounded contributes
one; a press after remaining grounded contributes zero. Other command
states do not automatically contribute another sample. The circular log
and this weighted measurement therefore have different meanings.

<MarginNote kind="brief">A recent-history array, a weighted score, and a consecutive counter are different measurements. Define which one a rule uses.</MarginNote>

## Context can change an apparently perfect pattern

The Macrodox discussion warns against combining it with automatic-jump
plugins. Such a plugin changes legitimate input behavior. Map conditions
and timing also affect what the detector observes. A goal of eliminating
false positives does not establish that the goal was achieved.

The inspected code queues flagged identities in a file and applies actions
on configured map cycles. Persisting an identity helps a server restart
retain a decision. It does not strengthen the underlying measurement.
Before an irreversible action, preserve the relevant trace, map, settings,
and detector version for review.

## Other plugins expose the same maintenance problem

SourceMod Anti-Cheat, or **SMAC**, divides checks into modules. An inspected
SMAC fork's February 2025 changelog removed a console-variable check after
a game update because the older rule could falsely ban players. A detector
must follow the rules of the game version it is protecting.

**Little Anti-Cheat**, also called Lilac, documents a case where scroll-wheel
attack input can trigger an autoshoot heuristic. Its original repository
was archived in September 2024. An archived detector can teach a design,
but it does not promise maintenance for later game updates.

The supplied CowAntiCheat case combines command counters, view changes,
server state, and client-reported settings. A client report must never be
allowed to disable a server check. A missing or unusual report calls for
separate handling. It does not prove either innocence or cheating.

A **threshold** is a chosen cutoff for a decision. Test thresholds against
legitimate trace data, including permitted devices and server settings.
Permanent bans and public accusations need more support than a heuristic
crossing its cutoff. These case studies explain measurements and their
failure modes; their implementation and tuning recipes are not reproduced.

---
## Lesson 15.4 — What Client Protection Can See
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/15/04/
Category: Anti-Cheat: How Games Defend Themselves
Estimated reading time: 8 minutes
Summary: Connect local integrity checks and kernel protection to boot trust, driver risk, privacy, and reliability.

Server validation protects accepted results. It cannot directly inspect
every change inside a player's local process. **Client protection** adds
observations on that machine, including file integrity, loaded code, and
access to the game process.

## User-mode checks inspect a limited view

**User mode** is the operating system's restricted execution environment
for ordinary applications. A local protection component can compare game
files with trusted hashes, inspect loaded modules, or record permitted
process-access events. Its permissions and operating-system interfaces
limit what it can observe.

A **handle** grants access to an operating-system object, such as a process.
An unexpected process with game-memory access can be relevant to an
investigation. A handle's existence alone does not establish a cheat.
Debuggers, crash reporters, and permitted overlays can also interact with
processes. Check the access rights, provenance, and game's supported tools.

[Lesson 13.3](/pages/13/02/) separates integrity checks from the trust in
the checking code. If a local checker and its reference are both under an
adversary's control, its successful report cannot establish an independent
truth. [Lesson 13.4](/pages/13/03/) makes the same distinction for debugger
signals: an observation and an enforcement decision are different jobs.

## Kernel privilege adds visibility and responsibility

The **kernel** is the operating system's privileged core. A **kernel driver**
is code loaded into that environment to perform operating-system services.
It can observe or enforce some boundaries unavailable to an ordinary
application. See [Lesson 12.6](/pages/11/05/) for this trust boundary.

That privilege also increases the consequences of a defect. A bad memory
access can crash the system rather than just the game. A vulnerable driver
can expose dangerous operations to other software. Signing identifies an
approved publisher and protects the signed bytes against alteration; it
does not prove that their implementation is free of security bugs.

Microsoft's vulnerable-driver blocklist illustrates an additional loading
policy. A known vulnerable signed driver can be refused even though its
signature is valid. An allowed driver still requires maintenance and
compatibility testing.

<Scene name="driver-trust-gate" />

Trend Micro documented ransomware abuse of a vulnerable Genshin Impact
anti-cheat driver. The lesson is broader than one game: a privileged
security component can become a security liability if its exposed
operations are unsafe. Driver revocation, updates, constrained interfaces,
and operating-system protections all matter.

## Boot trust and attestation answer narrower questions

Loading protection at boot can help it observe the environment before the
game starts. Loading it with the game limits its lifetime. Neither timing
choice makes privileged code infallible. A product may support different
modes on systems with different security guarantees.

**Secure Boot** checks that the boot chain uses components authorized by
the configured signing policy. A **Trusted Platform Module**, or **TPM**,
can retain protected keys and record boot measurements. A measurement is a
record of what was loaded, commonly represented by cryptographic hashes.

**Attestation** is a verifiable report about measured system state. A
verifier checks the signing identity, expected measurements, and a fresh
challenge so an old report cannot be reused as a current one. The protocol
must also bind the report to the intended session. The hash and signature
distinction from [Lesson 9.8](/pages/9/07/) applies here.

Such a report can support a claim about a measured boot environment. It
does not prove that every later action is fair, or that all possible
software and hardware behavior was measured. Server-owned rules remain
necessary.

<MarginNote kind="brief">More local privilege expands what protection can inspect. It also expands the damage its own defects can cause.</MarginNote>

## Collect what the defense needs

Protection should document its lifetime, privileges, collected information,
retention, and uninstall behavior. Limit collected data to its stated
purpose. Test updates against supported hardware and software, with a
recovery path for failures.

Privacy and reliability are engineering constraints. A protection system
that repeatedly crashes honest players or cannot explain its data use
weakens trust in the game it is trying to protect.

---
## Lesson 15.5 — How Detections Work
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/15/05/
Category: Anti-Cheat: How Games Defend Themselves
Estimated reading time: 8 minutes
Summary: Compare detector signals and count the real people behind a false-positive rate.

A detector turns observations into a signal. To assess that signal, ask
what was observed, what rule matched, and how often it makes mistakes in
the population where it runs. Its output is not automatically a verdict.

## Different signals measure different things

A **signature detector** matches a known pattern. A byte signature can
identify a known code sequence, as in [Lesson 5.4](/pages/7/04/). A file hash
can identify exact bytes. Matching a pattern is only as meaningful as its
uniqueness and the trust in the observation.

A **heuristic** is a rule based on an expected pattern rather than an exact
identity. Repeated input timing or an unlikely view change might trigger
one. Legitimate devices, accessibility controls, or gameplay changes can
also produce that pattern.

A **behavioral detector** studies actions over time. It may compare input
edges, aiming transitions, or movement consistency. A statistical model
describes the distribution of these observations. A machine-learning
model learns relationships from labeled examples. Both need evaluation
on legitimate cases outside the data used to build the model.

An **integrity signal** compares observed state with an expected reference.
Hardware and account signals describe another part of the environment or
its history. A new account or private profile is not itself proof of an
unfair game action. Combining signals requires attention to what each
actually measures.

## Count a rare event before trusting a flag

The **base rate** is how common a condition is in the population being
tested. Use a hypothetical population of 100,000 players. Assume one in
1,000 cheats. Then `100,000 ÷ 1,000 = 100` cheat, and
`100,000 − 100 = 99,900` are honest.

Now assume the detector catches 99 percent of cheaters and wrongly flags
1 percent of honest players. These are chosen teaching assumptions, not
claims about a real anti-cheat product.

Among the 100 cheaters, `0.99 × 100 = 99` are caught. The remaining
`100 − 99 = 1` is missed. Among the 99,900 honest players,
`0.01 × 99,900 = 999` are wrongly flagged. The remaining
`99,900 − 999 = 98,901` are correctly left unflagged.

The flagged group therefore contains `99 + 999 = 1,098` people. Only
`99 ÷ 1,098 ≈ 0.0902`, or about 9 percent, are cheating.

<Scene name="detector-base-rate" />

The picture groups nine flagged people into each dot. Nine is chosen
because it divides both flagged counts exactly: `99 ÷ 9 = 11` dots for cheating,
and `999 ÷ 9 = 111` dots for honest players. Together they make 122 dots. It depicts
the flagged group, rather than every person in the original population.

**Detection precision** is the fraction of flags that are correct. In this example
it is about 9 percent, even though the detector catches almost all cheaters.
**Detection recall** is the fraction of cheaters caught: here `99 ÷ 100 = 99%`.
The two numbers answer different questions.

<MarginNote kind="brief">A small error rate applied to a large honest population can produce more false flags than true ones.</MarginNote>

## Match the response to the evidence

A hard rule violation, such as an impossible purchase against server-owned
inventory, can be prevented immediately. A weak behavioral flag can send a
trace for review without publicly naming the player.

Rechecking with another observation can help, but its errors may be
correlated with the first check. Two models trained on the same mislabeled
examples are not two independent witnesses. Measure the combined decision
on real legitimate cases instead of multiplying error rates by assumption.

Delaying enforcement can allow further validation and group related cases.
It also leaves time for harm, so prevention and mitigation must continue.
Human reviewers need the trace and its context, clear decision criteria,
and a way to correct mistakes. A human verdict is not automatically
error-free either.

---
## Lesson 15.6 — Layers, Trust, and Review
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/15/06/
Category: Anti-Cheat: How Games Defend Themselves
Estimated reading time: 7 minutes
Summary: Combine game, platform, league, and server observations without treating duplicated reports as independent proof.

A match can have several protection layers. The game validates its rules.
A platform provides account and service signals. A league may add its own
client requirements and review process. A community server may run plugins
with local policies. These layers need not see the same facts or impose
the same consequences.

## Know which observation a layer owns

The game server knows its accepted inventory and simulation. Client
protection sees parts of the local software environment. An account service
can know historical enforcement records. A replay reviewer sees whatever
the recording retained. Each observation has a time, scope, and source.

**Provenance** records where information came from and how it was obtained.
Keep the originating event identifier, game version, server state, and
detector version when forwarding a signal. Otherwise, a later service may
misinterpret a copied report as a new measurement.

## Three reports can describe one event

Label a toy event A. The game logs it, a plugin forwards it, and a player
report references it. That creates three notifications. Their common
origin means they still describe one event.

<Scene name="evidence-correlation" />

A later event B adds another observation. Now there are two distinct
events. Distinct does not automatically mean statistically independent:
both might have been affected by the same game bug or network condition.

**Correlation** means observations vary together. When several detectors
share inputs or assumptions, their mistakes can occur together too. Count
unique events and evaluate the combined policy on legitimate cases. Do
not turn a copied signal into extra confidence merely by routing it
through additional services.

<MarginNote kind="alternative">Preserve the original event identity across services. Combine its context before deciding how much weight it deserves.</MarginNote>

## Matchmaking risk is different from a cheating verdict

A **trust score** summarizes risk or expected match quality for a policy.
It may guide matchmaking or prioritize review. It is not necessarily an
assertion that the account cheated in a particular match.

Valve's published CS:GO Trust Factor explanation illustrates that
distinction: it describes matchmaking using account and play observations,
while leaving changing details undisclosed. An account score does not
replace a rule-specific explanation for an enforcement decision.

New accounts, shared hardware, changing devices, and unusual but permitted
play can complicate such signals. Keep the scope of a consequence tied to
the evidence and documented rules. A community server's local removal is
different from a platform-wide sanction.

## Delayed enforcement has tradeoffs

A **ban wave** applies accumulated enforcement decisions in a batch.
Grouping cases can give investigators time to validate them and make
immediate detector feedback less revealing. The delay also allows further
harm unless other controls prevent or mitigate it.

Use durable case records and preserve the rule version that made each
decision. If an update causes a false-positive cluster, pause the affected
enforcement rule, investigate its shared cause, and correct affected cases.
A general recovery process should exist before a large batch is applied.

Review queues need clear prioritization and limited data access. A report
can be valuable without being sufficient evidence for a ban. Repeated
reports from the same source or the same incident should not automatically
increase the penalty. The purpose of layering is to add useful coverage
and context, not to hide responsibility behind a majority of flags.

---
## Lesson 15.7 — Cheat Categories from the Defender's Side
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/15/07/
Category: Anti-Cheat: How Games Defend Themselves
Estimated reading time: 8 minutes
Summary: Connect different locations of unauthorized code and automation to the observations and boundaries a defender can use.

A defender benefits from knowing where an unfair advantage originates.
That location affects which observations and protections are available.
It does not change who should own the game's accepted results.

## Process location changes local observations

An **external** tool runs outside the game process. An **internal** tool
runs code inside it. Depending on permissions and operating-system
interfaces, a defender may observe process access, loaded modules, or
unexpected integrity changes. Legitimate development and accessibility
software can create some of the same observations.

**Cheat Engine** is a development and modding tool with memory inspection,
debugging, and scripting capabilities. Those capabilities can be useful in
an owned offline program, like the memory examples earlier in this book.
The presence of a general-purpose tool is different from proving an unfair
action in a protected match. Nor does changing client memory automatically
change the server's inventory or simulation.

Do not assume that a project having publicly visible source settles every
license or distribution question. Check the actual components and current
terms before redistributing software. This lesson studies tool categories;
it does not ask you to install or use them against protected games.

## Privilege is one boundary, information is another

**Kernel-assisted** abuse uses privileged operating-system code. It expands
the local access problem described in Lesson 15.4. Defenders can combine
driver policy, integrity protections, updates, and server validation.
These controls cover different parts of the problem.

**Direct memory access**, or **DMA**, lets hardware devices transfer memory
without having the CPU copy every byte. [Lesson 12.7](/pages/11/06/) explains
why device access needs isolation. An **IOMMU**, an input-output memory
management unit, restricts which memory regions a device can access under
the configured policy. Firmware and operating-system configuration affect
whether that protection is actually in place.

Neither greater software privilege nor device access creates a hidden
server value that was never sent. In the picture, the server sends the
player's own health but excludes an unrelated hidden enemy. Observing the
client's received memory yields only the available information.

<Scene name="information-boundary" />

This is why local protection and server disclosure rules complement one
another. Audit other channels too. Sounds, event messages, timing, or team
updates can reveal information that one position filter withheld.

## Screen-based automation changes the observation problem

**Computer vision** extracts information from images. A vision-based
automation system can act on the ordinary game view and emulate input.
It may not need access to the game's internal memory.

The server still sees resulting commands and their timing. Behavioral
signals, supported-input policy, and review can contribute evidence.
Unusual input consistency also occurs with some permitted devices, so a
pattern alone needs legitimate-device testing and context.

<MarginNote kind="brief">Defend the result and the information boundary as well as the location of code. Different tool categories can produce similar commands.</MarginNote>

## Network and asset changes need their own controls

Network abuse can involve invalid messages, repeated requests, excessive
work, or inconsistent session claims. Parse bounded input, authenticate
the session, validate actions against current state, and define retry
behavior. A cryptographically protected connection does not make the
authenticated player's requests truthful.

An **asset** is stored game content such as a model, texture, or sound.
Unauthorized replacement can change the information or visibility a game
intends to provide. A server can require an approved asset set where the
rules call for it. Use signed manifests and trusted references rather than
letting the client select both the content and the expected checksum.
See [Lesson 9.8](/pages/9/07/).

Permitted mods have a separate policy and supported loading path. They
should not be silently treated as cheating merely because their bytes
differ from the stock installation. Define the protected mode, authorized
extensions, and review procedure before interpreting a local mismatch.

---
## Lesson 15.8 — Anti-Cheat in Modern Games
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/15/08/
Category: Anti-Cheat: How Games Defend Themselves
Estimated reading time: 8 minutes
Summary: Compare documented protection boundaries and lifetimes without treating product names as proof of effectiveness.

This comparison was checked on **October 5, 2026**. Products change their
requirements, supported games, and detection systems. The examples show
documented architecture, rather than a ranking or a guarantee that any
particular match is free of cheating.

## VALORANT and Vanguard

Riot describes Vanguard as a game-time client component and a kernel
driver. Its traditional mode starts the driver at boot so protection can
observe the environment before the game client starts.

On June 24, 2026, Riot announced optional **on-demand** sessions for
sufficiently secured PCs. In this mode, protection starts with a Riot
game and runs while it is being played. The published prerequisites include
an appropriate Windows version, Secure Boot, a TPM, virtualization-based
security, code-integrity protection, and an IOMMU. Boot-managed operation
remains a different mode; it is inaccurate to describe every Vanguard
installation as always starting at boot.

VALORANT also illustrates why client protection cannot replace server
design. Its server-side visibility policy limits hidden information sent
to a client. Local privilege and server disclosure are separate controls.

## Protection lifetime is a concrete difference

A kernel component's privilege describes what it may access. Its lifetime
describes when it runs. The two properties are separate. The diagram
compares illustrative boot-managed and session-managed lifetimes. Its
animation time is slowed for viewing, rather than measuring a real boot.

<Scene name="protection-session" />

The bars preserve the period each component was active. Ending a
session-managed monitor when the game stops does not mean it had lower
privilege while the game was running.

## Counter-Strike and Valve's layers

**VAC**, Valve Anti-Cheat, contributes client-side detection and server
enforcement of VAC status. The game still needs its own validation and
review systems. The public material does not provide a complete recipe for
VAC or VAC Live detections, so do not infer one from a product label.

Valve's August 19, 2024 update described initial limited-match testing of
VacNet 3.0 and asked for details of incorrectly cancelled matches. That
dated announcement does not establish a universal current rollout or a
measured detection rate.

Valve's April 25, 2024 Counter-Strike 2 notes added an **Overwatch** system
for match-demo review by trusted partners. This is a dated description of
review support, not a promise that every account can access the old CS:GO
review interface.

The earlier CS:GO **Trust Factor** documentation describes matchmaking
using account and play observations, with changing factors left
undisclosed. Matchmaking risk, detection, and a reviewed sanction are
different decisions. A historical FAQ cannot establish today's internal
CS2 scoring formula.

## Call of Duty and RICOCHET

Activision's current description combines server-side systems and
investigation with a PC kernel driver. It states that the driver operates
only while a protected Call of Duty title runs, and monitors software
interacting with those titles.

Server-side protections can also affect console players through shared
services and cross-play. The presence of a PC driver does not imply that
every participant uses the same local component.

## Easy Anti-Cheat and BattlEye

Epic's **Easy Anti-Cheat** integration through Epic Online Services supports
client-server and peer-to-peer architectures. In client-server mode, game
network code carries opaque messages between the client and server
protection modules. **Opaque** means the game transports the data without
interpreting its internal format. The developer still owns game-rule
validation and must integrate the required session and message lifecycle.

BattlEye describes user-mode and kernel-mode protection, proactive
prevention, and detection. These descriptions establish parts of its
design, rather than an independent measurement of how well it protects
every supported title.

<MarginNote kind="alternative">Compare what a system sees, when it runs, and who owns the decision. Marketing names do not answer those questions alone.</MarginNote>

A useful comparison also includes supported platforms, privacy, reliability,
appeals, and the game's own authority model. Public ban counts lack the
undetected cases and legitimate population needed to calculate precision
or recall. Lesson 15.5 explains those missing denominators.

---
## Lesson 15.9 — Designing a Game That Is Hard to Cheat In
Canonical page: https://mustcodeal.github.io/rust-game-hacking-book/pages/15/09/
Category: Anti-Cheat: How Games Defend Themselves
Estimated reading time: 8 minutes
Summary: Place authority, disclosure, retries, evidence, and permissions into the game's design from the beginning.

The strongest defense often removes an opportunity before a detector is
needed. Decide who owns each result, what a client may learn, and what
must happen when a request is repeated or delayed.

## Write the rule at its owning boundary

An **invariant** is a condition that must remain true across valid
operations. Examples include an item being consumed at most once, a
balance remaining within its permitted range, or a purchase granting only
the reward paid for.

Put these rules beside the state they protect. A user-interface check can
improve feedback, but it cannot replace the server's purchase validation.
An authenticated session establishes the requester; it does not establish
that every requested action is permitted.

Check object ownership and current state when applying an action. A valid
earlier snapshot can become stale before the request arrives. A pickup
observed by two players still represents one available world object.

## Make retries safe

**Idempotence** means repeating an operation has the same effect as applying
it once. Network retries are common when a reply is lost. Reward operations
need an identity and a committed result so the same request cannot earn
another reward.

The toy server owns one coin, labelled C, and begins at score zero. The
first permitted pickup consumes C and adds one point: `0 + 1 = 1`. A later
delivery repeats that pickup. The server finds its committed result and
returns it without adding another point.

<Scene name="validated-pickup" />

Commit the reward and consumption together. If another request can run
between the availability check and consumption, both might observe an
available coin. Use the appropriate transaction or synchronization for
the owning system. Remember that a transaction's scope must include all
state needed to preserve the invariant.

Repeated delivery here explains a normal network condition. Handling it
safely is better evidence of sound design than treating every retry as a
reason to ban its sender.

## Keep observations small and relevant

Construct each client's permitted observation on the server. Include
information needed for responsive presentation, but exclude unrelated
hidden state. A label hidden on screen is not information removed from
client memory.

Bound parsing, queued work, history, and requests per client. Use explicit
overflow and disconnect policies. Test normal delays, packet duplication,
lost replies, and concurrent actions in a synthetic offline harness.
Those cases expose trust and lifetime errors without requiring a real
cheater or a live service.

Keep authoritative records distinct from predictions and presentation.
That distinction lets a reviewer understand whether a mismatch changed the
shared world or merely corrected a local view.

## Plan enforcement and recovery together

Record the reason, rule version, and context for a decision. Minimize
personal data and restrict access to case records. Preserve enough
information for a correction without retaining unrelated private content.

Start new heuristic rules in an observation mode against representative
legitimate play. Inspect error clusters after game and device updates.
Have a way to stop a faulty enforcement rule and correct its consequences.
Deploying more privileged protection does not remove that responsibility.

<MarginNote kind="brief">A repeatable decision and a recovery path protect honest players as well as the game.</MarginNote>

## Permissions remain part of the project

Keep learning experiments inside programs, captures, servers, and mods
you own or have explicit permission to test. Written scope should identify
the systems, allowed data, permitted actions, and when testing stops.
Do not collect other players' private data to make a lesson example.

Technical access does not settle copyright, license, contract, privacy,
or computer-access questions. These depend on the applicable rules and
permissions. Verify the actual license and terms for the work you intend
to distribute; seek appropriate advice for consequential legal decisions.
The defensive designs here do not require claims about the outcome of a
particular lawsuit or permission to interfere with an online match.

If you discover a defect in an authorized test, preserve a minimal
reproduction and report it through the owner's stated process. Share only
the data needed to explain the problem. A reliable fix, bounded evidence,
and a clear permission boundary complete the engineering work.

  <section class="glossary-group" aria-labelledby="glossary-numbers">
    <div class="glossary-group__letter"><h2 id="glossary-numbers">0–9</h2><a href="#glossary-top">Top</a></div>
    <dl class="glossary-list">
      <dt id="term-2d"><dfn>2D</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Two-dimensional: a position needs two coordinates, usually horizontal <code>x</code> and vertical <code>y</code>. Screen pixels, menus, and tile maps are common 2D spaces.</dd>
      <dt id="term-3d"><dfn>3D</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Three-dimensional: a position needs three coordinates. A 3D engine transforms points through several coordinate systems before they become 2D pixels.</dd>
      <dt id="term-32-64-bit"><dfn>32-bit / 64-bit</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The width of the architecture and its usual pointer size. A 32-bit process normally uses four-byte pointers; a 64-bit process normally uses eight-byte pointers. This changes layouts, addresses, registers, and which DLL can load.</dd>
    </dl>
  </section>

  <section class="glossary-group" aria-labelledby="glossary-a">
    <div class="glossary-group__letter"><h2 id="glossary-a">A</h2><a href="#glossary-top">Top</a></div>
    <dl class="glossary-list">
      <dt id="term-a-star"><dfn>A*</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">A-star</span></dt>
      <dd>A graph-search algorithm that combines the cost already paid with a heuristic estimate of the cost remaining. With an admissible heuristic it finds a cheapest path; unlike breadth-first search, it can aim toward promising nodes.</dd>
      <dt id="term-abi"><dfn>ABI</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Application Binary Interface</span></dt>
      <dd>The machine-level agreement between compiled pieces: register use, stack layout, calling convention, type layout, symbol naming, and more. An <a href="#term-api">API</a> describes how source code calls something; an ABI describes how the resulting machine code fits together.</dd>
      <dt id="term-abstraction"><dfn>Abstraction</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A simpler interface that hides details behind a promise. A safe memory reader can expose “read this typed value” while containing handle management, byte counts, and raw pointers internally.</dd>
      <dt id="term-access-mask"><dfn>Access mask</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A bit field describing requested or granted operations on a Windows object. Ask for the smallest set needed; a process handle is not simply “open” or “closed,” because its access mask limits what it can do.</dd>
      <dt id="term-access-right"><dfn>Access right</dfn></dt>
      <dd>One named permission inside an access mask, such as querying process information or reading memory.</dd>
      <dt id="term-access-token"><dfn>Access token</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The Windows object that describes a process or thread’s security identity, groups, privileges, and integrity level. Windows compares the caller’s token with the target object’s security rules before granting a handle.</dd>
      <dt id="term-address"><dfn>Address</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A number naming a byte location in an address space. An address is not automatically valid, readable, writable, or the start of the value you expect.</dd>
      <dt id="term-address-space"><dfn>Address space</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The set of virtual addresses a process can use. Two processes can use the same numeric virtual address while mapping it to different physical memory.</dd>
      <dt id="term-alignment"><dfn>Alignment</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A requirement or preference that data begin at an address divisible by a particular power of two. Compilers insert <a href="#term-padding">padding</a> so fields satisfy their alignment.</dd>
      <dt id="term-algorithm"><dfn>Algorithm</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A finite, repeatable method for turning input into output. The code is one implementation; the underlying steps are the algorithm.</dd>
      <dt id="term-anti-aliasing"><dfn>Anti-aliasing</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">MSAA / FXAA / TAA</span></dt>
      <dd>Hiding the stair-steps on the edge of a diagonal shape. MSAA tests coverage at several points inside each pixel, FXAA blurs high-contrast edges in the finished picture, and TAA shifts the camera a little every frame and blends the results over time. They cost memory, a full-screen pass, and a history buffer respectively.</dd>
      <dt id="term-anti-cheat"><dfn>Anti-cheat</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Controls that protect game rules against unauthorized advantages, including server validation, client protection, investigation, and enforcement.</dd>
      <dt id="term-anti-debugging"><dfn>Anti-debugging</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Behavior that detects or reacts to debugger-related conditions. Defensive analysis names the observable artifact and tests it; it does not assume every delay, exception, or unusual branch proves a debugger check.</dd>
      <dt id="term-anti-rollback"><dfn>Anti-rollback</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A check that refuses genuinely signed but older software by comparing each image's security version with a minimum kept in fuses. It stops anyone reinstalling a version with a known security hole.</dd>
      <dt id="term-api"><dfn>API</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Application Programming Interface</span></dt>
      <dd>A documented way for one piece of software to request work from another. A function name, its parameters, return value, and error rules form part of an API contract.</dd>
      <dt id="term-argument"><dfn>Argument</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A value supplied to a function call. The calling convention determines where machine code places arguments; the function signature explains what those values mean.</dd>
      <dt id="term-array"><dfn>Array</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A fixed-size sequence of same-type elements stored contiguously. Given the base, index, and element size, an element address is <code>base + index × size</code>.</dd>
      <dt id="term-ascii"><dfn>ASCII</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The standard table that gives English letters, digits, and common symbols the numbers 0 to 127; for example <code>0x41</code> is <code>A</code>. Bytes from <code>0x20</code> (a space) to <code>0x7E</code> are printable.</dd>
      <dt id="term-aslr"><dfn>ASLR</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Address Space Layout Randomization</span></dt>
      <dd>An operating-system defense that varies where images and other regions are mapped. A module-relative location can stay stable while its absolute virtual address changes between launches.</dd>
      <dt id="term-assessment"><dfn>Assessment</dfn></dt>
      <dd>An interpretation made from one or more signals. Keep the measured signal separate from the assessment so a later test can challenge the interpretation without rewriting the observation.</dd>
      <dt id="term-assembly"><dfn>Assembly language</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A human-readable notation for machine instructions. It exposes registers, memory operands, branches, and calls more directly than a high-level language, but each line still needs architectural and calling-convention context.</dd>
      <dt id="term-asset"><dfn>Asset</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A reusable game resource such as an image, model, sound, or character definition. Several running instances can share an asset while keeping different identities and changing state. See <a href="../pages/1/03/#shared-assets-create-separate-instances">Game Fundamentals</a>.</dd>
      <dt id="term-attack-surface"><dfn>Attack surface</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The set of inputs, interfaces, privileges, and trust transitions through which a system can be influenced. Reducing unnecessary parsers, handles, loaders, and exposed commands reduces the surface.</dd>
      <dt id="term-authenticode"><dfn>Authenticode</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Microsoft’s format and verification system for signing Windows files. A valid signature links the exact signed bytes to a certificate chain; it does not prove the program is harmless or bug-free.</dd>
      <dt id="term-authenticated-encryption"><dfn>Authenticated encryption</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Encryption that also detects unauthorized modification, usually through an AEAD construction. Confidentiality hides plaintext; authentication detects tampering. Both properties matter and are different.</dd>
      <dt id="term-authoritative-state"><dfn>Authoritative state</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The one copy of a value whose contents decide what happens next, such as the simulation's entity object or, in a multiplayer game, the server's record. Checks that protect a value must run against this copy, not a cached or displayed one.</dd>
      <dt id="term-authority-boundary"><dfn>Authority boundary</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The separation between a request and the party permitted to decide its result.</dd>
    </dl>
  </section>

  <section class="glossary-group" aria-labelledby="glossary-b">
    <div class="glossary-group__letter"><h2 id="glossary-b">B</h2><a href="#glossary-top">Top</a></div>
    <dl class="glossary-list">
      <dt id="term-bare-metal"><dfn>Bare-metal programming</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Programming that runs without an operating system providing application services. The image needs a suitable startup arrangement, memory layout, and hardware interfaces; Rust's <code>no_std</code> alone does not supply them.</dd>
      <dt id="term-base-address"><dfn>Base address</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The starting virtual address of a mapped image or region. A live image address is commonly <code>module base + RVA</code>.</dd>
      <dt id="term-base-rate"><dfn>Base rate</dfn></dt>
      <dd>How common a condition is in the population being observed. Rare cheating can make false flags outnumber true flags even with a small false-positive rate.</dd>
      <dt id="term-batch-processing"><dfn>Batch processing</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Processing a collected group of data together, such as recalculating a leaderboard from finished-match results. Stream processing instead handles an ongoing sequence of events as they arrive.</dd>
      <dt id="term-behavior-tree"><dfn>Behavior tree</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A tree of conditions and actions that an NPC evaluates from the root every tick. A selector node tries its children until one succeeds; a sequence node runs its children until one fails.</dd>
      <dt id="term-bfs"><dfn>BFS</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Breadth-first search</span></dt>
      <dd>A graph search that visits all nodes one edge away, then two edges away, and so on. On an unweighted graph it finds a path with the fewest edges.</dd>
      <dt id="term-binary"><dfn>Binary</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Either base-two notation or a compiled file made of bytes. Context decides which meaning is intended.</dd>
      <dt id="term-bit"><dfn>Bit</dfn></dt>
      <dd>One binary digit, <code>0</code> or <code>1</code>. Flags often pack several yes/no facts into the bits of one integer.</dd>
      <dt id="term-bootloader"><dfn>Bootloader</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Software that selects, checks, or loads another program to run next. It can support updates or recovery; the application's runtime startup still has its own initialization responsibilities.</dd>
      <dt id="term-boot-rom"><dfn>Boot ROM</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The first code a chip runs at power-on, written into the chip when it is made and unchangeable afterwards. In secure boot it checks the first stage that can be updated.</dd>
      <dt id="term-border"><dfn>Border</dfn></dt>
      <dd>In Lua, a key whose value is present while the next key's value is missing. The length operator <code>#</code> may return any border, so a table with a hole in its sequence has no single length.</dd>
      <dt id="term-boundary-scan"><dfn>Boundary scan</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A test method in which a cell between each chip pin and the chip's logic can capture the pin's level or drive a chosen level. The cells form a shift register, so every connection on a board can be tested through one serial chain.</dd>
      <dt id="term-bounding-volume"><dfn>Bounding volume</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A simple shape, such as a sphere or a box, that stands in for an object's real shape in fast tests: contact, picking, and deciding whether to draw it. It is a rough fit on purpose, so touching the shape is not always touching the model.</dd>
      <dt id="term-branch"><dfn>Branch</dfn></dt>
      <dd>An instruction that may change which instruction runs next. Conditional branches implement decisions; unconditional jumps always transfer control.</dd>
      <dt id="term-breakpoint"><dfn>Breakpoint</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A debugger stop condition attached to an instruction, memory access, or event. A breakpoint gives you one observation point; it does not by itself explain why execution arrived there.</dd>
      <dt id="term-bsp"><dfn>BSP</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Binary Space Partitioning</span></dt>
      <dd>A map format used by Source games. Its sections store compiled world geometry and related level data. It is a level description; it is not the archive that groups many separate game assets.</dd>
      <dt id="term-buffer"><dfn>Buffer</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A memory area reserved to hold bytes temporarily. Correct code tracks both capacity and current length and never trusts an external length before checking it.</dd>
      <dt id="term-bug-check"><dfn>Bug check</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Blue screen, stop error</span></dt>
      <dd>Windows deliberately halting the whole machine after a kernel-mode failure it cannot safely recover from, showing a stop code and writing a crash dump.</dd>
      <dt id="term-build-fingerprint"><dfn>Build fingerprint</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A set of evidence used to identify one exact program build—such as file size, timestamp, version fields, section layout, and cryptographic hash. Multiple signals are stronger than a filename alone.</dd>
      <dt id="term-bypass"><dfn>Bypass</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A way of reaching an outcome without satisfying the control that was meant to guard it. Rigorous analysis states the intended invariant, the observable check, and the unguarded path; defensive work then repairs the invariant rather than merely adding another fragile check.</dd>
      <dt id="term-byte"><dfn>Byte</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Eight bits and the smallest addressable unit on the systems in this book. Types give groups of bytes a size and meaning.</dd>
      <dt id="term-bytecode"><dfn>Bytecode</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Instructions for a software virtual machine rather than the physical CPU. Lua source may be compiled into Lua VM bytecode before the VM executes it.</dd>
    </dl>
  </section>

  <section class="glossary-group" aria-labelledby="glossary-c">
    <div class="glossary-group__letter"><h2 id="glossary-c">C</h2><a href="#glossary-top">Top</a></div>
    <dl class="glossary-list">
      <dt id="term-cache"><dfn>Cache</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A faster storage layer that keeps copies of recently or predictably useful data. CPU caches are not extra variables visible in source; they are part of how memory accesses are served.</dd>
      <dt id="term-call-frame"><dfn>Call frame</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">stack frame</span></dt>
      <dd>The part of a thread’s stack used by one active function call, commonly holding a return address, saved registers, local values, and spilled arguments.</dd>
      <dt id="term-call-stack"><dfn>Call stack</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The ordered chain of active function calls on one thread. Reading it answers “who called whom?” only when unwind information and stack state are trustworthy.</dd>
      <dt id="term-callback"><dfn>Callback</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A function handed to other code so that code can call it later, at a moment it chooses. You register a callback instead of calling it yourself. Event loops, debuggers, Lua hosts, and game engines all run code this way.</dd>
      <dt id="term-calling-convention"><dfn>Calling convention</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The ABI rules for a function call: where arguments and results go, which registers a callee must preserve, who adjusts the stack, and how the stack is aligned.</dd>
      <dt id="term-camera-space"><dfn>Camera space</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">view space</span></dt>
      <dd>Coordinates expressed relative to the camera. The view transform moves the world so the camera becomes the origin with a chosen forward direction.</dd>
      <dt id="term-canonical-state"><dfn>Canonical state</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The state a game actually consumes to decide an effect. A menu copy, render cache, or old snapshot can resemble canonical state without owning the decision.</dd>
      <dt id="term-chain-of-trust"><dfn>Chain of trust</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The sequence of secure-boot stages, each trusted only because the stage before it checked its signature. It starts at a root of trust that nothing checks, because nothing can change it.</dd>
      <dt id="term-change-detection"><dfn>Change detection</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Letting a system ask only for the components written since it last ran. The engine stamps each write with a frame counter, and a write counts as a change <em>even when the new value equals the old one</em>, so a tool that rewrites a value every frame makes everything triggered by that change run every frame.</dd>
      <dt id="term-cheat-code"><dfn>Cheat code</dfn></dt>
      <dd>For an old console game, an address and a value: either a byte substituted when the game reads that address, or a value written to RAM once every frame. It works because those games keep their variables at fixed addresses.</dd>
      <dt id="term-checksum"><dfn>Checksum</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A compact value used mainly to detect accidental corruption. Unlike a keyed MAC or digital signature, an ordinary checksum does not prove who produced the data.</dd>
      <dt id="term-circular-array"><dfn>Circular array</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Fixed-capacity storage whose write position returns to the beginning and replaces the oldest slot.</dd>
      <dt id="term-client-area"><dfn>Client area</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The part of a window a program draws into, without the title bar and borders. The window rectangle includes them, so converting between window and screen positions uses the client area's own origin.</dd>
      <dt id="term-client-protection"><dfn>Client protection</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Checks and controls running on a player's machine, with observations limited by permissions and trust in that environment.</dd>
      <dt id="term-clip-space"><dfn>Clip space</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The homogeneous coordinate space produced by a projection matrix. Clipping happens here before dividing <code>x</code>, <code>y</code>, and <code>z</code> by <code>w</code> to obtain NDC.</dd>
      <dt id="term-clock-cycle"><dfn>Clock cycle</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Cycle</span></dt>
      <dd>One tick of a processor's clock. Emulators count the cycles each instruction takes, so the emulated CPU, graphics, and sound stay in step as they did in the original hardware.</dd>
      <dt id="term-closure"><dfn>Closure</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A function value together with the outside values it captures. In Lua, captured locals live through <a href="#term-upvalue">upvalues</a>.</dd>
      <dt id="term-code-cave"><dfn>Code cave</dfn></dt>
      <dd>An unused executable byte range large enough to hold added instructions. “Unused” must be proven for the exact build; padding-looking bytes may still be data, alignment, or a branch target.</dd>
      <dt id="term-code-section"><dfn>Code section</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A PE section intended to contain executable instructions, usually named <code>.text</code>. Section names are conventions; protection flags and verified layout carry more weight.</dd>
      <dt id="term-committed-memory"><dfn>Committed memory</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Virtual address space for which the operating system promises backing storage. Committed does not mean the page is currently resident in RAM.</dd>
      <dt id="term-compilation"><dfn>Compilation</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Translating code from one representation to another. Rust commonly compiles source to native machine code before a program runs; Lua compiles source to virtual-machine bytecode when it loads a chunk.</dd>
      <dt id="term-compression"><dfn>Compression</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A reversible transformation that represents data with fewer bytes. It is not encryption: compressed data may look irregular, but no secret key is required to restore it.</dd>
      <dt id="term-compute-shader"><dfn>Compute shader</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A GPU program that is not part of drawing: it runs once for each item in a grid of work and reads and writes buffers. Engines use it for particles, culling, mesh deformation, and post-processing.</dd>
      <dt id="term-concurrency"><dfn>Concurrency</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Multiple tasks making progress during overlapping time. Parallelism means work literally runs at the same instant; concurrent tasks may instead take turns.</dd>
      <dt id="term-console-variable"><dfn>Console variable</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">cvar</span></dt>
      <dd>A named setting an engine exposes through its in-game console, which can be read or changed while the game runs. Toggling one gives a clean experiment: whatever changes in memory at the same moment is connected to that feature.</dd>
      <dt id="term-context-switch"><dfn>Context switch</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Saving one thread's registers and loading another's so a core can run a different thread. Switching to a thread of another process also loads that process's page tables into <code>cr3</code>.</dd>
      <dt id="term-contradiction"><dfn>Contradiction</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Evidence that two claims cannot both satisfy the stated model—for example, a decision says “denied” while the correlated game effect still changes canonical state.</dd>
      <dt id="term-control"><dfn>Control</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Logic intended to preserve an invariant, such as validating a command before applying it. This differs from <a href="#term-control-flow">control flow</a>, which describes instruction order.</dd>
      <dt id="term-ioctl"><dfn>Control code</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">IOCTL</span></dt>
      <dd>A 32-bit number sent with <code>DeviceIoControl</code> that packs a device type, the access the caller's handle must hold, a function number, and a buffer method.</dd>
      <dt id="term-control-flow"><dfn>Control flow</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The order in which instructions execute, shaped by sequential steps, calls, returns, branches, exceptions, and threads.</dd>
      <dt id="term-convar"><dfn>ConVar</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Console variable</span></dt>
      <dd>A named game-engine setting with a current value and flags. Flags can control who may change it, whether the server replicates it, and whether another process may query it.</dd>
      <dt id="term-coordinate-system"><dfn>Coordinate system</dfn></dt>
      <dd>An origin, axes, units, and orientation used to describe positions. Numbers are meaningless until you know which space and convention they belong to.</dd>
      <dt id="term-correlation"><dfn>Correlation</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A tendency for observations to vary together. Shared inputs or defects can make detector errors occur together.</dd>
      <dt id="term-correlation-id"><dfn>Correlation ID</dfn></dt>
      <dd>An identifier attached to events from one logical action so observations from different threads or stages can be joined without assuming timestamps alone prove causality.</dd>
      <dt id="term-coverage"><dfn>Coverage</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The exact bytes, fields, branches, states, or cases examined by a check. A result is only meaningful for what the check actually covered.</dd>
      <dt id="term-coverage-bypass"><dfn>Coverage bypass</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A meaningful change that falls outside what a control measures, allowing the checked subset to remain valid while the larger promised relation becomes false.</dd>
      <dt id="term-cpu"><dfn>CPU</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Central Processing Unit</span></dt>
      <dd>The processor that executes machine instructions. Registers hold immediate working values; caches and memory supply code and data.</dd>
      <dt id="term-cross-validation"><dfn>Cross-validation</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Confirming a field with independent checks that all agree, such as the instructions that access it, how its value changes when the game changes, the object it belongs to, and its range relative to other fields.</dd>
      <dt id="term-crash-dump"><dfn>Crash dump</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A captured subset of process state around a failure, often including threads, registers, stacks, modules, and selected memory. It is evidence from one moment, not a full recording of everything that happened earlier.</dd>
      <dt id="term-culling"><dfn>Culling</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Skipping work for what cannot be seen: objects outside the camera's view volume (frustum culling), triangles facing away (back-face culling), or objects hidden behind others (occlusion culling). Culling happens before drawing; the <a href="#term-depth-buffer">depth buffer</a> decides per fragment afterward.</dd>
    </dl>
  </section>

  <section class="glossary-group" aria-labelledby="glossary-d">
    <div class="glossary-group__letter"><h2 id="glossary-d">D</h2><a href="#glossary-top">Top</a></div>
    <dl class="glossary-list">
      <dt id="term-dacl"><dfn>DACL</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Discretionary Access Control List</span></dt>
      <dd>The Windows rules that allow or deny requested access to a securable object. The object’s DACL, the caller’s token, and the requested access mask participate in the access check.</dd>
      <dt id="term-data-model"><dfn>Data model</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The values, relationships, and constraints chosen to describe a problem. A character model names attributes and owned items; a save or message format describes how selected model data is represented. See <a href="../pages/9/01/#the-data-model-shapes-the-questions-you-can-ask">storage models</a>.</dd>
      <dt id="term-data-structure"><dfn>Data structure</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A layout and set of rules for organizing values so operations such as lookup, insertion, traversal, or deletion have useful costs.</dd>
      <dt id="term-dead-zone"><dfn>Dead zone</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A range around the centre of a stick or trigger that the game treats as zero, so a resting stick that reads 0.06 does not make a character drift. Engines usually rescale the rest of the range so the output starts from 0 instead of jumping.</dd>
      <dt id="term-debouncing"><dfn>Debouncing</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Suppressing repeated triggers until an input has stayed stable or enough time has passed. It turns noisy changes into one intentional event.</dd>
      <dt id="term-debug-build"><dfn>Debug build</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Release build</span></dt>
      <dd>A build made for finding mistakes, with most optimizations left out. Engine code that loops over thousands of entities can run many times slower in it than in a release build, so a frame time means little until you know which kind of build produced it.</dd>
      <dt id="term-debugger"><dfn>Debugger</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A tool that controls and observes a running program: pausing threads, reading registers and memory, stepping instructions, and receiving debug events.</dd>
      <dt id="term-debugger-artifact"><dfn>Debugger artifact</dfn></dt>
      <dd>An observable condition associated with debugging, such as a flag, handle, exception path, timing change, or modified instruction byte. Each artifact has false positives and can disappear across versions, so treat it as evidence rather than proof.</dd>
      <dt id="term-dedicated-server"><dfn>Dedicated server</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A server process that runs the shared simulation without a local player client. A listen server hosts the simulation while its owner also plays through a client.</dd>
      <dt id="term-deferred-command"><dfn>Deferred command</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A request such as “spawn a bullet here” or “despawn brick 7” that a system records instead of doing at once. The engine applies the queue at a safe point, so a spawned entity is first seen by systems that run later, or by every system on the next frame.</dd>
      <dt id="term-dpc"><dfn>Deferred procedure call</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">DPC</span></dt>
      <dd>Driver code queued by an interrupt service routine to run shortly afterward at a lower priority, where it finishes the device work and completes waiting requests.</dd>
      <dt id="term-delta-time"><dfn>Delta time</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The time since the previous frame or step, in seconds. Movement is scaled by it (distance = speed × delta time) so a character's speed does not depend on the frame rate.</dd>
      <dt id="term-depth-buffer"><dfn>Depth buffer</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A per-sample store used to decide which fragment is in front. Its values are produced by projection and are often nonlinear; it is not simply “distance from the camera.”</dd>
      <dt id="term-detection-precision"><dfn>Detection precision</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The fraction of flagged cases that actually have the condition being detected.</dd>
      <dt id="term-detection-recall"><dfn>Detection recall</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The fraction of cases with the condition that the detector successfully flags.</dd>
      <dt id="term-detection-rule"><dfn>Detection rule</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A precise query over observations that identifies evidence of a stated condition. A useful rule names its inputs and possible false results instead of hiding them behind an unexplained score.</dd>
      <dt id="term-detector"><dfn>Detector</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Logic that reports evidence that a condition or invariant failure may be present. A detector can be noisy, incomplete, or independent from the control that prevents the failure.</dd>
      <dt id="term-detour"><dfn>Detour</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A redirection that sends execution into your own code and then back. You overwrite instructions at a chosen point with a jump; a correct detour only ever replaces whole instructions, keeps a copy of the originals, and provides a way back so the interrupted function finishes normally.</dd>
      <dt id="term-device-register"><dfn>Device register</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A small storage location inside a device that software reads to learn the device's state or writes to command it. Unlike RAM, reading or writing a register can have side effects, such as removing data from a queue.</dd>
      <dt id="term-differential-comparison"><dfn>Differential comparison</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Running the same code on two inputs that differ in one known way and comparing the outputs. For an XOR-based value transform the key cancels out, so the comparison exposes the rest of the transform without knowing the key.</dd>
      <dt id="term-digital-signature"><dfn>Digital signature</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A cryptographic value that lets a verifier detect byte changes and check that a holder of a particular private key signed the data. Trust still depends on key identity and certificate policy.</dd>
      <dt id="term-disassembler"><dfn>Disassembler</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A tool that decodes machine-code bytes into assembly instructions. Decoding does not recover original variable names, types, comments, or guaranteed function boundaries.</dd>
      <dt id="term-dll"><dfn>DLL</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Dynamic-Link Library</span></dt>
      <dd>A Windows PE image designed to be mapped into a process and share code or data through exported functions and other interfaces.</dd>
      <dt id="term-dllmain"><dfn>DllMain</dfn></dt>
      <dd>An optional DLL entry routine Windows calls for loader events. It runs under loader constraints, so substantial initialization should occur later under application-controlled synchronization.</dd>
      <dt id="term-dma"><dfn>DMA</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Direct Memory Access</span></dt>
      <dd>A hardware mechanism that lets a device move data without the CPU copying every byte. Physical-memory evidence still requires address translation, consistent snapshots, and structure validation before it has meaning.</dd>
      <dt id="term-dot-product"><dfn>Dot product</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Two vectors' matching parts multiplied and added: <code>a.x × b.x + a.y × b.y</code>. For two unit vectors it equals the cosine of the angle between them.</dd>
      <dt id="term-draining"><dfn>Draining</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A shutdown phase that refuses new work while existing users finish. Hook code and callback state must remain alive until the active count reaches zero.</dd>
      <dt id="term-draw-call"><dfn>Draw call</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A command submitting geometry for rendering with the currently bound pipeline state. A draw call does not carry every fact by itself; textures, shaders, buffers, transforms, and tests may already be bound elsewhere.</dd>
      <dt id="term-driver"><dfn>Driver</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Device driver</span></dt>
      <dd>Software that lets the operating system control or communicate with hardware or a kernel service. Kernel-mode drivers have broad authority and therefore a much larger failure and trust boundary than ordinary process code.</dd>
      <dt id="term-driver-signing"><dfn>Driver signing</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The rule that 64-bit Windows loads kernel-mode drivers only with a valid digital signature; since Windows 10 version 1607, with Secure Boot on, new drivers must be signed through Microsoft's hardware developer program.</dd>
      <dt id="term-driver-stack"><dfn>Driver stack</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The drivers layered on one device: optional filter drivers that watch or adjust requests, the function driver that operates the device, and the bus driver for the bus it is plugged into.</dd>
      <dt id="term-dynamic-recompilation"><dfn>Dynamic recompilation</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Dynarec, JIT</span></dt>
      <dd>Translating guest machine code into host machine code while the program runs, one block at a time, and reusing the stored translation. It is much faster than interpreting, but it needs memory that is written and then executed, and it must discard translations when the guest rewrites its code.</dd>
      <dt id="term-dynamic-typing"><dfn>Dynamic typing</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Values have types, but a variable can refer to values of different types while the program runs. Lua permits assigning a number and later a string to the same variable; an invalid operation on the current value can fail at run time.</dd>
    </dl>
  </section>

  <section class="glossary-group" aria-labelledby="glossary-e">
    <div class="glossary-group__letter"><h2 id="glossary-e">E</h2><a href="#glossary-top">Top</a></div>
    <dl class="glossary-list">
      <dt id="term-easing"><dfn>Easing</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Reshaping the fraction used in an <a href="#term-interpolation">interpolation</a> so a motion starts gently, ends gently, or both, instead of moving at one constant speed.</dd>
      <dt id="term-ecs"><dfn>ECS</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Entity component system</span></dt>
      <dd>A design in which <a href="#term-entity">entities</a> are only identities, components are plain data attached to them, and systems are functions that run over every entity that has a given set of components. Behavior comes from which components an entity has.</dd>
      <dt id="term-effect-boundary"><dfn>Effect boundary</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The shared point where a requested operation becomes canonical game state. Preconditions are strongest when enforced here rather than on a distant UI flag or copied value.</dd>
      <dt id="term-efuse"><dfn>eFuse</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">One-time programmable fuse</span></dt>
      <dd>A bit on a chip that can be changed once, from 0 to 1, and never back. Chips keep settings that must not be undone in fuses, such as a locked debug port, a key hash, or an anti-rollback counter.</dd>
      <dt id="term-emulator"><dfn>Emulator</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A program that imitates another computer's hardware closely enough that the other computer's software runs on it unchanged. The imitated machine and its software are the guest; the computer running the emulator is the host.</dd>
      <dt id="term-encoding"><dfn>Encoding</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A conventional representation of information, such as UTF-8 for text or Base64 for bytes. Encoding changes form, not secrecy.</dd>
      <dt id="term-encoded-value"><dfn>Encoded value</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The stored result of a reversible representation transform. Its bytes must be interpreted through the exact operation width, key or parameter, and inverse order used by the program.</dd>
      <dt id="term-endianness"><dfn>Endianness</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The byte order used to store a multi-byte number. Little-endian stores the least significant byte first; network byte order is conventionally big-endian.</dd>
      <dt id="term-entry-point"><dfn>Entry point</dfn></dt>
      <dd>The image-relative address where the loader begins executing a PE image after mapping and initialization. It is not necessarily the source-language <code>main</code> function.</dd>
      <dt id="term-encryption"><dfn>Encryption</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A key-controlled reversible transformation that hides plaintext. Encryption alone may not detect modification; authenticated encryption combines confidentiality with integrity checking.</dd>
      <dt id="term-entity"><dfn>Entity</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A distinct thing in game state, such as a player, projectile, or unit. Engines may represent entities as objects, IDs into tables, or bundles of components.</dd>
      <dt id="term-etw"><dfn>ETW</dfn> <span class="glossary-alias">Event Tracing for Windows</span></dt>
      <dd>A Windows system for structured, timestamped events from the kernel and applications. ETW shows emitted events; absence of an event is not proof that an action never occurred.</dd>
      <dt id="term-evasion"><dfn>Evasion</dfn></dt>
      <dd>Changing observable behavior so a detection or validation rule does not fire. A defensive analysis models the rule, its blind spots, and stronger invariants without assuming one bypass generalizes to other products or versions.</dd>
      <dt id="term-event"><dfn>Event</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A record that something happened — a key press, an arriving network message, an expired timer, a resized window — delivered to code that responds to it.</dd>
      <dt id="term-event-driven-programming"><dfn>Event-driven programming</dfn></dt>
      <dd>A program structure built around waiting for events and running a handler for each one, instead of running from top to bottom. Window procedures, debuggers, and servers work this way; a game combines it with a loop that runs every frame.</dd>
